items.title: 1. The electrical heart: foundations for recognising arrhythmias
items.los: IT_PO 1.7; SS_IC 1.37; AT_RT 1.1; IT_RT 1.1 (tachycardia/bradycardia); SS_CS 1.4 (cardiac rhythm)
items.body:
## Why it matters

- An arrhythmia is dangerous not because the monitor displays an unfamiliar rhythm but because **electrical activation no longer produces adequate mechanical circulation**, or because the rhythm can deteriorate suddenly into cardiac arrest.
- The first skill is therefore to connect the electrical diagnosis to the patient's cardiac output, coronary perfusion and systemic perfusion.
- A heart rate of 40/min may be entirely normal in a fit athlete, whereas 50/min with severe aortic stenosis and hypotension may be life-threatening.
- Similarly, sinus tachycardia of 140/min from haemorrhage is an adaptive response: ablating the rate without treating bleeding makes the problem worse.

The four useful questions are: (1) Is there a pulse? (2) Is the rhythm causing instability? (3) Is the QRS narrow or broad, regular or irregular? (4) What reversible cause is driving it? These questions remain useful whether the patient is awake, anaesthetised, ventilated or in intensive care.

## Normal conduction explains the ECG

- The sinus node near the superior vena cava–right atrial junction initiates most normal rhythms.
- Depolarisation spreads through atrial tissue to the AV node, whose slow conduction gives the ventricles time to fill; conduction then accelerates through the His bundle, bundle branches and Purkinje network to synchronise ventricular contraction.
- Autonomic inputs alter sinus rate and AV-node refractoriness; ischaemia, electrolyte disturbances, drugs and structural disease change the capacity to generate or conduct impulses.

| ECG feature | What it represents | Why it is clinically useful |
|---|---|---|
| P wave | Atrial depolarisation | Presence, morphology and relation to QRS distinguish sinus, atrial and junctional mechanisms. |
| PR interval (normally 120–200 ms) | Atrial-to-ventricular conduction | A prolonged PR suggests first-degree AV block; progressive or intermittent failure reveals higher block. |
| QRS (<120 ms usually narrow) | Ventricular depolarisation | Broad QRS may indicate ventricular origin, bundle branch block, pacing, hyperkalaemia or pre-excitation. |
| QT/QTc | Ventricular depolarisation plus repolarisation | A prolonged QT predisposes to torsades; measure carefully in AF, BBB or paced QRS. |
| ST–T | Repolarisation/ischaemia patterns | New ischaemia may cause or complicate arrhythmia, but baseline conduction abnormalities confound interpretation. |

**Why rate and rhythm matter to circulation:**

- Tachycardia shortens diastole more than systole, reducing ventricular filling and predominantly diastolic left-coronary perfusion; it also raises myocardial oxygen demand.
- Bradycardia decreases cardiac output if stroke volume cannot rise sufficiently (CO = HR × SV).
- Loss of atrial contraction in AF is particularly important in stiff ventricles, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, severe aortic stenosis and mitral stenosis.
- Ventricular dyssynchrony from a broad QRS or RV-only pacing may reduce mechanical efficiency even when the displayed pulse rate is adequate.

## A rhythm-recognition method that works under pressure

Read an adequate ECG systematically rather than guessing from the display:

- 1. Rate and regularity: regular versus irregularly irregular; check whether the monitor counted artefact, pacing spikes or large T waves.
- 2. P waves: present? consistent morphology? is there one P for each QRS, or AV dissociation?
- 3. PR relationship: constant, progressively lengthening, intermittently non-conducted, or no relationship.
- 4. QRS width and morphology: narrow or wide; compare previous ECG for bundle-branch block or paced rhythm.
- 5. QT, ST–T and context: ischaemia, potassium, magnesium, medications, temperature and acid–base status.
- 6. Mechanical correlation: palpate pulse or observe arterial line/plethysmography. Electrical activity without a pulse is cardiac arrest, not a stable dysrhythmia.

- A 12-lead ECG provides diagnostic information; intraoperative leads II and V5 may aid rhythm and ischaemia monitoring but cannot replace it for difficult diagnoses.
- Telemetry can exaggerate apparent rates with electrocautery, neuromuscular stimulation, shivering, movement and poor electrode contact.
- New arrhythmias also warrant review of previous tracings and medication history: baseline AF with a ventricular response of 85/min is not the same problem as sudden AF at 170/min during induction.

## Mechanisms: automaticity, triggered activity and re-entry

- **Increased automaticity** generates impulses outside the sinus node (catecholamines, hypoxaemia, ischaemia, electrolyte shifts).
- **Triggered activity** involves afterdepolarisations: early afterdepolarisations in prolonged repolarisation predispose to torsades; delayed afterdepolarisations may occur with digoxin toxicity or calcium overload.
- **Re-entry** requires a circuit with differing conduction and refractory characteristics, producing AVNRT, AVRT and many monomorphic VTs.
- These mechanisms explain why adenosine can interrupt AV-node-dependent SVT but does not treat atrial fibrillation or a scar-based ventricular tachycardia reliably.

**Exam focus.** Describe the ECG phenotype first, assess the circulation second, and then choose electrical or pharmacological treatment. ANZCA examiners have specifically highlighted misinterpretation of Mobitz II as complete block and preparation for defibrillation instead of pacing; the treatments are not interchangeable.

items.title: 2. An arrhythmia during anaesthesia: assess, stabilise, find the cause
items.los: AT_RT 1.1; IT_RT 1.1; IT_RT 1.2 (haemodynamically compromising arrhythmias); IT_PO 1.7
items.body:
## Why it matters

- Anaesthesia removes compensatory sympathetic responses, changes preload and afterload, and can conceal symptoms such as palpitations or chest pain.
- Arrhythmia may therefore first present as falling blood pressure, ETCO₂ or oxygen saturation.
- But tachycardia and bradycardia are often **signs of another emergency** rather than independent diseases.
- An appropriate response treats reversible physiology while preparing definitive rhythm treatment where necessary.

## Immediate assessment: decide whether the patient is stable

- When the monitor suddenly shows an abnormal rhythm, **announce the problem, call for help early, assess airway/oxygenation/ventilation, check pulse and arterial pressure, and obtain rhythm confirmation**.
- If pulseless, activate the ANZCOR arrest algorithm immediately.
- Otherwise evaluate clinical instability: hypotension/shock, altered consciousness, acute chest pain/ischaemia, pulmonary oedema, or evidence of severe tissue hypoperfusion.
- The heart rate alone is insufficient: a well-perfused patient with AF at 125/min need not be cardioverted, whereas VT at 120/min with shock may require immediate cardioversion.

- In the anaesthetised patient, look for BP trend, pulse pressure, arterial waveform, plethysmography, falling ETCO₂ (possible abrupt drop in cardiac output), central/peripheral perfusion and new ST change.
- Check equipment: ECG cables, diathermy, pulse-ox artefact, cuff error and pacing spikes.
- **Synchronised cardioversion treats an unstable perfusing tachyarrhythmia; unsynchronised defibrillation treats VF/pulseless VT (and unstable polymorphic VT when synchronisation cannot be achieved).**

## Reversible causes: work from the most likely to the most dangerous

| Clinical pattern | High-yield causes | What to correct first |
|---|---|---|
| Sinus tachycardia | Light anaesthesia/pain, hypovolaemia or haemorrhage, hypercapnia, hypoxaemia, fever/sepsis, anaphylaxis, PE | Verify perfusion and ventilation; treat precipitant, not rate in isolation. |
| New AF/SVT | Adrenergic stimulation, atrial stretch, acute ischaemia, K/Mg abnormalities, sepsis, catecholamines | Correct physiology; decide stability and rhythm-specific therapy. |
| Regular broad-complex tachycardia | VT until proven otherwise, SVT with aberrancy, ventricular pacing, hyperkalaemia | Assume VT if uncertain and seek cardiology/critical care input. |
| Bradycardia | Vagal reflex (laryngoscopy, ocular traction, pneumoperitoneum), hypoxaemia, neuraxial block, opioids, propofol, beta-blockers, CCBs | Stop stimulus, oxygenate, assess perfusion; treat with atropine/adrenaline/pacing as indicated. |
| AV block/ventricular escape | Ischaemia (especially inferior MI), degenerative conduction disease, drug effect, hyperkalaemia, cardiac surgery | Prepare pacing and address cause; avoid delaying rescue in high-grade block. |

- Also consider the **Hs and Ts** when physiology is severely abnormal: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hydrogen ion/acidosis, hypo-/hyperkalaemia and metabolic causes, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis (coronary/pulmonary).
- If the patient is haemorrhaging, correct volume/blood loss rather than reflexively giving esmolol for compensatory tachycardia.
- If bradycardia develops during insufflation, ask the surgeon to stop insufflation immediately and reassess the circulation.

## Perioperative management sequence

- **Preoperative:** recognise baseline AF, conduction disease, unexplained syncope, medication-induced bradycardia and pre-excitation; assess the clinical risk of proceeding. Correct important K/Mg abnormalities, treat active ischaemia/HF, and plan pacing or defibrillation support for high-risk patients.

**Intraoperative:**

- Minimise triggers through adequate anaesthesia, oxygenation, normocapnia, temperature and volume management.
- When an arrhythmia appears, verify it, determine whether it is the cause of instability, correct precipitating factors and treat the rhythm promptly when needed.
- Record a 12-lead ECG when possible without delaying urgent intervention.
- Select antiarrhythmics according to LV function and the actual rhythm rather than treating all tachycardias with amiodarone.

**Postoperative:**

- Distinguish a transient, reversible event from a persistent rhythm disorder; obtain ECG, electrolytes, troponin/echo if clinically indicated, consider monitored care, review anticoagulation/stroke prevention in AF and arrange appropriate device/cardiology follow-up.
- If cardioversion or antiarrhythmic drugs were required, document the rhythm, treatment, response and subsequent plan.

![Electrical emergency decision sequence](set12-fig1.png)

## Electrical therapy: the essential decision

- For haemodynamic compromise attributable to a perfusing tachyarrhythmia, prepare **synchronised cardioversion**, providing sedation/anaesthesia if feasible but not at the cost of delaying rescue.
- Confirm synchronisation markers on R waves before every shock and reassess after each attempt.
- The 2025 AHA ALS guideline considers an initial biphasic **200 J** reasonable for AF or flutter; local device-specific and ANZCOR algorithms should govern actual practice.
- For unstable monomorphic VT, a synchronised initial 100 J is commonly recommended by AHA, escalating as required.
- If synchronisation fails in a critically unstable VT, do not delay an unsynchronised shock.
- For polymorphic VT/VF or pulseless VT, deliver unsynchronised defibrillation and ALS.

- For **VF/pulseless VT**, ANZCOR's 2025 electrical therapy guideline recommends **200 J default biphasic** (or device-supported alternative), with escalation if unsuccessful and rapid resumption of compressions.
- Pad positions may be anterior–lateral or anterior–posterior; keep pads **ideally ≥8 cm from an implanted generator**, but do not delay a life-saving shock.
- A controlled airway, oxygen, appropriately delivered shocks and prevention of long CPR pauses matter more than perfect pad geometry.

items.title: 3. Atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter and supraventricular tachycardias
items.body:
## Why they matter

- Atrial tachyarrhythmias increase myocardial oxygen consumption, shorten filling time and reduce cardiac output.
- In AF, disorganised atrial activation also causes **loss of the effective atrial contribution to ventricular filling**.
- This is especially consequential in a stiff LV, mitral stenosis, severe AS or RV failure.
- Thrombus formation in the left atrial appendage creates a second problem: cardioverting a patient may restore haemodynamics but does not erase stroke risk.

- Atrial flutter is an organised macro-reentrant circuit, commonly with an atrial rate around 250–350/min; **2:1 conduction can present as a regular narrow-complex rate around 150/min**.
- AF is typically irregularly irregular without discrete P waves.
- AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT are often abrupt-onset, regular narrow-complex tachycardias; sinus tachycardia rises and falls according to physiological stimuli.

## Preoperative implications: diagnose, grade and protect

- Establish whether the rhythm is new or chronic, symptomatic or asymptomatic, rate-controlled or uncontrolled.
- Ask about exercise tolerance, heart failure, valvular disease, prior stroke/TIA, bleeding history, anticoagulation adherence, prior cardioversion/ablation and precipitants (thyroid disease, OSA, sepsis, alcohol).
- Examine heart rate, BP, signs of HF and murmurs.
- Review 12-lead ECG, echo where structural disease is suspected or status has changed, electrolytes/creatinine/thyroid testing as indicated.
- Stable rate-controlled AF alone does not automatically require postponement of non-cardiac surgery; **new AF with uncontrolled ventricular response, acute decompensation, unstable symptoms or suspected ACS does**.

- Stroke prevention is a separate decision from immediate rate control.
- The 2024 ESC guideline uses **CHA₂DS₂-VA** (without sex category) for stroke-risk assessment; other jurisdictions continue to use CHA₂DS₂-VASc.
- Oral anticoagulation is recommended in higher-risk patients, usually with a DOAC unless there is a **mechanical valve or moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis**, in which case VKA is indicated.
- Antiplatelets do not replace anticoagulation for AF stroke prevention.
- Bleeding risk scores help correct modifiable hazards rather than justify withholding treatment automatically.

- For elective cardioversion, **duration matters**.
- Under 2024 ESC guidance, AF lasting **>24 h or of uncertain onset** generally requires at least **3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or TOE exclusion of atrial thrombus** before elective cardioversion.
- Continue anticoagulation for at least **4 weeks afterward** in most patients; long-term treatment depends on thromboembolic risk, not whether sinus rhythm appears to have returned.
- This is a stricter threshold than the older 48-hour shortcut; emergency cardioversion for haemodynamic collapse is not delayed to complete anticoagulation.

## Intraoperative management of AF or flutter

- First ask **is rapid AF the cause of shock or a response to another problem?** Hypovolaemia, sepsis, anaphylaxis, ischaemia and PE may provoke rapid AF; correcting those causes can be more important than an antiarrhythmic.
- However, if haemodynamic instability is attributable to AF/flutter, **synchronised cardioversion is first-line**, with resuscitation and later stroke-prevention planning.

For stable patients, choose rate or rhythm control based on duration, symptoms, physiological tolerance and LV function:

| Option | Mechanism/role | Important cautions |
|---|---|---|
| Beta-blocker (e.g. metoprolol/esmolol) | Slows AV conduction and sympathetic drive; useful for rapid AF with stable pressure. | May worsen shock, severe bradycardia, AV block or acute decompensated HF; titrate rather than bolus indiscriminately. |
| Diltiazem/verapamil | AV-node slowing for AF/flutter with preserved LV systolic function. | Avoid in significant HFrEF, hypotension, high-grade block and pre-excited AF. |
| Digoxin | Slows AV conduction through vagal effects; sometimes useful in HF or when BP limits alternatives. | Slow onset, less effective in high catecholamine states; adjust for renal function, potassium and drug interactions. |
| Amiodarone | Rhythm/rate control in selected critically ill or structurally abnormal hearts. | Can cause hypotension, bradycardia, QT prolongation, organ toxicity; conversion may occur and therefore carries thromboembolic implications. |
| Electrical cardioversion | Rapid restoration of coordinated rhythm when unstable or pharmacological strategy inappropriate. | Requires synchronisation, sedation if possible and post-cardioversion anticoagulation planning. |

- An initial target of **resting HR <100–110/min** is often a reasonable lenient-control strategy in a stable patient; it is not appropriate if the patient remains ischaemic, hypotensive or has severe mitral stenosis.
- **Rate control does not equal adequate ventricular filling:** in marked diastolic dysfunction, restoring sinus rhythm may have a larger haemodynamic effect than reducing the rate alone.

## Regular narrow-complex SVT: AVNRT and AVRT

- If unstable, synchronised cardioversion.
- If stable, use vagal manoeuvres (modified Valsalva if awake and cooperative), then **adenosine 6 mg IV rapid bolus with a brisk saline flush**, followed if required by **12 mg**, according to local ANZCOR protocol.
- Record ECG during administration when possible; transient AV block can expose atrial flutter and is diagnostic as well as therapeutic.
- Warn of flushing, chest discomfort, breathlessness and short-lived asystole.
- Use particular caution in severe reactive airways disease and heart transplantation; in a transplanted heart, much smaller initial doses may produce profound effects.

- **Avoid AV-nodal blockers in irregular broad-complex tachycardia with possible pre-excited AF.** In AF with WPW, rapid accessory-pathway conduction can degenerate into VF.
- Adenosine, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin and beta-blockers are unsafe in that scenario; urgent electrical cardioversion is usually the safest solution, with electrophysiology input when stable.
- Procainamide or ibutilide can be options in expert-managed stable cases where available, after assessment of contraindications.

## Postoperative/ICU implications

- New postoperative AF may reveal volume shifts, pain, inflammation, infection, hypoxaemia, PE, atrial stretch or myocardial injury.
- Treat causes and determine whether it persists or recurs.
- Monitor haemodynamics, electrolytes and bleeding.
- New AF after non-cardiac surgery is **not necessarily benign or permanently transient:** reassess stroke risk and consider long-term anticoagulation at follow-up, balancing recent surgery/haemostasis.
- In cardiac surgery, beta-blockers and selected prophylactic antiarrhythmics reduce POAF, while short-term treatment decisions must still reflect LV function and stroke risk.
- For perioperative anaesthesia, do not reflexively restart anticoagulation through an indwelling neuraxial catheter without checking the agent-specific interval.

**BJA Education reading:**

- Haysley et al., Perioperative atrial fibrillation (2025), is a particularly useful integration of AF mechanisms, perioperative triggers, risk and prevention.
- Major contemporary trials discussed later include **AFFIRM, RACE II and EAST-AFNET 4:** early rhythm-control evidence should not be interpreted as meaning every episode of rapid postoperative AF requires pharmacological conversion.

items.title: 4. Ventricular tachyarrhythmias, torsades and electrical emergencies
items.body:
## Why they matter

- Ventricular tachyarrhythmias can cause sudden loss of coordinated ventricular ejection.
- **Monomorphic VT** commonly reflects a stable re-entry circuit around scarred myocardium; **polymorphic VT** has changing QRS morphology and may reflect acute ischaemia, prolonged repolarisation or other electrical instability.
- **VF** produces chaotic activation with no effective cardiac output.
- A broad-complex tachycardia in a patient with structural heart disease is VT until convincingly proven otherwise.

- The underlying mechanism dictates treatment.
- Scar-based monomorphic VT may respond to cardioversion or a ventricular antiarrhythmic.
- **Torsades de pointes** is a polymorphic VT associated with a prolonged QT and often a pause-dependent initiation; its treatment focuses on magnesium, correcting QT triggers and sometimes increasing heart rate.
- Giving amiodarone indiscriminately for torsades can further prolong QT and worsen the problem.

## Recognition and immediate management

- If the patient is pulseless with VT or VF, **activate ALS, perform high-quality CPR and deliver unsynchronised defibrillation promptly**.
- If conscious/perfusing but unstable with **monomorphic VT**, attempt synchronised cardioversion; if polymorphic VT cannot be reliably synchronised or causes collapse, deliver unsynchronised high-energy shocks.
- For stable regular broad-complex tachycardia, obtain ECG, IV access, electrolytes, senior help and treat as VT.
- Do not administer verapamil to an undifferentiated wide-complex rhythm.

**Amiodarone:**

- ANZCOR peri-arrest guidance commonly uses **300 mg IV over 20–60 minutes** for stable regular broad-complex VT, followed by 900 mg over 24 h; for refractory unstable tachycardia after attempted cardioversion, the ANZCOR peri-arrest protocol uses 300 mg over 10–20 minutes before further cardioversion.
- These are not the same as the ALS arrest bolus regimen (**300 mg IV/IO after the third shock** for shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT, then 150 mg later according to the current arrest algorithm).
- Monitor for hypotension and bradycardia.
- Lignocaine can be considered for ventricular arrhythmias particularly in ischaemia or as an alternative in refractory VF/pVT, with locally recommended dosing and toxicity monitoring.

| Rhythm | Immediate treatment | Crucial distinction |
|---|---|---|
| Stable monomorphic VT | Rhythm confirmation, reversible causes, IV antiarrhythmic/experienced review, prepare cardioversion. | Never assume SVT just because BP is currently preserved. |
| Unstable monomorphic VT with pulse | Synchronised cardioversion; sedation if feasible. | Shock promptly if poor perfusion is attributable to VT. |
| VF or pulseless VT | CPR + unsynchronised defibrillation + ALS drugs/reversible causes. | Do not synchronise. |
| Polymorphic VT with collapse | Unsynchronised shock, treat trigger; check QT, ischaemia. | Synchronisation may not be possible. |
| Torsades with prolonged QT | Magnesium + remove offending drugs/correct K; shock if sustained/unstable. | Avoid QT-prolonging drugs including amiodarone. |

## Torsades de pointes: why magnesium and pacing work

- A prolonged repolarisation interval permits early afterdepolarisations, especially after a pause; the premature beat can initiate polymorphic VT.
- Risk factors include congenital long-QT syndromes, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia, female sex, severe illness and QT-prolonging drugs (some antiemetics, macrolides, antipsychotics, methadone and class III antiarrhythmics).
- A QTc of **≥500 ms** is an important warning threshold but is not diagnostic by itself; correct measurement and QRS duration matter.

- ANZCOR suggests **magnesium sulfate 5 mmol IV over approximately 10 min**, repeat once if needed, with further infusion (e.g. 20 mmol over 4 h) according to response and local protocol.
- Other adult resuscitation pathways use **2 g** (approximately 8 mmol) IV; do not combine the two into a single invented dose.
- Correct K towards the normal/high-normal range, stop precipitating drugs, treat ischaemia and monitor continuously.
- For **recurrent pause-dependent acquired torsades**, temporary overdrive pacing or isoprenaline may reduce episodes by preventing long pauses; **avoid isoprenaline in congenital long-QT syndrome**, where adrenergic stimulation can be hazardous.
- Unstable sustained torsades requires an electrical shock irrespective of magnesium preparation.

## Cause-directed perioperative care

- When VT occurs under GA, rapidly evaluate myocardial ischaemia, oxygenation, potassium/magnesium, acidosis, hypothermia, drug toxicity, catheter or guidewire irritation, and surgical stimulation.
- If structural heart disease, recent MI, recurrent sustained VT or an ICD is present, arrange electrophysiology/cardiology review and consider postoperative monitored care.
- Electrical storm (≥3 sustained VT/VF episodes or appropriate ICD therapies within 24 h, with varying consensus definitions) requires a coordinated approach: correct triggers, analgesia/sedation and sympathetic suppression, beta-blockade when appropriate, amiodarone or alternative, urgent ablation or mechanical support in refractory cases.
- ICD shocks alone do not correct the underlying problem.

**Exam emphasis.** Differentiate **synchronised cardioversion, unsynchronised defibrillation and temporary pacing** by indication. Be able to manage both a perfusing broad-complex tachycardia and pulseless VF, and explain why torsades is not ordinary monomorphic VT.

items.title: 5. Bradyarrhythmias and atrioventricular conduction disease
items.los: IT_PO 1.7; AT_RT 1.1; IT_RT 1.1 (bradycardia); SS_IC 1.37; IT_PO 1.4 (conduction disease)
items.body:
## Why it matters

- A slow rhythm becomes hazardous when the accompanying stroke volume cannot maintain adequate cardiac output.
- The ECG may identify a benign sinus bradycardia, a transient vagal reaction or irreversible infranodal disease.
- **The location of block predicts progression to asystole:** nodal Wenckebach during vagal stimulation is often transient; Mobitz II or complete heart block can indicate His–Purkinje system disease with an unreliable escape rhythm.
- Anaesthetic agents may suppress sinus and AV-node function, and loss of sympathetic drive at induction may unmask severe conduction disease.

## Recognise the conduction abnormality before choosing a treatment

| ECG diagnosis | Diagnostic pattern | Significance for anaesthesia |
|---|---|---|
| Sinus bradycardia | Each P wave precedes a QRS; sinus rate <60/min | Often physiological; treat if hypoperfusion or concerning cause. |
| First-degree AV block | PR >200 ms, all P waves conducted | Usually no treatment alone; investigate symptoms, multiple conduction defects or relevant drugs. |
| Mobitz I (Wenckebach) | Progressive PR prolongation then dropped QRS | Often AV-nodal/vagal; can be reversible. Unstable patients still require treatment. |
| **Mobitz II** | Constant PR intervals in conducted beats with sudden non-conducted P | Usually infranodal and prone to progression; prepare pacing, even before overt shock. |
| High-grade AV block | ≥2 consecutive non-conducted P waves | Treat as potentially unstable; pacing likely required. |
| Complete heart block | Atrial and ventricular impulses independent (AV dissociation), escape rhythm | Slow broad escape is particularly unreliable; risk of asystole. |
| Sick sinus / tachy–brady | Sinus pauses, chronotropic incompetence, alternating AF and pauses | Assess symptoms and medication effects; may require permanent pacing. |

**2:**

- 1 block cannot reliably be labelled Mobitz I or II from the rhythm strip alone because there are not two successive conducted PR intervals to compare.
- Assess QRS width, clinical context and other ECG clues; seek cardiology input.
- A broad escape rate of 30/min with syncope is different from a narrow junctional escape at 55/min with preserved BP.
- Likewise, newly recognised LBBB is not itself complete heart block but may signal structural disease or additional conduction-system vulnerability.

## Immediate treatment of symptomatic bradycardia

The purpose is to restore perfusion, not a particular heart rate. Apply oxygen if hypoxaemic, obtain IV access, connect defibrillation/pacing pads if deterioration is possible, stop vagal/surgical triggers, evaluate drugs and electrolytes, and assess for MI, hyperkalaemia or high neuraxial block. If pulseless, move immediately to cardiac arrest management.

**ANZCOR adult peri-arrest bradycardia:**

- Atropine **500–600 micrograms IV**, repeat every **3–5 minutes** to a total of **3 mg** if necessary.
- If ineffective or likely to fail (especially high-grade infranodal block), use **transcutaneous pacing as a bridge to transvenous or epicardial pacing**, and an appropriately titrated catecholamine infusion.
- ANZCOR describes adrenaline **2–10 micrograms/min** and isoprenaline **2–5 micrograms/min** as options.
- Local resuscitation protocols, coronary ischaemia and structural disease should influence agent choice; these doses are not automatically interchangeable with AHA protocols.

**Atropine works by removing vagal inhibition from the SA/AV nodes:**

- It may do little in infranodal block with severe conduction-system failure, so do not wait for repeated ineffective doses before pacing a deteriorating patient.
- A transplanted, denervated heart typically will not respond and may exhibit paradoxical conduction effects: prioritise direct support and pacing as appropriate.
- Isoprenaline may provoke tachyarrhythmia/ischaemia; epinephrine is often preferable when BP also needs support.
- If beta-blocker or calcium-channel-blocker toxicity is responsible, initiate specific toxicology management (e.g. calcium for CCB, glucagon for selected beta-blocker toxicity, high-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy and vasopressors where indicated) rather than treating only the rate.

**Hyperkalaemia is a cause to identify quickly:**

- A broadening QRS, loss of P waves, sine-wave pattern, bradycardia or ventricular arrest may occur even without textbook sequential changes.
- Give IV calcium promptly for ECG toxicity, shift K intracellularly with insulin/glucose and other measures and remove K from the body; pacing may fail until membrane excitability is restored.

## Preoperative implications

- Ask about syncope, exertional presyncope, falls, fatigue, chronotropic limitation, prior pacemaker indication and previous ECGs.
- Review AV-nodal blockers (beta-blocker, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin), amiodarone, lithium and toxin exposures; test electrolytes and consider TTE for structural disease.
- A patient with symptomatic Mobitz II, advanced block or complete block generally warrants urgent specialist assessment and pacing strategy before elective anaesthesia.
- Emergency surgery may proceed only with effective external pacing immediately available, invasive monitoring when appropriate and a definitive rescue pathway.

Temporary or permanent pacing decisions depend on symptoms, reversibility and type of block; **permanent pacing is indicated for acquired Mobitz II, high-grade AV block or third-degree block not due to reversible causes even without symptoms** under ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia guidance. Conversely, asymptomatic sinus bradycardia by itself does not demand a pacemaker.

## Intraoperative implications

- Exaggerated vagal stimulation during traction on the globe, carotid sinus, peritoneum or viscera can produce profound bradycardia.
- **Stop the stimulus** first, support airway/BP and give appropriate vagolytic/vasopressor therapy.
- High spinal/epidural block can produce bradycardia through reduced venous return and sympathetic block; treat preload deficit and SVR reduction while preparing pacing for refractory instability.
- Bradycardia with severe hypotension following regional anaesthesia may be a pre-arrest state, not merely an uncomfortable HR number.

- For unstable or pacing-dependent patients, attach external pads **before induction**, use continuous ECG plus mechanical pulse monitoring and ensure a functioning rescue device.
- If an implanted pacemaker is present, evaluate for oversensing/inhibition by electrocautery rather than assuming the heart itself suddenly failed.
- Distinguish failure to pace (no output spikes), failure to capture (spikes without QRS) and failure to sense (inappropriate spikes) in the next chapters.

## Postoperative implications

- Watch for recurrence as anaesthetic agents, hypoxaemia, analgesics and electrolyte shifts change.
- After temporary pacing, ensure a documented plan for daily threshold checks, lead security, monitoring and removal.
- Long-standing symptomatic or infranodal block warrants electrophysiology evaluation and consideration of permanent device placement.
- Any episode of syncope, ventricular standstill or high-grade block should appear in the postoperative handover.

items.title: 6. Arrhythmias in intensive care and recovery
items.body:
## Why ICU arrhythmias need a different approach

- In critical illness, arrhythmias frequently reflect **sepsis, inflammation, catecholamine administration, hypoxaemia, metabolic derangement or changing cardiac loading conditions**.
- Treating the ECG without correcting these conditions produces recurrence and sometimes shock.
- New-onset AF is common in sepsis and after cardiac surgery; recurrent ventricular ectopy may be the first signal of ischaemia, hypokalaemia or significant myocardial dysfunction.
- The decision is therefore not simply drug versus shock, but whether the rhythm is causing or signalling failure of organ perfusion.

The ICU sequence is:

- Establish stability.
- Obtain a diagnostic 12-lead ECG.
- Compare baseline.
- Check K, Mg, ionised calcium, ABG, Hb, lactate, renal function, drug infusions and troponin when indicated.
- Use bedside echo to assess LV/RV function and filling.
- Correct the precipitant and decide whether rate/rhythm correction is needed.

- **A falling arterial pressure and ETCO₂ with a new arrhythmia is an emergency**, while isolated premature beats in a stable patient may only need treatment of electrolyte and sympathetic triggers.

## Postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF)

- POAF often develops on postoperative days 1–4, especially after thoracic/cardiac surgery.
- Atrial stretch, inflammation, increased sympathetic tone and oxidative stress all contribute.
- Assess sustained rapid response, symptoms, ischaemia, heart failure and duration.
- If shocked because of the rhythm, cardiovert.
- If stable, control triggers and rate using beta-blocker, diltiazem/verapamil (only if LV function appropriate) or amiodarone in selected cases.
- Correct congestion without assuming every patient needs a fluid bolus.
- Reassess after recovery because a seemingly transient episode may recur and confer thromboembolic risk.

**Stroke prevention:**

- Anticoagulation after surgery requires individualised assessment of AF duration, recurrence, CHA₂DS₂-VA/CHA₂DS₂-VASc and surgical bleeding risk.
- Do not start full-dose anticoagulation on day 0 simply because AF occurred; nor assume AF after surgery carries no future stroke risk.
- Withhold or restart anticoagulants according to procedure, renal function and neuraxial guidelines.
- At discharge, document the duration of AF, plans for surveillance and who will reassess anticoagulation.

## Bradycardia and cardiac surgery

- Following cardiopulmonary bypass, AV block may reflect surgical trauma, oedema, ischaemia, electrolyte changes or medications.
- Temporary epicardial leads can provide atrial or ventricular support; the exact mode depends on intact atrial activity, AV conduction, capture and the haemodynamic value of AV synchrony.
- **Complete heart block needs ventricular capture**—atrial-only pacing is inadequate because impulses cannot reliably reach the ventricles.
- Reassess rate, threshold and battery/connection every shift and after clinical deterioration.
- High-grade block persisting after recovery may require permanent pacing, with timing determined by operation type and surgical/cardiology advice.

## Common ICU medication traps

- **Amiodarone** can cause IV hypotension/bradycardia and interacts with warfarin, digoxin and other QT-active agents; it is unsuitable as reflex treatment for every abnormal rhythm.
- **Beta-blockers** may be helpful for adrenergic AF or ventricular ectopy but can aggravate acute low-output shock; the short half-life of esmolol facilitates a carefully observed trial.
- **Digoxin** has a narrow therapeutic index; hypokalaemia and renal impairment increase toxicity risk. Bidirectional VT is classic but not always present. Correct electrolytes and obtain expert advice regarding digoxin-specific Fab when severe toxicity is suspected.
- **Vasopressors and inotropes** can provoke atrial/ventricular ectopy; treat shock with the least catecholamine burden that restores perfusion and reassess whether a change in agent or dose is possible.
- **QT-prolonging combinations** (antiemetics, antibiotics, antipsychotics, methadone, electrolyte depletion) increase risk; check QTc, Mg and K and stop avoidable contributors.

## When to request additional monitoring and specialist intervention

- Seek cardiology/electrophysiology input for sustained VT, recurrent symptomatic SVT, new unexplained high-grade AV block, suspected inherited channelopathy, recurrent ICD therapy, pre-excited AF or persistent AF with failed rate control.
- Use echo and possibly PA catheter when arrhythmia overlaps with complex shock or advanced PH.
- Haemodynamic instability despite reasonable therapy may need pacing, catheter ablation or temporary circulatory support; these are individualised, not routine ICU measures.

**Practical bedside distinction:**

- If a patient develops rapid AF and hypotension in sepsis, first determine whether AF is causing low output or merely accompanying vasodilation.
- In a patient with severe mitral stenosis, AF may itself precipitate pulmonary oedema, making urgent rhythm intervention much more important.
- In a patient with severe RV failure, loss of atrial contribution can suddenly reduce RV filling and systemic output; maintaining AV synchrony becomes a resuscitation target.

items.title: 7. Cardiac pacing: concepts, modes and device types
items.los: SS_CS 1.10; SS_CS 1.11; SS_CS 1.12; IT_PO 1.4 (conduction abnormalities/pacemakers); BT_RT 1.37
items.body:
## Why pacing works—and when it does not

- Pacing delivers an electrical impulse strong enough to depolarise myocardial tissue and trigger contraction.
- It may rescue dangerously slow rhythms, maintain AV synchrony, prevent pause-dependent VT, or resynchronise dyssynchronous ventricles.
- **A visible pacing spike is not proof of effective pacing:** it may fail to depolarise tissue, or electrical activation may not produce mechanical output in profoundly shocked myocardium.
- Always confirm an appropriate QRS and arterial/plethysmographic pulse.

- A pacing system has a **pulse generator**, a lead/electrode, a sensing circuit and programming parameters.
- The generator supplies voltage/current for a defined pulse width; capture depends on the stimulus exceeding the myocardial threshold.
- Sensing allows the generator to detect intrinsic cardiac signals and inhibit or trigger pacing appropriately.
- Energy and battery longevity depend on voltage, pulse width, resistance and rate.
- Capture threshold rises with myocardial oedema, fibrosis, acidosis, hypoxaemia, hyperkalaemia, lead displacement and certain drugs.

## The five-position NBG pacemaker code

The North American Society of Pacing and Electrophysiology/British Pacing and Electrophysiology Group (NBG) code tells you **what is paced, what is sensed, how the device responds, whether it is rate adaptive, and whether multisite pacing is used**.

| Position | Meaning | Common letters |
|---|---|---|
| I | Chamber paced | A = atrium; V = ventricle; D = both; O = none |
| II | Chamber sensed | A, V, D, O |
| III | Response to sensing | I = inhibited; T = triggered; D = dual (triggered/inhibited); O = none |
| IV | Rate modulation | R = rate-responsive; O/blank = no rate response |
| V | Multisite pacing | A, V, D, O (used where relevant) |

**Examples:**

- VVI = ventricular pacing and sensing, inhibited by intrinsic ventricular activity
- AAI = atrial pacing inhibited by sensed atrial activity, requiring reliable AV conduction
- DDD = paces/senses both chambers with coordinated triggered/inhibited responses
- DDDR adds rate responsiveness
- VOO/DOO = asynchronous pacing with no sensing (so cannot inhibit when spontaneous activity occurs).
- **DDDR does not mean “paces the ventricle continually”:** the programmed timing allows intrinsic conduction when appropriate.

### Pacing modes chosen for physiology

| Rhythm and conduction | Mode that may be useful | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Complete AV block with sinus atrial rhythm | DDD, or VVI for temporary rescue | DDD tracks atrial activity and preserves AV synchrony; VVI provides reliable ventricular escape when atrial lead absent. |
| Sinus-node dysfunction with intact AV conduction | AAI/AAIR in selected patients, or DDD/DDDR | Preserves AV synchrony and can support chronotropic response. |
| Persistent AF with slow ventricular response | VVI/VVIR | No useful atrial tracking; maintain ventricular rate. |
| Perioperative EMI in a pacing-dependent pacemaker patient | Asynchronous VOO/DOO depending on system | Avoids oversensing and inhibition, with an R-on-T risk if intrinsic rhythm competes. |
| LBBB or dyssynchrony with indicated HF phenotype | CRT pacing (often biventricular) | Coordinates LV/RV activation and can improve pump function in carefully selected patients. |

- **Pacemaker syndrome:** loss of AV synchrony (e.g. VVI pacing with preserved retrograde atrial activation) can produce hypotension, cannon a waves, fatigue, dyspnoea or HF. The problem is not simply pacing rate but atrial contraction against a closed AV valve and impaired filling. DDD pacing can restore synchrony in appropriate patients.

## Core programming terms

- **Lower rate limit** is the minimum paced rate in a demand mode.
- **Upper tracking rate** limits how fast a dual-chamber system will track atrial activity; **upper sensor rate** limits rate-adaptive pacing.
- **AV delay** permits atrial-to-ventricular conduction before ventricular pacing; excessive or very short delay may harm ventricular filling.
- **PVARP** (postventricular atrial refractory period) helps prevent inappropriate atrial tracking and pacemaker-mediated tachycardia.
- **Hysteresis** may permit rates temporarily below the nominal lower rate to encourage intrinsic conduction.
- **Rate response** increases pacing according to activity measured by accelerometer, minute ventilation or other sensors; mechanical ventilation, electrocautery or handling may falsely activate some sensors.

**Capture threshold:**

- Smallest output (at a defined pulse width) resulting in depolarisation.
- Programmers set a safety margin, commonly **2–3 times the measured threshold** for temporary pacing (institution/device dependent).
- **Sensing threshold:** the smallest intrinsic signal detectable at a given sensitivity setting.
- Sensitivity is expressed in **mV**, with an essential inversion: **lower programmed mV = greater sensitivity**.
- Thus, changing a ventricular sensing setting from 5 to 2 mV makes the device more likely to sense small signals, not less.
- Excess sensitivity risks oversensing interference or T waves; insufficient sensitivity risks asynchronous impulses landing on intrinsic activity.

## Types of pacing

- **Transcutaneous pacing** sends current between skin pads and is rapidly available but causes pain and skeletal muscle stimulation; it is a bridge.
- **Transvenous pacing** inserts a temporary electrode, usually through a central vein to the RV endocardium, producing more reliable capture with lower outputs but carries vascular, infection, arrhythmia and perforation risks.
- **Epicardial pacing** uses temporary wires placed surgically on atrial and/or ventricular epicardium, common after cardiac surgery; capture thresholds may rise over days as inflammation develops.
- **Permanent transvenous systems** contain generator and endocardial leads, while **leadless pacemakers** are implanted inside the ventricle and may have different magnet responses and AV synchrony capabilities.
- **CRT** uses coordinated ventricular activation, often a coronary-sinus LV lead; **ICDs** sense and terminate malignant ventricular tachyarrhythmias and may also provide pacing.

### What a pacemaker ECG can tell you

- Ventricular pacing usually creates a broad QRS with a pacing spike (although modern bipolar, conduction-system and leadless pacing may have tiny/obscured spikes or narrower QRS).
- A pacing spike without a subsequent depolarising QRS suggests failure to capture.
- P waves and paced QRS with a consistent AV delay suggest atrial sensing/tracking.
- A pacemaker may not fire because it correctly senses intrinsic rhythm; **absence of spikes does not prove a device fault**.
- Conversely, a monitor may hide spikes owing to filtering, so always correlate with the pulse and device interrogation when indicated.

items.title: 8. Temporary pacing: practical programming and troubleshooting
items.body:
## Why this is an ANZCA Final priority

- The 2026.1 Final SAQ specifically examined **complete heart block after bypass requiring epicardial pacing**, asking for justified rate/mode selection and troubleshooting intermittent loss of capture in a pacing-dependent ICU patient.
- Examiner feedback emphasised that candidates must take the actual patient's haemodynamics into account and propose **alternative rescue modalities**; a generic description of the pacemaker controls was insufficient.
- The most teachable sequence is therefore: what circulation do we need? → which chamber must be paced? → is there capture? → is there sensing? → what is the fallback plan?

## When to apply external defibrillation/pacing pads before surgery

- In a patient at risk, apply multifunction pads **before induction** rather than finding a defibrillator after deterioration.
- Typical indications include severe symptomatic bradycardia or high-grade AV block
- Temporary epicardial or transvenous pacing dependence
- Significant risk of VT/VF or recurrent electrical storm
- A patient with an ICD whose tachytherapies will be suspended
- Severe cardiomyopathy or a procedural situation where immediate external pacing/defibrillation rescue is likely to be required
- Selected unstable cardiac/EP procedures.
- Pad placement is a risk-based decision, not a mandate for every patient with a pacemaker.
- Where there is a generator, place pads ideally **≥8 cm away** and do not delay emergency shocks to satisfy the distance.

## A. External transcutaneous pacemaker: how to programme it

- **1.** Confirm the indication: unstable symptomatic bradycardia/high-grade AV block as a bridge, or prophylactic rescue readiness in a high-risk patient. If pulseless, apply arrest management first.
- **2.** Explain to an awake patient and provide appropriate analgesia/sedation where circulation permits; transcutaneous pacing may be painful.
- **3.** Apply multifunction pads in an accepted anterior–lateral or anterior–posterior position; keep them at least 8 cm from an implanted generator if feasible. Connect ECG monitoring with adequate sensing leads.
- **4.** Choose **demand mode** (synchronous, sensing intrinsic beats) where reliable; some circumstances require fixed/asynchronous mode if signal artefact inhibits pacing. Choose an initial rate **70–80/min**, then individualise to cardiac output, myocardial ischaemia, haemodynamics and patient size.
- **5.** Increase current/output (mA) from a low level (ANZCOR suggests e.g. **30 mA**) until each pacing impulse produces a clear paced QRS, then verify **mechanical capture** with arterial waveform, palpated pulse where reliable, or echocardiography.
  - Increase to a reasonable safety margin above threshold; manufacturer-specific settings vary.
- **6.** Continue monitoring patient comfort, perfusion, pad contact and skin. If pacing is ineffective or needed for more than a short rescue interval, arrange temporary transvenous pacing or definitive treatment, while using an adrenaline infusion as indicated.

- **Why electrical versus mechanical capture matters:** chest wall muscle twitch may mimic a pulse during transcutaneous pacing. The reliable endpoint is a paced ventricular depolarisation associated with a true arterial pressure waveform and improved perfusion, not simply the number on the machine.

## B. Temporary transvenous pacing

- Common indications are drug-refractory unstable bradycardia, high-grade or complete AV block, recurrent pause-dependent torsades when rate support is needed, and bridging while awaiting recovery or permanent implantation.
- Venous access is commonly internal jugular or femoral; place with sterile technique, ultrasound-guided vascular access and ECG/fluoroscopic or echocardiographic confirmation according to circumstance.
- Advance the lead to appropriate RV position while monitoring for ectopy, ventricular perforation and tamponade.
- Secure it carefully and confirm consistent electrical and mechanical capture.

- An RV lead can provide **VVI or VOO** depending on available generator/sensing and EMI.
- Set the lowest adequate rate, check threshold and use a safety margin.
- Watch for failure due to lead displacement, rising thresholds or generator/connection problems, especially during transfers and position changes.
- Complications include infection, thrombosis, ventricular ectopy, pneumothorax from venous access, valve injury, perforation and tamponade.
- Continuous monitoring and a backup rescue plan are essential for pacing-dependent patients.

## C. Epicardial pacing after cardiac surgery

- Epicardial wires may be placed on the right atrium and right ventricle and connected to a temporary external pulse generator.
- Atrial pacing (AAI) can improve output when sinus-node dysfunction coexists with intact AV conduction
- **DDD or sequential AV pacing** can preserve atrial contribution and ventricular capture when both atrial and ventricular wires work
- **VVI** is the essential rescue option when AV conduction is absent or atrial sensing/capture is unreliable.
- A pacing-dependent patient must have dependable ventricular output before relying on atrial synchrony.

### Programming a complete-heart-block patient after CPB

**Step 1 — protect perfusion:**

- Check arterial pressure, pulse, lactate, oxygenation and underlying rhythm; connect external pads and have a second generator or transcutaneous rescue available.
- Obtain appropriate pacing mode and settings from cardiac surgery/ICU context.
- For complete block, choose ventricular-capable pacing: **DDD when both leads and atrial rhythm are reliable; VVI if the atrial lead is absent/unreliable or rapid AF is present**.
- Explain your choice.

**Step 2 — choose a rate for output:**

- Start around **70–90/min** according to haemodynamics and postoperative cardiac physiology (some patients benefit from 80–100/min, others become ischaemic or poorly filled at higher rates).
- A generic 60/min without justification may be inadequate after CPB.
- Look at arterial waveform and stroke-volume response rather than merely the displayed HR.

**Step 3 — check capture thresholds:**

- With an adequate escape/backup arrangement, reduce output carefully until capture is lost, identify the threshold, then restore output with an appropriate **2–3× safety margin** or local/device policy.
- Repeat for each used chamber.
- Do not deliberately provoke prolonged asystole in a dependent patient to measure a threshold without a rescue pathway.

**Step 4 — check sensitivity:**

- For demand pacing, confirm that intrinsic signals appropriately inhibit or trigger pacing.
- Adjust the mV setting to sense intrinsic R/P signals reliably without oversensing artefact; lower mV means more sensitive.
- Set and test AV delay, upper rate and other parameters if in DDD.
- If electrocautery/artefact is significant or sensing is unreliable in a pacing-dependent patient, temporary asynchronous mode may be needed with continuous monitoring.

**Step 5 — documentation/handover.** Record rate, mode, atrial and ventricular output, pulse width, sensing settings, capture threshold, underlying rhythm and any dependence, wires used, backup plan, and next check. Keep wires and generator secured, clear and accessible.

## D. Intermittent failure of capture: patient → circuit → myocardium

**First stabilise the patient.** Is there hypotension, altered mentation, low output or asystole? Call help; apply transcutaneous pacing and start vasoactive support as required while correcting the cause. Do not spend several minutes adjusting generator controls while the patient becomes pulseless. Check arterial output to prove true loss of capture.

| Level of problem | What to check | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| **Patient / myocardium** | Hypoxaemia, acidosis, hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, ischaemia, oedema after CPB, drug effects | Correct cause; increase output safely while establishing backup pacing. |
| **Lead / connections** | Loose lead plugs, crossed polarity, wire fracture, displacement, poor contact after turning | Reconnect, correct ports/polarity, secure wires, check CXR/echo and obtain specialist review/replacement if needed. |
| **Generator / programme** | Battery, wrong chamber/mode, output below threshold, pulse width, excessive sensing of noise | Replace battery/generator, reprogramme, raise output, correct sensing/mode. |
| **Alternative rescue** | Does a second epicardial wire, transcutaneous pad, transvenous wire or catecholamine infusion provide support? | Implement immediately when dependent or unstable; prepare definitive pacing. |

- **Differentiate three malfunctions:**

- **Failure to pace/output:** no pacing spikes when the device should deliver them. Think battery, disconnection, oversensing, inappropriate inhibition or programme.
- **Failure to capture:** pacing spikes are delivered, but no corresponding P/QRS or arterial pulse occurs. Think low output, lead problem, threshold rise or severe metabolic disturbance.
- **Failure to sense:** pacing spikes occur inappropriately despite native beats (undersensing) or fail to occur because noise/T waves are falsely detected (oversensing). Adjust sensitivity thoughtfully: **smaller mV setting = more sensing**.

**Overdrive pacing** may terminate some re-entrant rhythms or prevent recurrent acquired pause-dependent torsades, but can provoke arrhythmia and is not a casual substitute for expert electrophysiological management. Pacing a patient with a ventricular tachyarrhythmia must never delay indicated electrical cardioversion/defibrillation.

items.title: 9. Permanent pacemakers, implantable defibrillators and CRT
items.los: IT_PO 1.4 (conduction abnormalities and pacemakers); SS_CS 1.11; SS_CS 1.12; SS_CS 1.8; SS_CS 1.4 (rhythm)
items.body:
## Why they matter

- Patients with cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) have **two separate sources of perioperative risk:** their underlying cardiac disease and interactions between the procedure and the device.
- A stable DDDR pacemaker may become inhibited by electrocautery in a patient whose ventricle is entirely pacing-dependent; an ICD may misinterpret electromagnetic interference (EMI) as VF and deliver an inappropriate shock.
- Conversely, a patient whose ICD tachyarrhythmia treatment has been suspended has no implanted defibrillation rescue until therapies are restored.

- A magnet is **not a universal “safe-mode” switch**.
- The response depends on the **device type, make/model, programming, battery status and magnet position**.
- For many conventional pacemakers a magnet causes asynchronous pacing; for most ICDs it suspends shock/antitachycardia treatment **without changing bradycardia pacing**.
- Some leadless devices (for example Medtronic Micra) have **no magnet response**; certain newer leadless devices differ.
- Only a confirmed patient-specific plan is safe.

## Device types and what they actually do

| Device | Main function | Specific perioperative issue |
|---|---|---|
| Permanent pacemaker (PPM) | Treats symptomatic bradyarrhythmia, AV block or sinus-node disease | Pacing inhibition from EMI in a dependent patient; mode/rate and magnet response. |
| ICD | Detects/treats VT/VF by antitachycardia pacing and/or shock; may provide brady pacing | Inappropriate shocks from EMI or loss of VT/VF treatment if therapies disabled. |
| CRT-P / CRT-D | Coordinates ventricular activation; CRT-D also defibrillates | Loss of biventricular capture can impair low-output patients; CRT-D inherits ICD precautions. |
| Leadless pacemaker | Intracardiac generator/electrode; often ventricular pacing | Magnet response may be absent; programme rather than rely on magnet when dependent. |
| Subcutaneous ICD | Detects and shocks VT/VF without traditional transvenous pacing | Does not provide routine bradycardia pacing; magnet and position must be confirmed. |
| Implantable loop recorder | Records arrhythmias only | No pacing or shocks; EMI may create false recordings. |

## A. Preoperative implications: patient, device and procedure

- **Patient:** establish indication for implantation, underlying rhythm, **pacing dependence**, HF/EF, recent syncope, shocks, arrhythmia burden and exercise tolerance. A high percentage of paced beats alone suggests, but does not always prove, complete dependence. Sedation or anaesthesia may increase dependence by suppressing native escape or sinus rate.

**Device:**

- Identify manufacturer/model and generator location from device card, records, CXR or interrogation.
- Review **recent interrogation** for battery longevity, lead impedance, sensing, capture thresholds, percentage atrial/ventricular pacing, stored arrhythmias, tachytherapy status and magnet response.
- AHA 2024 notes interrogation within about **3 months** can be informative for dependence and device function in many circumstances, but an urgent interrogation is determined by recent status, symptoms, surgical risk and local CIED guidance—not by an automatic date alone.
- A pacemaker with nearly exhausted battery may respond differently to a magnet and has less safety reserve.

**Procedure:**

- Identify surgical site relative to generator/leads
- Likelihood of monopolar diathermy, radiofrequency ablation, lithotripsy or other EMI
- Patient position (can magnet be reliably secured or removed?)
- Expected haemodynamic stress, ability to access chest and postoperative destination.
- **EMI is particularly relevant for monopolar cautery above the umbilicus**, although generator location and current pathway matter more than a simplistic line across the abdomen.

### A preoperative decision table

| Situation | Safe strategy to consider |
|---|---|
| Pacing-dependent PPM with significant EMI anticipated | Programme asynchronous AOO/VOO/DOO (depending on chamber configuration), or use a verified reliably maintained magnet if appropriate. |
| Pacing-dependent transvenous ICD with significant EMI | **Reprogramme pacing to asynchronous and suspend tachytherapy**; a magnet alone only suspends ICD tachytherapy. |
| Non-dependent ICD with significant EMI | Suspend tachytherapies using programmed setting or verified magnet; have external pads/defibrillator immediately ready. |
| Little/no EMI anticipated away from device | Often leave programming unchanged, with monitoring and contingency plan. |
| Leadless pacemaker requiring asynchronous pacing | Arrange device-specific programming; do not assume the magnet works. |

- Seek CIED team input and provide an **explicit written plan** specifying what setting changes occur, when and by whom they will be restored.
- Do not assume all implanted devices require reprogramming for every operation.
- For emergency surgery without device records, prioritise haemodynamic monitoring, external pacing/defibrillation access and pragmatic magnet use only according to the likely device type, with specialist input as soon as possible.

## B. Intraoperative implications: make the electrical environment safe

- Use **bipolar diathermy** or non-electrical haemostasis when practical. If monopolar cautery is necessary, use short, intermittent bursts at the lowest effective power and position the return electrode so the current path does not traverse the generator or leads.
- Maintain standard ECG plus a **mechanical pulse signal** (pulse oximetry or arterial line) because EMI can obscure the ECG. If the heart is pacing-dependent and inhibition is possible, have transcutaneous pacing rescue ready.
- Place external defibrillator pads before induction in high-risk patients; place them **ideally ≥8 cm away from the generator**, without delaying resuscitation. External shocks are permitted when needed despite the device; assess device function afterwards.
- If tachytherapies are disabled, ensure someone explicitly owns the responsibility for **external defibrillation** during surgery and for restoration afterward. A magnet may become dislodged during prone or lateral positioning.
- Avoid arrhythmogenic physiology: hypoxaemia, severe acidosis, potassium abnormalities, ischaemia, deep anaesthetic depression and sympathetic surges. Preserve electromechanical capture rather than assuming spikes guarantee perfusion.

**Device-specific examples:**

- A patient with a biventricular CRT-D and EF 25% undergoing upper abdominal surgery may need both VT/VF therapy suspension and a pacing plan preserving resynchronisation; simply converting to RV-only asynchronous pacing can reduce output.
- In an emergency, external pads and immediate support take priority, but subsequent electrophysiology input should refine the plan.
- For planned cardioversion/defibrillation, position pads away from the generator and interrogate afterwards if clinically indicated or if device function may have changed.

## C. Postoperative implications: restore and check

- **Never discharge a patient from monitored care while ICD tachytherapies remain inadvertently disabled.** When a magnet was used, remove it and verify return to the expected device state; where the programmer changed the mode, restore the intended settings and verify with the CIED team.
- Interrogate after major EMI exposure, external shocks, significant arrhythmias, suspected malfunction or reprogramming according to local protocol.
- Document restoration clearly and communicate with the ward/recovery team.

- Monitor for arrhythmias, pacing failure, myocardial injury when indicated, and device or wound complications after implantation.
- Patients with severe underlying HF may require monitored recovery irrespective of device function.
- A device-specific handover states: underlying rhythm/dependence, perioperative changes, magnet response, tachytherapy status, external pads or rescue requirements and confirmation of restoration.

## D. Special circumstances and complications

**ICD storm:**

- Repeated shocks may be appropriate or inappropriate.
- Check rhythm and device telemetry, treat arrhythmia/ischaemia/electrolyte causes and apply analgesia/sedation.
- Inappropriate shocks from lead fracture or EMI may be temporarily inhibited by a magnet **provided external defibrillation remains available**; never use a magnet reflexively in a patient with ongoing true VF/VT without a rescue plan.

- **Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia:** in DDD systems retrograde VA conduction may create an endless-loop tracking tachycardia. Reprogramming PVARP or applying a verified pacemaker magnet can interrupt it, but do not mislabel every rapid paced rhythm as PMT. **Runaway pacemaker** is uncommon with modern devices; immediate expert input and supportive care are required.

**Device implantation and anticoagulation:**

- The **BRUISE CONTROL** trial showed lower clinically important pocket haematoma with uninterrupted warfarin (3.5%) versus heparin bridging (16%) in higher-thrombotic-risk patients having CIED implantation.
- This does not mean all surgery on warfarin is safer without interruption; it applies to the device-pocket procedure and its specific studied population.
- DOAC management and pocket bleeding risks are addressed with the device team and proceduralist.

- **Exam application:** In the ANZCA 2022.2 DDDR pacemaker SAQ, high-quality answers identified the **NBG code, patient's underlying rhythm/percentage paced, battery, magnet response, operative site and diathermy plan**. Do not substitute a generic full cardiac history for the requested device-focused answer.

items.title: 10. Right-ventricular physiology, echo and cardiac shunts
items.los: SS_CS 1.4 (RV systolic function, pulmonary artery pressure and shunts); BT_PO 1.5 (right HF/PH supporting physiology)
items.body:
## Why the RV behaves differently from the LV

- The **right ventricle is a thin-walled, highly compliant pump** normally ejecting against a low-resistance, high-compliance pulmonary circuit.
- Its crescentic geometry, longitudinal free-wall shortening and interventricular septal contribution differ from LV contraction.
- It accommodates modest increases in volume reasonably well, but an abrupt **increase in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR)** greatly raises wall tension and oxygen demand, impairs RV ejection and leads to dilatation.
- As the RV enlarges, the interventricular septum shifts toward the LV, reducing LV filling and systemic output—**ventricular interdependence**.

The haemodynamic trap is a vicious circle: **↑ PVR → ↑ RV pressure and dilatation → tricuspid regurgitation/septal shift → ↓ LV preload and systemic BP → ↓ RV coronary perfusion → RV ischaemia → worse RV contractility**. The anaesthetic objectives therefore simultaneously protect the RV from excessive afterload and maintain enough systemic pressure for its own perfusion.

- At normal pressures, the RV receives coronary perfusion during systole and diastole; with severe RV hypertension, systolic perfusion falls and the RV becomes increasingly dependent on adequate **aortic diastolic pressure relative to RV pressure**.
- Simply giving more fluid to a distended RV may exacerbate septal shift and congestion without improving stroke volume.
- Conversely, a genuinely underfilled RV may respond to a small assessed fluid challenge.
- This is why **fluid responsiveness, congestion and fluid tolerance are separate questions**.

## Pulmonary haemodynamics and equations

- **PVR = (mean PAP − PAWP) / cardiac output**, expressed in Wood units.
- PAWP approximates mean left atrial pressure under appropriate conditions; it is not automatically LVEDP in mitral stenosis or distorted pressure conditions.
- PVR is a calculated pressure–flow relationship, not a directly measured vessel property, and changes with lung volume, oxygen tension, CO₂, pH, airway pressures, haematocrit and vasoactive medication.
- Pulmonary arterial compliance is often markedly reduced in chronic PH and makes the RV more sensitive to pulsatile load even if a single PVR value appears modest.

**Lung volume matters:**

- PVR tends to increase at both very low and very high lung volumes.
- At low volumes, extra-alveolar vessels narrow; at high volumes, alveolar capillaries are compressed.
- Excessive PEEP, high plateau pressures, hyperinflation and auto-PEEP can therefore precipitate RV dysfunction.
- Positive-pressure ventilation also lowers systemic venous return, though appropriately titrated PEEP improves oxygenation and may decrease hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.

## Assess RV size, function and pressure using TTE/TOE

Start with qualitative assessment: is the RV dilated? Is the septum flattened? Is RV systolic performance visibly reduced? Is significant TR present? Then use quantitative measures in context.

| Echo measure | Common reference or interpretation | Important caveat |
|---|---|---|
| RV basal diameter | >41 mm suggests dilatation in conventional adult echo references | Plane and body size matter; compare with LV, serial trends. |
| TAPSE | <17 mm suggests impaired longitudinal RV systolic function | Angle- and load-dependent; does not assess all regions of RV. |
| Tissue Doppler S′ | <9.5 cm/s suggests reduced basal longitudinal motion | May be misleading after cardiac surgery or with altered loading. |
| RV FAC | <35% suggests impaired RV area shortening | Requires careful endocardial tracing and appropriate view. |
| RV:LV end-diastolic diameter | Ratio >1 suggests dilatation/strain | Not diagnostic of PE or PH by itself. |
| TR velocity | RV–RA gradient ≈4v²; plus estimated RAP estimates RVSP | Only approximates PASP without RVOT/pulmonary obstruction and with reliable TR signal. |
| Septal flattening / D-shaped LV | RV pressure overload (systolic) or volume overload (often diastolic) | Interpret timing, ventilation, congenital shunt and image plane. |
| IVC size and collapse | Supports estimate of RAP with multiple clinical clues | Poor predictor of fluid responsiveness, particularly on positive pressure. |

**Advanced RV indices:**

- RV free-wall longitudinal strain (more negative values generally better), three-dimensional RVEF and pulmonary artery acceleration time can add information when available.
- Normal TAPSE does **not** exclude significant PH, and a high TR velocity is not diagnostic in isolation.
- Echo estimates the probability of PH; **right-heart catheterisation defines haemodynamics and classifies PH** when diagnosis/management requires certainty.

### Pulmonary artery catheter: what it adds

- A PAC can measure RA pressure, RV/PA pressures, PAWP, mixed venous oxygen saturation and thermodilution output; derived PVR and cardiac index can help distinguish RV pressure overload, left-heart congestion and low output in selected complex patients.
- It is **not routine for every patient with PH** and can cause arrhythmias, vessel injury and misleading estimates if transducer zeroing or respiratory measurement is poor.
- Severe TR, intracardiac shunts, mechanical ventilation and low flow can distort derived measurements.
- Use trends and echo together with perfusion rather than interpreting a single CVP or PAWP as definitive.

## Intracardiac shunts: why direction matters

- A shunt alters the flow of blood between systemic and pulmonary circulations.
- **Left-to-right shunts** (ASD, VSD, PDA) initially increase pulmonary blood flow and chamber loading.
- With longstanding high flow, progressive pulmonary vascular disease can raise PVR until the shunt becomes bidirectional or right-to-left (**Eisenmenger physiology**).
- **Right-to-left shunts** cause systemic desaturation, paradoxical embolism risk and often major sensitivity to changes in SVR and PVR.
- A PFO is frequently functionally closed at normal atrial pressure relationships but may open with elevated RAP, straining, positive-pressure ventilation or RV failure.

| Lesion | Physiological pattern | Anaesthetic relevance |
|---|---|---|
| ASD | LA→RA flow; right-heart volume loading | RV dilatation, atrial arrhythmias, late PH; paradoxical embolism if R→L occurs. |
| VSD | LV→RV flow; flow depends on defect size and PVR:SVR | Large lesions cause increased pulmonary flow, HF and pulmonary vascular disease; acute shifts in SVR/PVR change shunt. |
| PDA | Aorta→pulmonary artery | Pulmonary overcirculation and LV volume load; reverse differential cyanosis in advanced shunt reversal. |
| PFO | Interatrial potential R→L under high RAP | **De-air all IV lines**; avoid air and prevent acute RV pressure rise. |
| Eisenmenger | High PVR with R→L/bidirectional shunt | Protect systemic perfusion/SVR, avoid ↑PVR, prevent air embolism; high perioperative risk. |

**Qp:**

- Qs is the ratio of pulmonary to systemic blood flow.
- Approximate oximetric calculation uses oxygen-content differences: (systemic arterial − mixed venous O₂ content)/(pulmonary venous − pulmonary arterial O₂ content), assuming reliable samples and negligible confounders.
- Qp:Qs >1 indicates net L→R flow, <1 net R→L.
- A ratio of 1.5:1 or more often marks a haemodynamically important L→R shunt, but closure decisions also depend on PVR, symptoms, ventricular size, pulmonary vascular disease and defect type.
- **Do not close an Eisenmenger shunt** reflexively: it may serve as an essential decompression route for the failing RV.

**Perioperative priorities with shunts:**

- Preserve adequate preload and SVR, avoid hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, acidosis and elevated airway pressures that increase PVR, and meticulously de-air all infusions and injection ports.
- Consider air filters for high-risk R→L shunts when compatible with treatment.
- Pulmonary vasodilation or systemic vasoconstriction can markedly change shunt direction.
- An acute fall in SVR from neuraxial sympathectomy can worsen R→L shunting, whereas excessive catecholamine-induced increases in SVR may augment L→R flow when PVR remains low.
- Technique must be individualised with congenital-heart expertise for complex lesions.

items.title: 11. Pulmonary hypertension: from haemodynamics to anaesthetic care
items.los: BT_PO 1.5 (pulmonary hypertension); SS_CS 1.4 (RV function/PA pressure and shunts)
items.body:
## A. Why it matters

- Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is not simply a high pressure on an echocardiogram.
- It is a state in which **the right ventricle faces increased resistance, reduced pulmonary vascular compliance or abnormal pulmonary blood flow** and may have limited capacity to adapt to anaesthesia and surgical stress.
- A patient may be comfortable at rest yet decompensate with induction-induced hypotension, hypoxaemia, mild hypercapnia or an episode of AF.
- The major perioperative catastrophe is **acute RV failure**, which reduces LV preload, systemic perfusion and RV coronary flow in a self-reinforcing cycle.

- PH is associated with important perioperative morbidity, including arrhythmias, hypoxaemia, low-output shock, respiratory failure, prolonged ventilation and death.
- In a systematic review/expert consensus statement of noncardiac/nonobstetric procedures, reported mortality in PH cohorts ranged approximately **2–18% for elective surgery and 15–50% for emergency surgery**.
- These are heterogeneous observational populations, **not** a universal predicted risk for an individual patient.
- Severity of RV dysfunction, functional class, exercise limitation and surgical urgency matter far more than one echo-estimated PAP number.

## B. Definition and classification

- The **2022 ESC/ERS definition** requires **mPAP >20 mmHg at rest measured by right-heart catheterisation**.
- Distinguish pulmonary arterial hypertension (a disease subgroup) from pulmonary hypertension due to left-heart, lung or thromboembolic disease.
- The pressure rises as blood flow increases or left atrial pressure rises, even when PVR is normal; therefore pressure alone does not equal precapillary vascular disease.

| Haemodynamic category | Right-heart catheter criteria | Clinical meaning |
|---|---|---|
| PH, any group | mPAP >20 mmHg | Raised pulmonary pressure; mechanism not yet defined. |
| Precapillary PH | mPAP >20, PAWP ≤15, PVR >2 WU | Increased resistance across pulmonary vascular bed. |
| Isolated postcapillary PH | mPAP >20, PAWP >15, PVR ≤2 WU | Elevated LA pressure transmitted backwards, e.g. left-heart HF/valves. |
| Combined pre/postcapillary PH | mPAP >20, PAWP >15, PVR >2 WU | Left-heart congestion plus pulmonary vascular remodelling. |

**Five clinical groups:**

- (1) pulmonary arterial hypertension—idiopathic, heritable, drug-associated, connective-tissue disease, congenital-heart-associated
- (2) due to left-heart disease (systolic/diastolic HF or valves)
- (3) due to lung disease/hypoxia including COPD, ILD and sleep-disordered breathing
- (4) chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) and other pulmonary artery obstruction
- (5) complex/multifactorial mechanisms.
- The group matters because **PAH-specific vasodilators are not standard treatment for all PH**, and can worsen pulmonary oedema in postcapillary PH.

## C. Pathophysiology: why routine anaesthesia can precipitate crisis

- Chronic PVR elevation causes RV hypertrophy and eventually dilatation, worsening TR and reduced ventricular compliance.
- When pulmonary resistance acutely rises, RV output falls and leftward septal shift impairs the LV.
- Systemic hypotension reduces right-coronary perfusion and makes RV ischaemia more likely.
- Meanwhile, hypoxaemia and acidosis constrict pulmonary arterioles, causing an escalating spiral.

- **Avoidable rises in PVR** include hypoxaemia (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction), hypercapnia, acidosis, pain/catecholamine surges, hypothermia, pulmonary embolism, high airway pressures, excessive PEEP or lung hyperinflation and nitrous oxide in selected high-risk cases.
- **Avoid systemic hypotension** because a well-oxygenated RV may still fail if coronary perfusion collapses.
- Do not chase an isolated PAP value without considering RV output, perfusion and congestion.

## D. Preoperative implications

### 1. Establish the PH phenotype, functional severity and progression

- History should identify diagnosis/group, previous right-heart catheter results, symptoms of exercise limitation, exertional syncope, chest pain, worsening dyspnoea, dependent oedema/ascites, recent admissions and prior PH crisis.
- Ask about home oxygen, continuous prostacyclin infusions, established PH therapies, diuretics, anticoagulation (particularly CTEPH) and planned surgery.
- Functional status is often described using WHO functional class I–IV; **class III/IV, recent syncope and poor 6-minute walk distance are red flags**.
- Determine whether the patient is clinically compensated or recently decompensated.

Examination: oxygen saturation (including baseline), HR/rhythm, BP, JVP, peripheral perfusion, oedema, hepatomegaly, right-ventricular heave, loud P2, TR murmur and signs of left-heart disease. A loud P2 supports raised PA pressure but neither absence nor presence grades risk accurately.

### 2. Targeted investigation and risk assessment

| Investigation | What matters | How it changes decisions |
|---|---|---|
| ECG | Right-axis deviation, RV strain, right atrial enlargement, RBBB, AF | Rhythm vulnerability; a normal ECG does not exclude PH. |
| TTE/FOCUS | RV size/function, TAPSE/S′/FAC, septal flattening, TR velocity, LA/LV, significant valve lesion | Identifies RV reserve and likely PH phenotype; compares with earlier studies. |
| BNP/NT-proBNP | Right-heart wall stress; interpret CKD/obesity/AF context | Rising values may signify decompensation and prompt PH-team review. |
| 6-minute walk / exercise assessment | Functional limitation, desaturation | Useful trend and severity marker; not a standalone clearance test. |
| RHC (selected) | mPAP, PAWP, CO/CI, PVR, RA pressure, SvO₂ | Definitive phenotype and risk clarification, when result changes therapy. |
| ABG/PFT/CT/VQ | Hypoxaemia, lung disease, CTEPH and alternate causes | Guides oxygen/ventilation and underlying disease treatment. |

- **High-risk markers** include WHO FC III/IV, syncope, markedly reduced exercise distance, elevated RA pressure, low cardiac index, substantial RV dysfunction, high BNP, recent right-HF decompensation and emergency/major surgery.
- Distinguish disease severity from surgical risk: long laparoscopy with pneumoperitoneum, major bleeding, sepsis or prolonged positive-pressure ventilation can be more threatening than a short peripheral regional procedure.
- Discuss significant PH cases with a **PH specialist, anaesthetist, surgeon and ICU team** and consider referral to an experienced centre.

### 3. Optimisation: don't stop essential pulmonary vasodilators

- Optimise volume to **euvolaemia:** decongest a swollen patient but avoid dehydration that reduces RV preload.
