> **Closing point:** New energy changes the complication profile; it does not abolish risk.

items.title: Which major AF trials matter in viva answers, and what did they show?
items.q: Which major AF trials matter in viva answers, and what did they show?
items.a:
- **AFFIRM**: rhythm control was **not superior to rate control for mortality** in the studied older AF population; anticoagulation and comorbidity management remained crucial.
- **RACE II**: a **lenient rate-control target** was acceptable for many stable patients with permanent AF.
- **EAST-AFNET 4**: **early rhythm control** improved cardiovascular outcomes in selected recently diagnosed AF patients.
- **CABANA**: catheter ablation improved AF recurrence and quality-of-life measures, but intention-to-treat mortality benefit was less clear.
- Viva application: do not say “rate control is always equivalent” or “all AF should be ablated”; match the evidence to the patient and time course.

> **Closing point:** AFFIRM explains why rate control is acceptable; EAST explains why early rhythm control is back in play.

items.title: Which landmark studies changed pacing/device and PAH practice?
items.q: Which landmark studies changed pacing/device and PAH practice?
items.a:
- **DAVID**: unnecessary RV pacing can worsen outcomes in some ICD patients, so avoid pacing the ventricle more than needed.
- **BLOCK-HF**: in AV block with reduced EF, biventricular pacing may outperform isolated RV pacing.
- **BRUISE CONTROL**: for CIED implantation, **uninterrupted warfarin** caused fewer pocket haematomas than heparin bridging in higher-thrombotic-risk patients.
- **AMBITION / SERAPHIN / GRIPHON / ZENITH / sotatercept studies**: modern PAH therapy is based on combination pathway treatment, and sotatercept adds a newer disease-modifying option in selected patients.
- Exam application: use these studies to explain **why** practice changed, not just to list acronyms.

> **Closing point:** Trial knowledge should clarify current pacing and PAH strategy, not replace physiology.

items.title: What advice matters after AF ablation?
items.q: What advice matters after AF ablation?
items.a:
- Continue OAC for at least 2 months under ESC 2024 (ACC/AHA 2023 at least 3), then by stroke risk.
- Delayed fever, dysphagia, chest pain or neurological symptoms may signal atrio-oesophageal fistula after thermal ablation.
- Urgent specialist review and contrast CT; avoid TOE/endoscopy when fistula is suspected.
- Review groin bleeding, tamponade symptoms and rhythm follow-up; apparent sinus rhythm does not automatically stop OAC.

> **Closing point:** Provide a clear anticoagulation and delayed-complication plan.

items.title: What must be handed over after a CIED procedure?
items.q: What must be handed over after a CIED procedure?
items.a:
- Actual device, dependence, programming/magnet changes and any events.
- Confirm tachy therapies/settings restored **before leaving monitoring**, with a named responsible clinician.
- Interrogate after reprogramming, external shocks, suspected malfunction or significant events according to the plan.
- Monitoring, emergency rescue, anticoagulant/drug plan and follow-up; CIED alone does not mandate ICU.

> **Closing point:** Never lose responsibility for an ICD that is still disabled.

items.title: Why is transvenous lead extraction an anaesthetic emergency risk?
items.q: Why is transvenous lead extraction an anaesthetic emergency risk?
items.a:
- Adherent chronic leads can tear SVC/heart, causing tamponade or massive haemothorax/bleeding.
### Preop

- expert centre, blood/access, immediate surgical/perfusion rescue, echo and pacing-dependence plan.
### Intraop

- monitor closely; sudden collapse needs urgent echo, resuscitation and surgical/balloon rescue rather than assuming anaesthetic hypotension.
### Postop

- monitor for delayed bleeding/tamponade, confirm pacing/device and infection-treatment plans.

> **Closing point:** Rescue capability must be present before extraction starts.

items.title: How does cardiac surgical arrest differ from routine ALS?
items.q: How does cardiac surgical arrest differ from routine ALS?
items.a:
- Use CALS-ANZ with a trained team; rapid rhythm confirmation and reversible-cause assessment.
- Witnessed monitored VF/pulseless VT may receive three stacked shocks; severe bradycardia/asystole may receive immediate epicardial pacing.
- Start CPR promptly if immediate treatment fails/is unavailable; arrange resternotomy within 5 minutes of arrest onset where indicated, including PEA/tamponade.
- This specialised pathway is for arrest after cardiac surgery, not a perfusing postoperative arrhythmia.

> **Closing point:** Prepare reopening and treat the arrest simultaneously.

items.title: 1. Catheter ablation of paroxysmal AF: anaesthetic plan
items.q: A 64-year-old man with symptomatic paroxysmal atrial fibrillation is booked for catheter ablation (pulmonary vein isolation). Outline the anaesthetic considerations and the complications you must watch for.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2021, "Atrial fibrillation, ablation, and the anaesthetist" (Maxwell, Potgieter, Bruessel).

## Why ablation

Pulmonary vein isolation uses radiofrequency, cryoballoon or **pulsed field ablation (PFA)** and improves symptoms/AF recurrence. **EAST-AFNET 4 tested early rhythm control (mostly drugs initially), not ablation alone**. **CABANA did not significantly reduce its primary death/disabling stroke/serious bleeding/cardiac arrest composite** on intention-to-treat analysis (8.0% vs 9.2%; HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.65–1.15; P=0.30); symptom and recurrence benefits must not be presented as a proven overall mortality benefit. Stroke prevention is based on thromboembolic risk, not apparent ablation success. [AF ablation consensus 2024](https://academic.oup.com/europace/article/26/4/euae043/7639428) [CABANA primary report](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6450284/)

## Preop

- Assess comorbidity (heart failure, OSA, obesity, renal function), **uninterrupted anticoagulation** (DOAC or warfarin), confirm anticoagulant adherence and whether thrombus-exclusion imaging (**TOE, appropriately timed delayed-phase CT or intracardiac echo**) is indicated by risk/protocol; imaging is not automatically required in every adequately anticoagulated low-risk patient, and electrolytes.
- The EP laboratory is a **remote location**: full anaesthetic equipment, suction, defibrillator, radiation protection and a clear plan for help. Pads on before the start.

## Intraop

- **GA with an endotracheal tube** is commonly selected, especially for prolonged RF mapping or airway risk, but deep/conscious sedation is also used successfully with suitable staff and monitoring: immobility is critical because small movements shift the 3D map, and sedation risks airway obstruction and coughing in a long case.
- Some centres use **jet ventilation or high-frequency, low-tidal-volume ventilation** to limit respiratory catheter movement. These are specialist techniques requiring CO2/airway-pressure surveillance; fixed tidal-volume/rate prescriptions are not transferable to every patient.
- Consider an arterial line according to risk and local workflow; capnography and haemodynamic surveillance are essential. **Oesophageal temperature monitoring** is used in some RF protocols but is not proven to prevent oesophageal injury and is not mandatory for all modalities. Track irrigant/IV volume and urine output; catheterisation is procedure-dependent. Maintain temperature. TOE guides transseptal puncture in some units.
- **Heparin before or immediately after transseptal access**, with ACT generally **at least 300 s** (often a 300–350/400 s institutional target); check frequently using the EP protocol. Protamine to facilitate haemostasis is an option, not obligatory in every case. Uninterrupted or minimally interrupted DOAC regimens follow the agreed evidence-based protocol; avoid unnecessary heparin bridging.
- **Cryoballoon:** phrenic nerve pacing is monitored, so avoid neuromuscular block.
- Cardioversion at the end if AF persists (synchronised).

## Complications — rates vary by modality, centre and population

| Complication | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Tamponade** | Hypotension, falling pulse pressure; echo, stop heparin and give protamine, pericardiocentesis, surgery |
| **Stroke or air embolism** | Anticoagulation, sheath flushing; supportive care and hyperbaric oxygen for air |
| **Oesophageal injury** (atrio-oesophageal fistula; delayed, days to weeks) | Fever, chest pain, neurological signs after discharge; avoid endoscopy and air insufflation; CT |
| **Pulmonary vein stenosis, phrenic palsy, vascular injury** | PV stenosis may present late; phrenic dysfunction may first be detected during ablation |
| **Large fluid load, pulmonary oedema** | Diuretic |

## Postop

Monitored recovery, ECG and groin/haemodynamic checks; overnight admission versus same-day discharge depends on protocol and risk. Continue OAC for **at least 2 months after ablation** under ESC 2024 (ACC/AHA 2023 specifies at least 3 months), then according to stroke risk. Give clear return advice for chest pain, dysphagia, fever or neurological symptoms: suspected atrio-oesophageal fistula requires urgent contrast CT/specialist surgical care; **avoid TOE and upper GI endoscopy** because insufflation/instrumentation may cause catastrophic embolism.

**PFA update:** nonthermal electroporation reduces collateral thermal injury but does not remove tamponade/embolism risks. Prepare for painful muscle/diaphragmatic contractions and modality-specific sedation needs; recognise **coronary spasm** and **haemolysis with AKI**, particularly with extensive applications. Monitor ECG, renal risk and dark urine as appropriate; hydration must be balanced against heart failure. [HRS/EHRA 2026](https://www.heartrhythmjournal.com/article/S1547-5271%2826%2900124-4/fulltext)

**Key evidence:** [BB21](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getcontentasset/381330f0-81cf-464d-a220-60a7da9dd1a0/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/blue-book_2021-version8.pdf?download=1&language=en) · [ABL](https://academic.oup.com/europace/article/26/4/euae043/7639428) · [PFA](https://www.heartrhythmjournal.com/article/S1547-5271%2826%2900124-4/fulltext) · [CABANA](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6450284/) · [EAST](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2019422)

## Self-marking checklist
- Distinguishes symptom/recurrence benefits from CABANA and early rhythm-control trial endpoints
- Assesses anticoagulation adherence, thrombus-imaging indications and remote-site rescue
- Selects GA or sedation with an airway/immobility and ventilation plan
- Uses risk-based monitoring and tracks irrigant/fluid balance
- Describes heparin timing, ACT ≥300 s and a protocol-based haemostasis plan
- Plans phrenic monitoring and suitable neuromuscular blockade for cryoablation
- Recognises tamponade, embolism and delayed fistula; avoids TOE/endoscopy for suspected fistula
- Recognises PFA coronary spasm and haemolysis/AKI and continues postoperative anticoagulation

items.title: 2. Fast AF with hypotension after surgery
items.q: A 72-year-old woman develops atrial fibrillation with a rate of 150 and a blood pressure of 85/50 two hours after a bowel resection. Outline your management and your long-term plan.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Anaesthesia for cardioversion" (2017); "Antiarrhythmic drugs and anaesthesia" parts 1 and 2 (2023 issue publication).

## Immediate assessment

AF is the commonest postoperative arrhythmia and is often a **symptom**. Assess ABCs, give oxygen, attach a monitor and obtain a 12-lead ECG. Establish whether she is **unstable** (hypotension, ischaemic chest pain, heart failure, reduced consciousness).

## Look for the trigger

Sepsis and anastomotic leak, **hypovolaemia and bleeding**, pain, hypoxia, **electrolyte deficiency (K, Mg, Ca; interpret units and renal function)**, pulmonary embolus, myocardial ischaemia, thyroid disease, drugs (catecholamines, beta-agonists), withdrawal of beta-blockers. Treat these in parallel with rhythm management. Establish whether AF is causing shock or compensating for another process: do not delay cardioversion when AF is driving instability.

## Unstable: synchronised DC cardioversion

- Sedate if conscious, apply pads (anterior-posterior), select **synchronise**, and give a biphasic shock at a manufacturer- and guideline-appropriate AF setting (often 200 J biphasic initially under contemporary AF protocols), escalating if required.
- If she is awake, cardioversion should not be delayed for fasting, and do not delay emergency cardioversion for TOE/anticoagulation; start anticoagulation as soon as appropriate after considering fresh surgical bleeding.
- **Amiodarone** (an AF regimen such as 300 mg IV over 30–60 minutes via a suitable vein, followed by 900–1200 mg/24 h according to protocol; monitor BP and QT) helps if cardioversion fails or AF recurs.

## Stable (or borderline)

- Correct volume, K and Mg, then **rate control**: beta-blocker (metoprolol or esmolol) if blood pressure allows; **digoxin** (slower onset, less effective in high adrenergic states, renal-adjusted) or carefully administered **amiodarone** in selected patients with LV dysfunction/limited alternatives; neither is a substitute for cardioversion in AF-driven shock, and IV amiodarone can worsen hypotension. Avoid verapamil or diltiazem when hypotensive or with poor LV function, and **avoid AV-nodal blockers including IV amiodarone in pre-excited AF**.
- Rhythm control with amiodarone, flecainide (no structural heart disease) or cardioversion using a rhythm- and stroke-risk-based plan; a reported onset within 48 hours is not blanket permission to cardiovert without anticoagulation assessment.

## Anticoagulation and follow-up

- Assess thromboembolic risk (**CHA2DS2-VA** in ESC 2024; CHA2DS2-VASc remains used in other guidance) and bleeding risk. **Do not wait automatically for 48 hours**. For non-emergency cardioversion with AF >24 h or uncertain duration, ESC 2024 advises ≥3 weeks of therapeutic OAC or TOE-guided exclusion of thrombus; generally ≥4 weeks of OAC afterwards, and longer by stroke risk. In the fresh postoperative patient, agree timing with the surgeon and cardiology. Anticoagulation during critical sepsis has uncertain benefit and needs individual assessment; recurrence and stroke-risk review remain necessary. [ESC AF 2024](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/45/36/3314/7738779)
- Echo, TSH, early review after discharge and reassessment by about 3 months, long-term anticoagulation by risk, and consider rhythm control or ablation if recurrent.

**Key evidence:** [AF](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/45/36/3314/7738779) · [AFUS](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11104284/) · [DRUG2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845544/)

## Self-marking checklist
- Assesses stability and looks for triggers (sepsis, bleeding, electrolytes, PE)
- Synchronised cardioversion for instability, with energy and sedation
- Amiodarone use and route
- Rate control choices appropriate to blood pressure and LV function
- Avoids AV node blockers in pre-excitation and verapamil when hypotensive
- Corrects K and Mg
- Assesses CHA2DS2-VASc and timing of anticoagulation against bleeding

items.title: 3. Antiarrhythmic drugs and their anaesthetic implications
items.q: Classify antiarrhythmic drugs and discuss the anaesthetic implications of amiodarone, beta-blockers, flecainide and digoxin.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Antiarrhythmic drugs and anaesthesia, parts 1 and 2" (2023 issue publication).

## Classification (modified Vaughan Williams)

| Class | Action | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | Sodium channel block | Ia procainamide, quinidine; Ib lidocaine, mexiletine; Ic flecainide |
| **II** | Beta-blockers | Metoprolol, esmolol, propranolol |
| **III** | Potassium channel block (prolong repolarisation) | Amiodarone, sotalol, ibutilide |
| **IV** | Calcium channel block | Verapamil, diltiazem |
| **Other** | | Adenosine, digoxin, magnesium, atropine |

## Anaesthetic implications

### Preop

Reconcile indication, dose, ECG/QTc/QRS, renal/liver function and electrolytes. Most established therapy is continued, with specialist review for toxicity or haemodynamic/conduction problems.

### Intraop

**Amiodarone** (class III with I, II and IV effects): long half-life (weeks), so effects persist. Prolongs QT; causes **bradycardia and hypotension at induction**, which may be resistant to atropine; interacts with other QT drugs; thyroid, pulmonary fibrosis and hepatic toxicity; **continue perioperatively**. IV amiodarone causes hypotension and phlebitis (central line).

**Beta-blockers:** continue (withdrawal causes rebound tachycardia and ischaemia). Do not start on the day of surgery (POISE). Expect bradycardia and hypotension; treat with glycopyrrolate, atropine, or in resistant cases glucagon and adrenaline. Esmolol is short-acting.

**Flecainide:** negative inotrope, **pro-arrhythmic** in structural heart disease or ischaemia; widens the QRS and raises pacing thresholds in pacemaker patients; toxicity (wide QRS, VT) is treated with resuscitation and **sodium bicarbonate** for sodium-channel blockade under toxicology advice; lipid emulsion is a rescue option in selected refractory cases, not routine co-treatment.

**Digoxin:** narrow therapeutic index; toxicity is worsened by **hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia**, renal impairment and amiodarone; look for bradyarrhythmia, atrial tachycardia with block, ventricular/bidirectional VT, GI/visual symptoms and, in acute major poisoning, **hyperkalaemia**. Avoid elective cardioversion in toxicity, but do not withhold a lifesaving shock for VF/unstable VT. **Digoxin-specific Fab** treats life-threatening toxicity; discuss severe hyperkalaemia with toxicology rather than teaching an absolute calcium prohibition. **Avoid digoxin in pre-excited AF**.

**Other points:** verapamil and diltiazem interact with beta-blockers (heart block) and potentiate neuromuscular block; adenosine is blocked by theophylline and potentiated by dipyridamole and may cause bronchospasm; check electrolytes and QTc.

### Postop

Resume the established regimen promptly, monitor after significant conduction/QT changes, and adjust digoxin/flecainide for renal dysfunction and interactions.

**Key evidence:** [DRUG1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9805968/) · [DRUG2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845544/) · [CAST](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1900101/) · [POISE](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18479744/)

## Self-marking checklist
- Classifies drugs correctly by class
- Amiodarone: long half-life, bradycardia, hypotension, QT, organ toxicity, continue
- Beta-blockers: continue and rebound risk, bradycardia treatment
- Flecainide: pro-arrhythmia, structural heart disease, bicarbonate for toxicity
- Digoxin: narrow window, electrolyte effects, avoid in pre-excitation, cardioversion risk
- Notes interactions (verapamil with beta-blockers, adenosine)
- Mentions electrolytes and QTc checks

items.title: 4. Brugada syndrome for inguinal hernia repair
items.q: Outline the anaesthetic management of a 38-year-old man with Brugada syndrome presenting for an inguinal hernia repair. How does this differ from arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC)?
items.a:
[BJA Education hereditary arrhythmias, parts 1 and 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7807910/) [LQTS/ARVC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7808061/)

## Brugada syndrome

A primary electrical disorder, sometimes associated with an SCN5A variant. A **type 1 pattern** has coved ST elevation ≥2 mm with T-wave inversion in V1/V2 (including high right-precordial positions). A pattern alone requires clinical interpretation and exclusion of phenocopies; not every asymptomatic pattern requires an ICD. VF risk is associated with arrhythmic syncope, previous arrest, fever and vagal predominance.

## Preop

- Clarify previous syncope/arrest, ICD therapies and specialist assessment. Review baseline ECG, potassium, calcium and magnesium, and all drugs against the specialist [Brugada drug resource](https://www.brugadadrugs.org/).
- Treat **fever promptly**; defer elective surgery with uncontrolled fever/arrhythmia. Discuss the plan with cardiology. Identify the safest local/GA technique for the patient and operation.
- If a CIED is present, use an **EMI-specific** plan. If tachy therapies must be suspended, apply external pads and continuous monitoring; ensure pacing requirements are addressed separately.

## Intraop

- Monitor ECG including right-precordial/ST changes where practical, pulse, temperature and routine anaesthetic variables. Avoid fever, marked bradycardia, vagal surges, electrolyte disorders and local-anaesthetic toxicity. Pneumoperitoneum/traction may be vagotonic.
- **Propofol induction boluses have been used safely**; prolonged/high-dose infusion has historically raised concern. Evidence is mainly observational, so weigh agent/duration and individual risk rather than declare every propofol dose contraindicated. Volatile techniques are established options. Etomidate is not proven universally safer and has also been associated with ST changes.
- Regional/neuraxial techniques can be used with careful dose/haemodynamic control. Prefer minimal effective local-anaesthetic exposure; short-acting lidocaine is often favoured over extensive bupivacaine exposure. Maintain perfusion and treat bradycardia: ephedrine, phenylephrine and anticholinergics have all been used; **do not teach a blanket ban on appropriate rescue drugs**. Titrate under ECG monitoring.
- Sugammadex avoids anticholinesterase-induced vagal effects; neostigmine with an anticholinergic has also been used cautiously. Avoid unnecessary sodium-channel blockers and check current drug advice.
- **VF/polymorphic VT: immediate unsynchronised defibrillation**, CPR if pulseless. Recurrent Brugada electrical storm needs urgent EP input, **isoprenaline** and often enteral **quinidine**; correct fever/triggers. Isoprenaline is not a substitute for an initial shock.

## Postop

Restore ICD therapies before leaving monitoring; maintain normothermia, electrolytes, analgesia and ECG surveillance. The 2018 BJA Education review recommends monitoring for **at least 36 hours** after anaesthesia; agree disposition/duration with the specialist according to phenotype, events and drug exposure rather than assuming routine unmonitored day discharge.

## How ARVC differs

ARVC is a structural arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, often desmosomal, with scar/fibrofatty change; it may involve both ventricles or be left dominant. VT often has LBBB morphology and is provoked by **exercise/sympathetic stimulation**, unlike the characteristic vagal/fever association in Brugada.

- **Preop:** assess arrhythmia burden and RV/LV function, continue beta-blockers/established antiarrhythmics and plan any ICD changes.
- **Intraop:** minimise sympathetic surges, abrupt preload/afterload changes and negative inotropy. Treat unstable VT electrically; amiodarone is an option for appropriate ventricular arrhythmias with specialist advice. Preserve RV perfusion; lifesaving catecholamines are not absolutely prohibited.
- **Postop:** continued monitoring appropriate to arrhythmia/ventricular risk, analgesia, drug resumption and confirmed ICD restoration.

**Key evidence:** [BRUGADA](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7807910/) · [LQTS](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7808061/)

## Self-marking checklist
- Recognises a type 1 Brugada pattern, phenotype/risk and fever/vagal triggers
- Reviews drugs, electrolytes, ICD status and specialist advice preoperatively
- Distinguishes propofol induction experience from prolonged infusion concerns
- Uses cautious local anaesthesia and treats hypotension/bradycardia rather than imposing blanket rescue-drug bans
- Defibrillates VF promptly and uses isoprenaline/quinidine for recurrent Brugada storm
- Plans postoperative monitoring and confirmed ICD restoration
- Contrasts structural/sympathetically triggered ARVC and its RV, beta-blocker and ICD considerations

items.title: 5. Eisenmenger syndrome for non-cardiac surgery
items.q: A 32-year-old woman with Eisenmenger syndrome (an unrepaired ventricular septal defect) requires an emergency laparoscopic appendicectomy. Outline the physiology and your perioperative management.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2021, "Anaesthetic considerations in the patient with Eisenmenger syndrome" (Toon, Graydon); Smith, "Pulmonary hypertension" (2015).

## Physiology

A large left-to-right shunt has caused pulmonary vascular remodelling (WHO group 1 PAH), so advanced pulmonary vascular disease produces **bidirectional/right-to-left shunting**, giving cyanosis, **secondary erythrocytosis**, hyperviscosity, iron deficiency, and risks of stroke, haemoptysis, endocarditis, arrhythmias and sudden death. The aim is to **preserve systemic perfusion/SVR and avoid acute rises in PVR**, and avoid anything that increases the shunt.

## Risks

Risk is high, especially with emergency surgery, infection, RV dysfunction and cyanosis; an old 30% estimate is not a universal prediction for modern non-cardiac surgery. Laparoscopy is a particular concern: pneumoperitoneum, CO2 (raising PVR), head-down tilt and reduced venous return.

## Preop

- **Transfer** to a centre with a congenital and PH service for elective work; for this emergency, resuscitate and seek urgent ACHD/PH/ICU advice; transfer if feasible without harmful delay, otherwise operate with the best available specialist-supported rescue plan.
- Continue PAH therapy (sildenafil, bosentan, prostanoids) without interruption.
- **Hydration:** minimise fasting and give IV fluid; avoid routine venesection: secondary erythrocytosis is adaptive. Specialist-directed isovolumic phlebotomy is reserved for persistent moderate/severe hyperviscosity, usually Hct >65%, after correcting dehydration and iron deficiency; Hb alone is not an indication. Check CBC/iron, platelets/coagulation and renal function; alert the laboratory if high Hct requires citrate adjustment.
- **Air filters on all IV lines** (paradoxical air embolism) and meticulous de-airing; give appropriate appendicitis/sepsis and surgical prophylactic antibiotics. Do not add blanket IE prophylaxis for every procedure solely because of Eisenmenger; follow local high-risk IE guidance and consider infected tissue/procedure type.
## Intraop

- Monitoring: arterial line before induction; CVC with caution (arrhythmias, infection); avoid PAC. Record the individual baseline saturation; a new fall requires assessment. Supplemental oxygen may help, but do not attempt to normalise a fixed shunt by injurious ventilation.
- **Technique:** avoid anything lowering SVR (large spinal or epidural boluses, volatile overdose, propofol bolus); GA with etomidate or ketamine, fentanyl, titrated and low-dose volatiles; **maintain SVR** with a titrated vasopressor, often noradrenaline or low-dose vasopressin in RV failure; phenylephrine can support SVR but may worsen PVR/bradycardia and requires context; avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia and pain, which raise PVR. Prefer **open surgery or low-pressure, short laparoscopy**.
- Arrhythmias are poorly tolerated: correct electrolytes and cardiovert early.
## Postop

- **ICU/HDU** for this high-risk emergency, with duration according to course, careful analgesia and ventilation, fluid/renal monitoring, continued PAH drugs and early recognition of RV failure. Individualise VTE/anticoagulant decisions because both thrombosis and bleeding risks are increased; therapeutic anticoagulation is not routine for all Eisenmenger patients.

**Key evidence:** [BB21](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getcontentasset/381330f0-81cf-464d-a220-60a7da9dd1a0/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/blue-book_2021-version8.pdf?download=1&language=en) · [ACHD](https://www.bjaed.org/article/S2058-5349%2825%2900066-6/pdf) · [PH](https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.00879-2022) · [IE](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/endocarditis/)

## Self-marking checklist
- Describes shunt reversal, cyanosis, erythrocytosis and risks
- States the aim: preserve systemic perfusion and avoid acute PVR rises
- Seeks expert advice and continues PAH therapy
- Meticulous de-airing/appropriate filters, surgical antibiotics and selective IE prophylaxis
- Arterial line and cautious central access, targeting baseline saturation
- Avoids drops in SVR; uses a context-appropriate vasopressor with awareness of PVR/heart-rate effects
- Avoids hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, and considers laparoscopy risk
- Plans ICU/HDU care

items.title: 6. Acute RV failure after pulmonary embolus
items.q: A patient develops acute right ventricular failure after a pulmonary embolus with hypotension and a CVP of 22. Explain the pathophysiology and outline your management.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2021, "Right ventricular failure – when the right heart goes wrong" (Falland et al.); Smith (2015).

## Pathophysiology

The thin-walled RV tolerates volume but not pressure. A sudden rise in PVR dilates the RV, which then (1) raises wall tension and oxygen demand, (2) reduces RV coronary flow, which depends on the **aortic–RV pressure gradient** and so is mainly diastolic at high RV pressure, (3) shifts the septum to the left (**ventricular interdependence**), reducing LV filling and cardiac output, and (4) provokes a vicious cycle of falling systemic pressure and RV ischaemia.

## Assessment

Clinical (raised JVP, hypotension, tricuspid regurgitation), ECG (right strain), echo (**dilated RV, D-shaped septum, TAPSE ≤17 mm and FAC ≤35% as supportive signs, with context; McConnell sign is not specific for PE**, TR jet), CVP, troponin, BNP, lactate. Identify the cause: PE, RV infarct, acute PH crisis, sepsis, positive pressure ventilation, volume overload.

## Management: treat the cause, then the RV

- **1.** **Maintain RV perfusion:** support systemic and RV coronary perfusion with **noradrenaline or carefully titrated low-dose vasopressin**. Individualise MAP according to systemic hypotension, RV/RA pressures and organ perfusion; do not treat “MAP above RV pressure” as a universally achievable numeric rule. Vasopressin has dose- and context-dependent effects, not guaranteed pulmonary neutrality.
- **2.** **Optimise preload:** the RV is often overfilled; a CVP of 22 suggests congestion but interpret with echo, ventilation and perfusion. Avoid reflex fluid loading; use a small challenge only when underfilling is plausible and reassess. **Diurese or ultrafilter** documented congestion while preserving perfusion, not simply because one CVP is elevated.
- **3.** **Reduce afterload:** avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia and acidosis; **inhaled nitric oxide or inhaled prostacyclin**; milrinone may reduce afterload and augment contractility but can cause systemic hypotension; oral sildenafil is not routine first-line rescue for shocked acute PE.
- **4.** **Improve contractility:** dobutamine or milrinone (with vasopressor).
- **5.** **Maintain sinus rhythm and AV synchrony:** cardiovert AF; pace if needed.
- **6.** **Ventilation:** use lung-protective tidal volume and individually titrated PEEP to balance recruitment against overdistension; avoid hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and high pressures. Intubation risks collapse but must not be withheld when necessary: use expert airway support with vasopressors/rescue ready.
- **7.** **Treat the cause:** urgent PE response/cardiothoracic/ICU review for **reperfusion** in PE with persistent hypotension: systemic thrombolysis, catheter intervention or surgical embolectomy according to bleeding risk, availability and urgency. Start appropriate anticoagulation unless contraindicated; recent surgery may alter the reperfusion choice. [2026 PE guideline](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2025.11.005); reperfusion for RV infarct.
- **8.** **Mechanical support:** **VA-ECMO** as a selected bridge to reperfusion/recovery; RVAD suitability depends on cause/afterload. **IABP is not routine effective support for isolated RV failure from severe pulmonary vascular obstruction**. Escalate before irreversible multiorgan failure.

**Key evidence:** [BB21](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getcontentasset/381330f0-81cf-464d-a220-60a7da9dd1a0/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/blue-book_2021-version8.pdf?download=1&language=en) · [RV](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13741-024-00397-5) · [PE](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2025.11.005) · [ASE](https://www.asecho.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/ASE-Right-Heart-Guidelines-May-2025.pdf)

## Self-marking checklist
- Explains RV pathophysiology: wall tension, coronary perfusion, interdependence
- Echo features of RV failure
- Treats the cause (PE, infarct, sepsis)
- Maintains perfusion pressure with vasopressor and avoids over-filling
- Reduces PVR (oxygen, avoid acidosis, inhaled vasodilators)
- Inotropes and keeps sinus rhythm
- Ventilation and mechanical support

items.title: 7. Pulmonary hypertensive crisis in a child under anaesthesia
items.q: A child with pulmonary hypertension becomes hypotensive and hypoxic after a surgical stimulus under anaesthesia. How do you recognise and manage a pulmonary hypertensive crisis?
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Smith, "Pulmonary hypertension" (2015). **BJA Education:** "Critical care management of pulmonary hypertension" (2017).

## Recognition

A sudden rise in PVR with RV failure, causing a **falling systolic pressure and end-tidal CO2**, hypoxia, rising CVP or PA pressure, arrhythmia, bradycardia and collapse. Triggers: hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia, pain or light anaesthesia, airway instrumentation, high airway pressure, catecholamine surges, tracheal suction and pneumoperitoneum.

## Principles

**Lower PVR, maintain SVR, restore cardiac output, remove the trigger.**

## Management

- **1.** **Call for help; 100% oxygen initially**, verify the airway/circuit and ventilation, correct hypoxaemia/hypercarbia and acidaemia. In a severe paediatric crisis, controlled short-term alkalinisation by ventilation or alkali can be a temporising measure while selective vasodilators arrive; do not impose PaCO2 30 mmHg or bicarbonate on every child, and avoid excessive airway pressure/overventilation, and ensure the circuit and tube are clear.
- **2.** Deepen anaesthesia and analgesia (opioid), and treat pain.
- **3.** **Inhaled pulmonary vasodilator:** nitric oxide 20 to 40 ppm (or inhaled prostacyclin / iloprost) first, because it is selective and does not lower SVR.
- **4.** **Maintain perfusion pressure** with noradrenaline or vasopressin, and use milrinone or dobutamine for low output.
- **5.** Maintain sinus rhythm; cardiovert arrhythmia.
- **6.** Treat the cause (obstruction, pneumothorax, bronchospasm, embolus).
- **7.** If refractory: **standard high-quality paediatric CPR immediately if arrest occurs**, with early **VA-ECMO/ECPR** activation when appropriate. Low pulmonary flow may make resuscitation difficult; this is not a reason to withhold compressions. IABP is not routine paediatric PH-crisis support. [AHA/AAP PALS 2025](https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/pediatric-advanced-life-support).

## Prevention

Pre-induction premedication, avoiding triggers, continuing PH drugs, and a plan for rescue (NO available before the case in a high-risk patient).

**Key evidence:** [PALS](https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/pediatric-advanced-life-support) · [PHOP](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36924225/)

## Self-marking checklist
- Recognises the crisis from physiological signs
- Lists triggers
- States the principle: lower PVR, maintain SVR, restore CO
- Gives oxygen, corrects ventilation/acidaemia and uses selective temporising alkalinisation when appropriate
- Uses inhaled nitric oxide or prostacyclin and a vasopressor
- Inotropes, treats cause, and cardiovert arrhythmia
- Starts standard CPR for arrest, considers ECMO early and explains prevention

items.title: 8. Fontan circulation for appendicectomy
items.q: A 20-year-old with a Fontan circulation presents for an appendicectomy. Describe the physiology and your anaesthetic management.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2021, "Anaesthesia for the adult patient with a Fontan circulation undergoing non-cardiac surgery". **BJA Education:** "Anaesthesia for non-cardiac surgery in adult congenital heart disease" (2025).

## Physiology

In a Fontan circulation (for single ventricle lesions, such as tricuspid atresia or hypoplastic left heart) systemic venous blood flows **passively** to the pulmonary arteries without a subpulmonary pump. Cardiac output depends on **low pulmonary vascular resistance, adequate systemic venous pressure/preload and good single-ventricle function with low filling pressure and effective rhythm**. Cardiac output reserve is limited, especially during stress; resting output and functional status vary, so not every well Fontan patient has a fixed low output.

## Risks

Arrhythmias (atrial, poorly tolerated), failing Fontan (protein-losing enteropathy, plastic bronchitis, ascites, liver disease), thromboembolism, cyanosis if there is a fenestration, and hepatic and renal dysfunction. A failing Fontan is a high-risk lesion: transfer to a specialist centre unless surgery is immediate.

## Preop

- Involve the congenital cardiology team; review the last echo, ECG, saturations and drugs (anticoagulants, diuretics, PAH agents); check for a **pacing system** (magnet response).
- **Fasting:** minimise and give IV fluid; maintain preload.
## Intraop

- **Monitoring:** arterial line; Fontan venous pressure is upstream pulmonary-circuit pressure, not a simple ventricular preload measurement; trend with perfusion/echo. Central access is only used if its benefit outweighs thrombosis and anatomical risks; select site/length using the actual surgical anatomy; avoid air in lines (fenestration). Prefer cautious fluids and avoid hypovolaemia.
- **Ventilation:** effective spontaneous breathing often assists Fontan pulmonary flow, but airway obstruction, respiratory fatigue and hypercarbia may outweigh that benefit, and requires an appropriate airway/ventilation strategy. If IPPV is needed, use **low mean airway pressure**, short inspiratory time, PEEP sufficient to avoid atelectasis without overdistension, avoid hypercarbia and hypoxia, and extubate early.
- Avoid large falls in SVR and negative inotropy (volatile overdose); phenylephrine or vasopressin; avoid increases in PVR (pain, acidosis, nitrous oxide).
- **Laparoscopy:** pneumoperitoneum reduces venous return and raises PVR, so discuss open versus carefully controlled laparoscopy; use the lowest workable pressure with haemodynamic/ventilation surveillance. No single pressure is guaranteed safe for all Fontan patients.
- **Arrhythmia:** treat urgently, with cardioversion early.
## Postop

- Monitored recovery/HDU appropriate to this operation and Fontan status; resume the agreed antithrombotic plan, PAH/heart drugs and careful fluid balance. Optimise analgesia, ventilation and early mobilisation; watch for arrhythmia, venous congestion and low output.

**Key evidence:** [BB21](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getcontentasset/381330f0-81cf-464d-a220-60a7da9dd1a0/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/blue-book_2021-version8.pdf?download=1&language=en) · [ACHD](https://www.bjaed.org/article/S2058-5349%2825%2900066-6/pdf) · [ACHD25](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001402)

## Self-marking checklist
- Describes passive pulmonary flow and the determinants of Fontan output
- Lists risks including a failing Fontan and arrhythmias
- Involves specialist team and considers transfer
- Preserves preload and monitors invasively
- Prefers spontaneous ventilation, and low mean airway pressure when ventilated
- Limits laparoscopy and avoids rises in PVR or falls in SVR
- Treats arrhythmia promptly, with HDU and thromboprophylaxis

items.title: 9. Regular narrow-complex tachycardia during laparoscopy
items.q: During a laparoscopic cholecystectomy a healthy 40-year-old develops a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 beats per minute with a blood pressure of 90/50. Outline your diagnosis and management.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Antiarrhythmic drugs and anaesthesia" (2023); "Anaesthesia for cardioversion" (2017).

## Diagnosis

A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190: most likely **AVNRT or AVRT** (accessory pathway); consider atrial flutter with 2:1 block (about 150), sinus tachycardia (rate alone does not exclude it; seek and treat the cause), atrial tachycardia. Confirm with a 12-lead if time allows.

Exclude causes that need treatment: **light anaesthesia and pain, hypercarbia (pneumoperitoneum), hypovolaemia, bleeding, malignant hyperthermia, thyrotoxicosis, drugs (ephedrine, adrenaline, pancuronium), hypoxia**. Tell the surgeon, **stop insufflation**, increase oxygen and deepen anaesthesia.

## Management by stability

**Unstable (hypotension, ischaemia, heart failure):** synchronised **DC cardioversion** (rhythm/device-specific energy, often 50–100 J for regular narrow-complex re-entry, escalating) under anaesthesia, which is already established.

**Stable or borderline:**
- **1.** **Vagal manoeuvres** are limited under GA (a carefully selected manoeuvre may be attempted if stable; avoid routine carotid massage or prolonged positive-pressure inflation in a hypotensive patient).
- **2.** **Adenosine** 6 mg rapid IV push into a large vein with a flush, then 12 mg (repeat 12 mg if needed under ANZCOR) if needed; warn of transient asystole, bronchospasm, and check interactions with dipyridamole or theophylline and the risk of significant bronchospasm. Reduce the initial dose when given centrally or in a transplanted heart according to protocol, and **pads on**.
- **3.** If adenosine fails or is contraindicated (asthma): **beta-blocker (esmolol) or verapamil/diltiazem**, once pre-excited AF is excluded, after checking BP/LV function and rhythm diagnosis. **Regular narrow orthodromic AVRT can respond appropriately to adenosine even in WPW; the dangerous exception is pre-excited AF**, not every accessory-pathway tachycardia.
- **4.** For AF with pre-excitation (broad irregular tachycardia): **cardiovert, or procainamide**; avoid AV-nodal blockers **including IV amiodarone**, digoxin, verapamil/diltiazem, beta-blockers and adenosine.

## After

Correct triggers, check electrolytes, 12-lead ECG after conversion, review for pre-excitation, and arrange cardiology and electrophysiology referral (ablation).

**Key evidence:** [ALS](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias) · [DRUG2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845544/) · [AFUS](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11104284/)

## Self-marking checklist
- Differentiates SVT mechanism and sinus tachycardia, with a differential diagnosis for intraoperative causes
- Removes triggers and stops insufflation
- Uses synchronised cardioversion for instability
- Adenosine dose, route and warnings
- Alternatives (beta-blocker, calcium channel blockers) and their caveats
- Recognises pre-excited AF and avoids AV nodal blockers
- Arranges follow-up and EP review

items.title: 10. Broad-complex tachycardia after cardiac surgery
items.q: A 60-year-old man with an ischaemic cardiomyopathy has a broad-complex tachycardia at 170 in the post-anaesthesia care unit. Outline your management.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death" (2017); "Antiarrhythmic drugs and anaesthesia" (2023).

## Approach

Broad-complex tachycardia is **VT until proven otherwise**, particularly with structural heart disease. Do not give verapamil or diltiazem. Check for a pulse and ABCs, call for help, oxygen, monitor, pads and a 12-lead ECG.

## Pulseless

VT without a pulse is **ALS**: CPR, immediate unsynchronised defibrillation, adrenaline and amiodarone as in VF.

## Pulse present, unstable (shock, ischaemic pain, heart failure, reduced consciousness)

For **monomorphic VT**, synchronised DC cardioversion using device/rhythm-appropriate energy (often 100–150 J initially), with sedation if feasible and no delay for shock. Recurrent/refractory VT may need **amiodarone by a controlled infusion**, with dose/rate set by the VT protocol and BP, rather than an automatic arrest-dose IV push. **Sustained polymorphic VT cannot be reliably synchronised: deliver an unsynchronised shock even if a pulse is present.**

## Pulse present, stable

- **Amiodarone** a monitored VT loading regimen (for example 300 mg IV over 20–60 minutes under the local protocol; avoid rapid administration in hypotension) (central line preferably) then 900 mg over 24 hours; or **lidocaine** 1 to 1.5 mg/kg (ischaemic VT); **procainamide**; avoid combining negative inotropes in LV failure.
- Correct hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia with renal-aware replacement; selected long-QT patients may have a high-normal potassium target, not a universal supra-normal target; treat ischaemia and hypoxia; review drugs prolonging QT.
- If **polymorphic with a prolonged QT (torsades)**: IV magnesium using the selected TdP protocol (ANZCOR 5 mmol over 10 min; other protocols MgSO4 2 g ≈8 mmol), correct K, overdrive pacing, isoprenaline only for selected **acquired** pause-dependent torsades under expert advice, not routine congenital LQTS, avoid amiodarone.

## ICD patient with storm

Repeated shocks: sedation and analgesia, amiodarone plus beta-blocker (esmolol or propranolol), **deep sedation or GA**, and urgent electrophysiology (ablation, stellate ganglion block); review stored electrograms and ICD programming urgently. Inappropriate shocks require temporary therapy suspension with external defibrillation immediately available. Repetitive appropriate shocks may also be reduced through expert reprogramming/ATP while actively treating VT, with external rescue and continuous monitoring. [EHRA storm consensus 2024](https://doi.org/10.1093/europace/euae049).

## Afterwards

ICU or CCU, ECG, echo, troponin, coronary assessment, electrolytes, and review for an ICD.

**Key evidence:** [ALS](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias) · [DRUG2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845544/) · [STORM](https://doi.org/10.1093/europace/euae049)

## Self-marking checklist
- Treats broad-complex tachycardia as VT and avoids calcium channel blockers
- Pulseless VT as ALS
- Synchronises unstable monomorphic VT; shocks sustained polymorphic VT unsynchronised even with a pulse
- Amiodarone or lidocaine for stable VT, with doses
- Corrects K and Mg and treats ischaemia
- Torsades: magnesium, pacing, avoid amiodarone
- Plans ICD storm management and follow-up

items.title: 11. Elective DC cardioversion for persistent AF
items.q: A 68-year-old man with persistent atrial fibrillation is booked for elective DC cardioversion. Outline the anaesthetic considerations.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Anaesthesia for cardioversion" (2017).

## Preop

- **Anticoagulation is essential:** at least 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation before, or a **TOE** to exclude left atrial thrombus; continue for at least 4 weeks after, and indefinitely by CHA2DS2-VASc. ESC 2024 uses **>24 hours or unknown duration** as the threshold for this non-emergency safety pathway; a short duration does not eliminate risk. Use CHA2DS2-VA (or the locally adopted score) for longer-term therapy. [ESC AF 2024](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/45/36/3314/7738779)
- Assess heart failure, LV function, thyroid function, electrolytes (correct K/Mg/Ca deficits and account for renal function), **digoxin toxicity** (defer elective cardioversion and treat toxicity; emergency lifesaving shocks are still indicated), and drugs (amiodarone loading improves success).
- Fasting as for GA, consent for a repeat shock and the risk of failure, embolism and arrhythmia.
- Location: resuscitation equipment, suction, airway equipment, a working defibrillator.

## Intraop

- Monitoring: ECG, SpO2, NIBP, capnography.
- **Short GA:** preoxygenate; **propofol** (titrated, 0.5 to 1 mg/kg) or etomidate for cardiovascular stability, with a short-acting opioid; maintain the airway with a mask. In reflux or full stomach, intubate.
- **Pads** anterior–posterior or anterolateral according to device, patient and protocol; good pad contact and current vector matter, and AP is not universally superior, and **synchronise**, checking the marker sits on the R wave.
- **Biphasic** shock at an appropriate AF energy (often 200 J initially, or the validated manufacturer/local setting; higher initial energy may improve success), escalating after failed shocks; if shocks fail, change pad position, improve pad contact using an approved insulated pressure technique if trained; never apply unprotected hand pressure during shock, and consider amiodarone or ibutilide.
- Be ready to treat **bradycardia (atropine)**, post-shock VF (unsynchronise), hypotension and aspiration.

## Complications

Skin burns, embolism, VF, bradycardia and sinus arrest (pacing), pulmonary oedema, transient myocardial stunning, and pacing-threshold changes in pacemaker patients (use pads away from the device).

## Postop

Observe until fully awake, 12-lead ECG, continue anticoagulation, and plan rate and rhythm therapy.

**Key evidence:** [AF](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/45/36/3314/7738779) · [AFUS](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11104284/)

## Self-marking checklist
- Anticoagulation before and after, or TOE
- Checks electrolytes, digoxin and thyroid
- Describes short GA with haemodynamically stable drugs
- Pad position and synchronisation on the R wave
- Biphasic energy and escalation
- Prepares for bradycardia, VF, hypotension
- Follow-up and continued anticoagulation

items.title: 12. Pulmonary arterial hypertension in late pregnancy: delivery
items.q: A 29-year-old woman at 36 weeks with pulmonary arterial hypertension is to be delivered. Discuss the risks and your anaesthetic plan.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Pulmonary arterial hypertension in pregnancy" (2023 issue; online 2022). **Blue Book:** Smith (2015); Toon, Graydon (2021).

## Risks

PAH is a **very high-risk pregnancy condition (mWHO IV)**, requiring explicit counselling against pregnancy and shared decision-making; not only severe pressure elevation carries risk. ESC 2025 reports contemporary maternal mortality **11–25%** across cited series, with marked variation by phenotype and RV status and highest in the **first weeks after delivery**. Physiology works against the RV: blood volume rises 40 to 50%, cardiac output rises, SVR falls, hypercoagulability, and the peripartum period brings autotransfusion with uterine contraction, pain, bleeding and fluid shifts.

## Preop — planning

- Multidisciplinary team (obstetrics, PH cardiology, anaesthesia, ICU) at a **tertiary centre**; individualised mode/timing of delivery, often a planned caesarean for controlled conditions, with a written haemodynamic/haemorrhage/rescue plan. **34–36 weeks is not a mandatory target**; at 36 weeks assess maternal trajectory and fetal factors without harmful delay. Continue PAH therapy (sildenafil, inhaled or IV prostanoids); avoid **endothelin receptor antagonists, riociguat and selexipag** during pregnancy per ESC 2025; avoid sotatercept because of fetal harm risk. Anticoagulation is indication-specific, not automatic for every PAH patient; when required, coordinate LMWH interruption (therapeutic dosing generally ≥24 hours before planned delivery/neuraxial intervention) and local neuraxial guidance.
- Pre-op echo, BNP, risk stratification, arterial line, and a plan for ICU or HDU for at least 48 to 72 hours.

## Intraop — delivery and anaesthesia

- **Aim:** maintain SVR and RV coronary perfusion, avoid increases in PVR, and keep preload.
- **Neuraxial:** a slowly titrated **epidural or combined spinal-epidural** (or low-dose, slow CSE) is favoured; single-shot spinal causes abrupt SVR fall and is avoided. GA reserved for emergencies or contraindications, but is high risk (induction hypotension, positive pressure ventilation).
- Arterial line before; central line with caution; avoid PAC.
- **Drugs:** vasopressor (phenylephrine or noradrenaline) ready; **avoid ergometrine and carboprost** (raise PVR); give oxytocin slowly in small boluses or an infusion (it lowers SVR and raises PVR). Consider **inhaled nitric oxide or prostacyclin** in the theatre.
- Tranexamic acid, cell salvage, and avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, pain and shivering.

## Postop — postpartum

ICU monitoring during delivery and postpartum, with duration individualised; **risk persists for many weeks to months**, so discharge at 72 hours does not end surveillance. [ESC pregnancy 2025](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/46/43/4462/8234487) continue PAH therapy; thromboprophylaxis; avoid fluid overload; contraception and counselling.

**Key evidence:** [BJAPREG](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9805939/) · [PREG](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/46/43/4462/8234487) · [PH](https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.00879-2022)

## Self-marking checklist
- Explains why pregnancy and the postpartum period are high risk
- Plans MDT and delivery timing; continues PAH therapy and avoids teratogens
- Chooses a titrated neuraxial technique and avoids single-shot spinal
- Arterial line and cautious central access
- Avoids ergometrine and carboprost and gives oxytocin cautiously
- Prepares inhaled pulmonary vasodilators and vasopressors
- Plans ICU care and contraception

items.title: 13. Bradycardia and hypotension after spinal anaesthesia
items.q: A patient develops a heart rate of 35 with hypotension 15 minutes after induction of spinal anaesthesia. Outline your assessment and management of perioperative bradycardia, including advanced AV block.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Perioperative management of CIEDs" (2016); ALS bradycardia algorithm.

## Immediate

Call for help, confirm a pulse, give 100% oxygen, and check the airway and breathing. **Treat the cause**: in a spinal, the Bezold–Jarisch reflex, a high block with cardiac accelerator block (T1 to T4) and vagal predominance. **Stop the surgical stimulus** (peritoneal traction, laparoscopic insufflation, eye or cervical traction), optimise venous return (supine/leg elevation; left uterine displacement if pregnant), assess block height and respiratory muscle weakness, and support ventilation/intubate for high spinal when needed, and give a **fluid bolus**.

## Look for causes

Vagal reflexes, a high neuraxial block, hypoxia, hypercarbia, hypothermia, hypothyroidism, raised ICP (Cushing), **drugs** (opioids, neostigmine, dexmedetomidine, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, amiodarone, suxamethonium in children), **myocardial infarction** (inferior), hyperkalaemia, pacemaker failure, and AV block (first, second Mobitz 1 or 2, and third degree).

## Drugs

- **1.** **Atropine** **500–600 micrograms IV** (ANZCOR), repeat every 3 to 5 minutes to 3 mg (low doses cause paradoxical slowing). Glycopyrrolate is slower and does not cross the blood–brain barrier.
- **2.** **Vasopressors with chronotropy:** ephedrine 5 to 15 mg, then **adrenaline** (10 to 100 mcg boluses, or 2 to 10 mcg/min infusion), or dopamine; **isoprenaline** when other measures fail (not in ischaemia).
- **3.** Suspected drug **toxicity**, not merely chronic use: toxicology consultation. Beta-blocker poisoning may need glucagon and high-dose insulin euglycaemia; calcium-channel-blocker poisoning may need calcium and high-dose insulin with glucose/K monitoring, alongside vasopressors. Avoid atropine in a transplanted heart where paradoxical high-grade block can occur; seek pacing/adrenergic support. [ANZCOR 11.9](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias)

## Pacing

**Transcutaneous pacing** at once if drugs fail or the rhythm is **Mobitz 2, complete heart block or asystole risk** (pads, rate 70 to 80, increase current until capture and check a mechanical pulse), with sedation for awake patients. Then **transvenous pacing** and a cardiology referral for a permanent pacemaker. Treat asystole by ALS.

## After

12-lead ECG, troponin, electrolytes, echo, monitored bed, and avoid precipitating drugs.

**Key evidence:** [ALS](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias) · [BRADY](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000628)

## Self-marking checklist
- Calls for help, removes the stimulus, flat position and fluid
- Lists causes including neuraxial block and vagal reflexes
- Atropine dose and limits; ephedrine, adrenaline, isoprenaline
- Distinguishes drug toxicity from chronic treatment and seeks appropriate toxicology-directed therapy
- Describes transcutaneous pacing technique and checking capture
- Plans transvenous pacing and cardiology review
- Investigations and monitored bed

items.title: 14. Tetralogy of Fallot and large left-to-right shunts
items.q: Describe the physiology of tetralogy of Fallot and of a large left-to-right shunt, and outline the anaesthetic implications of each for non-cardiac surgery.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Tetralogy of Fallot" (2019); "Anaesthesia for non-cardiac surgery in adult congenital heart disease" (2025).

## Tetralogy of Fallot (unrepaired)

Four features: **VSD, RV outflow obstruction (pulmonary stenosis), overriding aorta, RV hypertrophy**. Blood shunts right to left through the VSD according to the balance of SVR and the RVOT obstruction, causing cyanosis. **Tet spells** (hypoxic spells) occur with falls in SVR, rises in PVR or RVOT spasm from catecholamines, crying and dehydration.

**Anaesthesia:** keep SVR up and PVR down; avoid hypovolaemia, tachycardia and catecholamines; avoid agents that fall SVR. Treat a spell with **oxygen, flexed knees, fluid, phenylephrine, morphine, beta-blocker (esmolol) and correction of significant acidaemia** (bicarbonate only if indicated, not routine); ketamine is preferred over a big propofol dose. Ventilate with a low mean airway pressure.

## Repaired ToF (the usual adult patient)

Residual lesions include **pulmonary regurgitation with RV dilatation, RVOT obstruction, residual VSD, arrhythmia (atrial and ventricular), and RV failure**. They have risks of sudden cardiac death, a wide QRS (above 180 ms is high risk), and endocarditis. The ACHD classification is anatomical complexity (simple, moderate, great) plus physiological stage A to D, so repaired ToF may be IIA or IIC.

**Anaesthesia:** specialist review and recent echo, avoid increasing PVR, maintain preload and sinus rhythm, a defibrillator, and treat arrhythmia early.

## Large left-to-right shunt (VSD, ASD, PDA)

Excess pulmonary blood flow causes pulmonary overload and, in time, PH and Eisenmenger syndrome. **Anaesthesia:** avoid anything that lowers PVR excessively (which increases the shunt) or raises SVR sharply (also increases the shunt); the aim is a balance, titrate FiO2 to adequate oxygenation; avoid unnecessary hyperoxia/hypocapnia that markedly increases pulmonary overcirculation, but **never withhold needed oxygen**. meticulous de-airing; use appropriate **air-eliminating filters when right-to-left/bidirectional flow or transient reversal is possible**, without compromising required rapid resuscitation flow, endocarditis prophylaxis when indicated, and treatment of heart failure.

## Preop

Define unrepaired versus repaired anatomy, residual shunts/obstruction, saturation, ventricular function, arrhythmia burden and PH with the ACHD team. Review drugs, antithrombotics and an appropriate location; treat dehydration/iron deficiency/heart failure as indicated.

## Intraop

Use the lesion-specific goals above: avoid SVR collapse/dynamic RVOT obstruction in unrepaired ToF; balance systemic perfusion and pulmonary flow in a large L–R shunt. ASD usually volume-loads the **RV**, whereas a large VSD/PDA generally volume-loads the **LV** through excess pulmonary venous return. Monitor/rescue according to physiological risk, with careful de-airing and ventilation.

## Postop

Monitor saturation against baseline, rhythm and perfusion; provide analgesia, adequate ventilation, careful fluids and early resumption of the specialist regimen. Higher-risk physiology/major surgery warrants HDU/ICU; investigate new desaturation, low output or arrhythmia.

**Key evidence:** [ACHD](https://www.bjaed.org/article/S2058-5349%2825%2900066-6/pdf) · [ACHD25](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001402) · [IE](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/endocarditis/)

## Self-marking checklist
- Describes the four features and shunt direction in ToF
- Recognises and treats a tet spell
- Residual lesions and arrhythmia risk in repaired ToF
- Uses anatomical and physiological classification
- Large left-to-right shunt physiology and effect of changes in SVR and PVR
- Air filters and endocarditis considerations
- Specialist review and monitoring

items.title: 15. Severe hypoxia after induction in congenital heart disease
items.q: A patient with congenital heart disease becomes severely hypoxic soon after induction of anaesthesia. Discuss the differential diagnosis and management of increased right-to-left shunting.
items.a:
This is a high-priority rescue scenario. The key question is whether the patient has developed **or worsened a right-to-left shunt** because right atrial pressure now exceeds left atrial pressure, or whether another cause of hypoxaemia is masquerading as shunt physiology.

## Why it happens

A right-to-left shunt may occur through a known lesion (e.g. Eisenmenger physiology, unrepaired tetralogy, Fontan fenestration) or across a **previously functionally closed PFO/ASD** when **right atrial pressure rises above left atrial pressure** (for example, from increased RV afterload or reduced left-sided filling pressure).

## Differential diagnosis

- **Increased PVR / RV afterload:** hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis, pain/sympathetic surge, high airway pressures/PEEP, pulmonary hypertensive crisis, pulmonary embolism.
- **Reduced SVR:** induction-related vasodilation, neuraxial sympathectomy, sepsis, anaphylaxis.
- **RV failure / raised RA pressure:** RV infarction/failure, acute PH crisis, tamponade, tension physiology.
- **Preload problems:** hypovolaemia, excessive positive-pressure ventilation reducing venous return.
- **Other causes of desaturation to exclude quickly:** endobronchial intubation, circuit/oxygen failure, bronchospasm, aspiration, atelectasis, pneumothorax.
- **Paradoxical air or particulate embolism** is a special risk in patients with R→L shunts.

## Immediate management

- **1.** **Call for help** and give **100% oxygen**.
- **2.** Check the airway, tube position, ventilation, circuit and lungs; treat common reversible causes of hypoxaemia in parallel.
- **3.** Ask: is the patient losing SVR, gaining PVR, or both?

## Specific shunt-directed management

### Reduce PVR

- Treat **hypoxia, hypercapnia and acidosis**.
- Avoid excessive PEEP, high plateau pressures and hyperinflation.
- Deepen anaesthesia/analgesia appropriately to blunt surges.
- Consider **inhaled pulmonary vasodilator** (nitric oxide or inhaled prostacyclin) if PH/RV crisis is suspected.

### Support SVR and coronary perfusion

- Treat vasodilation promptly with **vasopressors**, commonly **noradrenaline** or **vasopressin**; phenylephrine may help selected patients where pure vasoconstriction is desirable.
- Avoid large drops in SVR, which can increase right-to-left shunting.

### Optimise preload and RV function

- Give a **small assessed fluid challenge** only if underfilled; avoid reflexive fluid loading of a distended RV.
- Support the RV with inotrope/vasopressor therapy if needed (e.g. noradrenaline ± dobutamine/milrinone depending on blood pressure and RV performance).

### Investigate the mechanism

- Use **arterial line/ABG** and consider urgent **TTE/TOE** to assess RV size/function, septal shift, shunt flow and tamponade.
- De-air all infusions and injection ports meticulously.

## Practical anaesthetic points

- Keep the patient warm, well oxygenated and haemodynamically supported.
- Avoid sudden changes in intrathoracic pressure or prolonged apnoea.
- Individualise whether to continue, postpone or abort surgery once the patient is stabilised.

**Key evidence:** [ACHD](https://www.bjaed.org/article/S2058-5349%2825%2900066-6/pdf) · [RV](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13741-024-00397-5) · [PH](https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.00879-2022)

## Self-marking checklist
- Explains that worsening right-to-left shunting follows raised right-sided pressure and/or reduced left-sided pressure
- Gives a differential including increased PVR, reduced SVR, RV failure and common non-shunt causes of hypoxaemia
- Starts immediate rescue with 100% oxygen and basic airway/circuit checks
- Describes how to reduce PVR (treat hypoxia/hypercapnia/acidosis and reduce injurious airway pressure)
- Supports SVR and avoids large vasodilatory drops
- Uses careful, assessed fluid and RV support rather than reflexive fluid loading
- Mentions urgent echo/ABG assessment and meticulous de-airing

items.title: 16. Arrhythmias after cardiac surgery in the ICU
items.q: Outline the common arrhythmias after cardiac surgery, their causes and your management of them in the first 48 hours.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Antiarrhythmic drugs and anaesthesia" (2023); "Anaesthesia for cardioversion" (2017). **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2021, RV dysfunction after CPB.

## Common arrhythmias and why

- **Atrial fibrillation or flutter (about 30%, peaking days 2 to 3):** inflammation, atrial stretch, pericarditis, electrolyte disturbance, catecholamines, beta-blocker withdrawal.
- **Ventricular ectopy, VT and VF:** ischaemia, graft occlusion, electrolytes, catecholamines, reperfusion.
- **Bradycardia and AV block:** conduction injury (valve surgery, particularly aortic and mitral), cardioplegia, drugs, oedema; usually transient.
- **Junctional rhythm** and SVT.

## General approach

- Confirm on a 12-lead ECG, with **atrial wire electrogram** if needed to distinguish flutter and junctional rhythm.
- Correct electrolyte deficits with renal-aware replacement and monitor serially; routine high potassium targets are not required in every postoperative patient, oxygenation, pain, tamponade and bleeding, and stop proarrhythmic infusions.

## Treatment

- **Unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse:** synchronise for AF/flutter/monomorphic VT; unsynchronised shock for sustained polymorphic VT. **Arrest after cardiac surgery:** use the local **CALS-ANZ** protocol with a trained team. Witnessed monitored VF/pulseless VT may receive **three rapid stacked shocks**; severe bradycardia/asystole may receive immediate epicardial pacing. Do not delay CPR when these immediate measures fail or are unavailable. Prepare **resternotomy within 5 minutes of arrest onset**, including PEA/tamponade—not only after three shocks. Do not apply resternotomy instructions to a perfusing arrhythmia. [ANZCOR 11.10](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-10-resuscitation-in-special-circumstances)
- **AF:** beta-blocker if stable; **amiodarone** (rate and rhythm); digoxin for rate control in heart failure; atrial overdrive pacing for flutter via epicardial wires. Review stroke and fresh surgical bleeding risks with the surgical team; postoperative AF may warrant a time-limited anticoagulation course once safe and reassessment for longer therapy/recurrence. Do not automatically defer all decisions until 48 hours.
- **Bradycardia and block:** **epicardial pacing** (AAI, VVI or DDD), with threshold checks daily; atropine or isoprenaline short term. Persistent high-grade block needs daily cardiology/device review; permanent-pacing timing is individualised by operation, recovery likelihood, escape rhythm and safety (often an observation period of several days, not an automatic day-7 rule).
- **VT:** amiodarone, treat ischaemia (angiography), and electrolytes.

**Key evidence:** [CALS](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-10-resuscitation-in-special-circumstances) · [TEMP](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10433321/) · [AFUS](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11104284/)

## Self-marking checklist
- Lists the arrhythmias and their causes
- Corrects electrolytes and looks for tamponade, ischaemia, bleeding
- Uses rhythm-appropriate shocks and the CALS-ANZ pathway for cardiac surgical arrest
- AF treatment with amiodarone, beta-blocker, overdrive pacing, and anticoagulation
- Epicardial pacing and threshold checks
- Treats VT with amiodarone and assesses for ischaemia
- Sees when a permanent pacemaker is needed

items.title: 17. Complete heart block after aortic valve replacement
items.q: A patient develops symptomatic complete heart block after aortic valve replacement and has temporary epicardial pacing wires. Describe how you would set up and programme an external pacemaker, and how you would troubleshoot failure to capture.
items.a:
[BJA Education: Temporary epicardial pacing after cardiac surgery, 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10433321/)

## Types of temporary pacing

Transcutaneous, transvenous and epicardial pacing are the principal rescue options; transoesophageal pacing mainly stimulates the atrium and is not reliable ventricular rescue for complete AV block.

## Set-up for this patient

- **1.** **Assess ABCs and perfusion**, call the cardiac surgical/ICU team, attach ECG and a pulse-based monitor, and have external pacing/defibrillation ready. Symptomatic complete block needs effective **ventricular** pacing; AAI cannot bridge AV block.
- **2.** Check the generator battery, correct leads/cables, labelled atrial/ventricular wire pairs, connector security, insulation and manufacturer instructions. **Bipolar epicardial wires have both poles in the myocardium**. A unipolar system needs a dedicated return electrode—often subcutaneous—not an assumed ordinary surface ECG electrode. Do not improvise the connection or touch exposed conductors (microshock risk).
- **3.** Select **VVI** for ventricular rescue if only ventricular wires, AF or unreliable atrial sensing. **DDD** can preserve AV synchrony with reliable atrial/ventricular wires in sinus rhythm. AAI is only suitable when AV conduction is intact. Avoid unmonitored asynchronous pacing because of competitive R-on-T risk; reserve DOO/VOO for a specific indication with continuous observation.
- **4.** Set a rate suitable for perfusion (often 70–90/min initially after adult cardiac surgery, then titrate). In urgent failure, increase output sufficiently to achieve capture; once stable establish the capture threshold safely. Set **output generally at least twice the measured threshold**, within generator limits. Rate/output/sensing values are patient-specific, not guaranteed by a default setting.
- **5.** For dual-chamber pacing, set AV delay (often around 150–200 ms initially, then optimise clinically) and both atrial/ventricular output and sensitivity. Confirm **electrical and mechanical capture**, not simply pacing spikes.

## Threshold and sensing checks

- Perform checks only with trained staff, continuous monitoring and an immediately available rescue plan. **Do not deliberately lose capture in an unprotected pacing-dependent patient**. Test according to the local protocol, with backup pacing where required.
- Capture threshold is the lowest output producing consistent depolarisation; a rising threshold prompts review of wires, temperature, electrolytes and myocardium. A threshold >10 mA is concerning and requires an urgent reliable alternative rather than accepting a small safety margin.
- Sensing threshold is the smallest intrinsic signal reliably detected. If no intrinsic rhythm exists, it cannot be safely measured in the usual way. Sensitivity is expressed in **mV: lower number = more sensitive**. A common programmed margin is about half the measured sensing threshold, while avoiding oversensing; follow the generator-specific protocol.

## Failure to capture

Pacing spike without atrial depolarisation or QRS, with absent expected pulse: **support perfusion and increase output immediately**. Check power, connections, correct port/polarity and wires; consider displacement/fracture, high threshold from oedema/ischaemia, hypothermia, acidosis/electrolytes or drugs. Check echo for tamponade/major postoperative causes of deterioration. Use functioning alternative wires or external pacing while arranging urgent transvenous/other rescue. Atropine may fail in infranodal block; a titrated adrenaline/isoprenaline infusion can bridge to pacing where appropriate, without delaying it.

## Failure to sense

**Undersensing:** intrinsic beats are missed and inappropriate spikes may land on T waves; check leads and lower the mV setting to increase sensitivity. **Oversensing:** EMI/myopotentials are mistaken for beats, inhibiting pacing and causing pauses; remove interference, check wires and increase the mV setting if appropriate. Any R-on-T VT/VF requires immediate resuscitation/defibrillation and expert correction of the pacing system.

## Ongoing care

Document settings, capture/sensing thresholds, dependence and backup plan; inspect/check regularly (usually at least daily early after surgery). Persistent AV block requires cardiology assessment; timing of a permanent device depends on operation, escape rhythm, recovery and stability rather than a compulsory day-7 rule.

**Key evidence:** [TEMP](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10433321/) · [BRADY](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000628)

## Self-marking checklist
- Recognises complete block requires reliable ventricular pacing and cannot be treated by AAI
- Checks labelled wires, battery, insulated connections and bipolar/unipolar return arrangements
- Selects VVI or DDD appropriately and confirms mechanical capture
- Sets rate, output, sensitivity and AV delay with a safe capture margin
- Avoids unprotected threshold testing in a pacing-dependent patient
- Troubleshoots failure to capture while providing immediate backup pacing
- Explains lower mV = greater sensitivity, oversensing pauses and undersensing R-on-T
- Documents daily checks, escalation and individualised permanent-pacing review

items.title: 18. Emergency laparotomy in a pacemaker patient with no technician
items.q: A 78-year-old man with a pacemaker needs emergency laparotomy for perforated bowel at 2 a.m. No technician is available. Outline your management, including the use of a magnet.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Perioperative management of patients with cardiac implantable electronic devices" (2016).

## Principle

Do not delay emergency surgery for a device check. **Manage the patient, not the device.**

## Preop — rapid device assessment

- Examine the chest (site of the generator), look for a **device card, wristband, or hospital record**, and check the ECG and chest X-ray: pacing spikes, number of leads (ICD has thick coils; CRT has three leads).
- Determine **dependence**: indication, ECG and available interrogation/underlying escape rhythm; pacing before every beat alone does not prove dependence. Palpate and monitor the pulse by plethysmography or arterial line.
- Last check date, battery and indication, if the record is available.

## Magnet

| Device | Magnet effect |
|---|---|
| **Pacemaker** | Usually asynchronous pacing at a fixed (manufacturer) rate; some devices do not respond or can be programmed to ignore it |
| **ICD** | Suspends tachycardia detection and shock therapy; **does not affect pacing** |
| **Micra leadless pacemaker** | No magnet response; reprogramming is needed if asynchronous pacing is required |
| **AVEIR leadless systems** | May respond to a magnet; verify model and reliable effect |
| **Loop recorder** | May mark/store an event or have model-specific effects; it has no pacing/shock therapy to suspend |

A magnet must be reliably positioned over the generator and remain accessible despite the operative field and patient position, and response/reliability depends on device, placement and positioning. If the magnet cannot be reliably held or the patient is dependent and monopolar diathermy is above the umbilicus, reduce EMI with **bipolar diathermy** or short monopolar bursts and appropriate return-electrode placement, but this does **not guarantee pacing**. Seek remote device expertise/urgent programming if feasible; ensure external capture and a plan for transvenous rescue when essential. A pacing-dependent ICD/CRT-D patient cannot be made asynchronous by magnet alone.

## Intraop

- **1.** **Pads** (external pacing and defibrillation) on before starting; defibrillator and pacing ready.
- **2.** **Diathermy:** bipolar if possible; otherwise monopolar in bursts of 1 to 2 s, with the return plate positioned so that the current path is away from the generator (below the umbilicus is a lower risk).
- **3.** Monitor ECG and pulse oximetry or arterial line; correct K and Mg.
- **4.** **ICD:** apply a magnet to suspend the shock therapy, with pads on, and reactivate as soon as possible. If a magnet is not available, accept the risk of inappropriate shock but be ready to treat.
- **5.** Atropine, isoprenaline and adrenaline are available.
## Postop

- **6.** Continue monitoring and external rescue until device function and any suspended ICD therapies are restored; arrange interrogation after this high-risk emergency/any suspected interference or reprogramming, and document the handover.

**Key evidence:** [CIED](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12068544/) · [NZCIED](https://nzmj.org.nz/journal/vol-137-no-1590/heart-rhythm-new-zealand-consensus-statement-on-the-practical-management-of-cardiac-implanted-electronic-devices-in-the-peri-ope)

## Self-marking checklist
- Does not delay emergency surgery
- Rapid device assessment: card, ECG, CXR, dependence
- Magnet response in pacemaker and in ICD
- Describes the limits of magnet use
- Applies pads, uses bipolar or short diathermy and a return plate
- Monitors pulse and corrects electrolytes
- Interrogation and restoration after surgery

items.title: 19. Leadless pacemakers and subcutaneous ICDs
items.q: Compare leadless pacemakers and subcutaneous ICDs with conventional transvenous devices, and outline the anaesthetic considerations for transvenous lead extraction.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Advances in management of electrophysiology and AF in the cardiac catheter laboratory" (2018); "Anaesthesia for extraction of long-term cardiac leads" (2022).

## Newer devices

| Device | Features | Anaesthetic relevance |
|---|---|---|
| **Leadless pacemaker** (for example Micra) | Self-contained capsule in the RV via the femoral vein; single-chamber ventricular devices, AV-synchronous ventricular options and newer dual-chamber systems exist; avoids a chest pocket/transvenous lead but still has vascular/perforation and device risks | **Micra has no magnet response; AVEIR may respond** (verify the actual system), so **reprogramming** is needed for asynchronous pacing; EMI can inhibit it; interrogate by programmer |
