| **Subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD)** | Left parasternal electrode and left lateral generator; delivers a shock of **80 J**; **no pacing** except brief post-shock; avoids vascular access | Magnet suspends shock therapy; no antibradycardia pacing, so unsuitable for pacing dependence; bipolar diathermy, pads anterior–posterior away from the can |
| **Conventional transvenous ICD or pacemaker** | Leads in the RA, RV (and coronary sinus for CRT) | Infection, lead fracture, venous occlusion |

A coronary sinus LV lead suggests conventional **CRT**, but lead number is not definitive: conduction-system pacing and other configurations exist. Assess current ventricular function rather than assuming severe failure from the radiograph.

## Transvenous lead extraction

Indications are infection, lead failure, venous occlusion or upgrade. It is performed with laser or mechanical sheaths and carries a risk of **SVC or RV tear, tamponade and haemorrhage** (risk depends on lead dwell time, infection, anatomy and centre; the ELECTRa registry reported major procedure-related complications **1.7%** and procedure-related mortality **0.5%**, not a universal individual risk estimate).

### Preop
- **GA** (or deep sedation in selected cases) in a hybrid theatre with **cardiac surgical back-up** and a perfusionist on standby, cell salvage, and blood crossmatched.
### Intraop

- Arterial line before induction; large-bore IV access (and femoral venous access if the SVC is torn); TOE or transthoracic echo available for tamponade.
- External **defibrillation and pacing pads**; temporary pacing ready for dependent patients; ICD therapy off.
- Be prepared for sudden haemodynamic collapse: pericardiocentesis, sternotomy, balloon occlusion of SVC, and massive transfusion.
### Postop

- After the procedure, a monitored recovery, echo, and reinterrogation or a new device placement.

**Key evidence:** [CIED](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12068544/) · [EXTRACT](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9463625/) · [ELECTRA](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28369414/)

## Self-marking checklist
- Describes leadless pacemaker features and magnet limitations
- Describes the stand-alone S-ICD (no chronic bradycardia pacing/ATP, limited post-shock pacing) and its anaesthetic implications
- Reviews device configuration and current ventricular function
- Lists lead extraction indications and complications
- Prepares for GA, arterial line and surgical back-up
- Pads, temporary pacing and ICD therapy off
- Has a plan for tamponade and haemorrhage

items.title: 20. MRI in patients with cardiac implantable electronic devices
items.q: Discuss the risks to a patient with a cardiac implantable electronic device from magnetic resonance imaging, electroconvulsive therapy, radiotherapy and lithotripsy, and outline how each is managed.
items.a:
[EHRA/HRS/APHRS interference consensus](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11636572/) [SCMR MRI consensus 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11211236/) [AHA CIED statement 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12068544/)

## General principles

Define the exact system (generator **and leads**), pacing dependence, battery status and procedure exposure. Interference may cause oversensing/pacing inhibition, inappropriate ICD therapy, reset or damage; MRI can additionally heat leads. Coordinate the procedural and device teams, establish monitoring/external rescue, and document who restores any changed settings. **One blanket magnet/off protocol does not suit all four procedures.**

## MRI

- **MR-conditional** means the entire implanted system meets the labelled conditions (field strength, leads, programming and scanning limits). A conditional generator alone is insufficient.
- Many **non-MR-conditional systems can also be scanned**, usually at 1.5 T, within a specialist risk-assessed pathway. Abandoned/fractured/epicardial leads need additional expert assessment; they are not accurately described as an absolute lifelong prohibition in every centre.
- Interrogate before scanning; set asynchronous pacing for dependence, a nonpacing mode such as ODO/OVO when appropriate in a nondependent patient, and disable ICD tachy therapies. Monitor ECG, SpO2 and BP with trained staff and immediate communication/rescue.
- Keep conventional defibrillation/resuscitation equipment outside the MRI magnetic exclusion area; if deterioration occurs, remove to the designated safe resuscitation location. Interrogate promptly after MRI and restore settings/therapies before leaving monitoring.

## ECT

ECT is usually feasible. Brief electrical stimulus/myopotentials may inhibit pacing or provoke inappropriate ICD therapy; the associated autonomic response can also provoke arrhythmia. Review recent device data and dependence. Suspend ICD tachy therapy with a verified magnet or programming; asynchronous pacemaker programming is selected when dependence/oversensing risk warrants it, rather than automatic for all. Use effective neuromuscular blockade to reduce seizure muscle activity/fasciculation artefact, ECG plus pulse monitoring, and rescue equipment. Restore/confirm device therapies afterwards; interrogate for events or suspected malfunction.

## Radiotherapy

Plan with radiation oncology/physics and the device service. Main risks are **generator dose, neutron-producing energy, device type and dependence**. EHRA uses generator-dose bands <2 Gy, 2–5 Gy and >5 Gy for increasing risk; neutrons from higher-energy photons/protons can cause reset even at low scatter dose. These are risk bands, not a universal safe maximum.

Keep the generator outside the direct treatment beam and minimise exposure while preserving tumour treatment. **External shielding has limited benefit** and is not the primary protective strategy. Routine relocation is not required unless the device prevents adequate tumour treatment. Arrange audiovisual observation for all, ECG/rescue according to risk, and **risk-based** interrogation/remote monitoring (not necessarily every fraction). Routine suspension of every ICD for every fraction is not recommended; consider it for selected high-risk exposure with external rescue and a restoration plan.

## Extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy

Modern ECG-gated systems generally produce little clinically important CIED interference. Avoid directing the beam/focus near the generator and monitor ECG/pulse. **Routine magnet application, ICD deactivation or conversion to VVI is not generally necessary solely for modern SWL** under EHRA guidance. Confirm manufacturer restrictions and individual device/stone location; seek a tailored plan for unusual exposure or malfunction.

## Preop / Intraop / Postop application

**Preop:** agree the procedure-specific device prescription and monitoring/rescue plan. **Intraop:** implement it, confirm pulse during artefact and respond promptly to inhibition/shocks. **Postop:** restore all changes, confirm ICD therapies before leaving monitoring, interrogate where required and hand over the plan.

**Key evidence:** [EMI](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11636572/) · [MRI](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11211236/) · [CIED](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12068544/)

## Self-marking checklist
- Identifies system, dependence, exposure and device-team responsibilities
- Distinguishes MR-conditional labelling from expert pathways for selected nonconditional systems
- Uses MRI programming, monitoring, safe rescue location and postscan interrogation
- Uses an individual ECT pacing plan with ICD therapy suspension and muscle-relaxation/monitoring precautions
- Explains radiotherapy dose/neutron risks and limited shielding value
- Uses risk-based radiotherapy checks rather than automatic deactivation/interrogation every fraction
- Recognises modern SWL usually needs beam avoidance and monitoring rather than routine reprogramming
- Restores changed settings and confirms ICD therapies before leaving monitored care

items.title: 21. Pulmonary hypertension: classifying haemodynamics before elective surgery
items.q: A patient referred for elective surgery has mPAP 32 mmHg, PAWP 10 mmHg and cardiac output 4 L/min on right-heart catheterisation. Echo shows TR velocity 3.5 m/s, TAPSE 14 mm and FAC 28%. Interpret these findings and outline the further assessment that guides perioperative risk.
items.a:
## Haemodynamic interpretation

PH is mPAP **>20 mmHg**. Calculate **PVR = (mPAP − PAWP)/CO = (32 − 10)/4 = 5.5 Wood units**, or 440 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵ (multiply WU by 80). PAWP ≤15 and PVR >2 indicate **precapillary PH**. This does not by itself establish group 1 PAH: lung/hypoxic disease, chronic thromboembolic disease and other causes must be considered. If PAWP were >15, this would be postcapillary PH; PVR >2 would indicate combined post-/precapillary physiology. [ESC/ERS](https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.00879-2022)

## Echo interpretation

TR velocity 3.5 m/s supports a high echocardiographic probability of PH. TAPSE 14 mm and FAC 28% support RV systolic dysfunction (ASE abnormal thresholds ≤17 mm and ≤35% respectively). Interpret image quality, load, regional/global RV function and any prior cardiac surgery; TAPSE alone can underestimate preserved global function after pericardiotomy. Review RV/RA dimensions, septal flattening, pericardial effusion, valves and LV function. [ASE 2025](https://www.asecho.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/ASE-Right-Heart-Guidelines-May-2025.pdf)

RVSP is **4 × TR velocity² + estimated RAP**. Here the TR gradient is 49 mmHg, but RAP is not supplied. RVSP approximates PASP only if there is no RVOT/pulmonary-valve obstruction. A poor/incomplete TR envelope or severe TR can mislead; echo is not a substitute for catheter diagnosis when management depends on accurate haemodynamics.

## Further assessment and risk

- Establish WHO group, duration and treatment response; consider PFT/DLCO, chest imaging, connective-tissue/other cause assessment and **V/Q scanning to screen for CTEPH**. A negative CTPA does not replace appropriate CTEPH screening.
- Ask about syncope, progression, chest pain, exercise capacity and right-heart-failure signs. Review WHO class, 6MWD/CPET, BNP/NT-proBNP, renal/liver function and oxygenation.
- Use a validated PAH risk model when appropriate; do not label this patient “moderate PH” from mPAP 32 alone. RV dysfunction, low cardiac index/high RAP, deterioration and surgical urgency matter more than a single pressure band.

## Preop

PH-specialist/anaesthetic review before elective surgery; optimise the underlying cause, volume, oxygenation, rhythm and established therapy. Consider deferral if decompensated. Agree the surgical approach, location, monitoring and crisis plan; further catheterisation is for a management-changing question, not automatically every operation.

## Intraop

Preserve systemic/RV perfusion and avoid acute PVR rises, overdistension and excessive fluids. Use risk-based invasive monitoring and access to selective inhaled vasodilators/inotropy/rescue for significant disease; select agents and ventilation by RV physiology.

## Postop

Plan monitored recovery/ICU according to RV dysfunction and surgical burden, continued PH drugs, careful fluids/analgesia and surveillance for hypoventilation, arrhythmia and RV failure. Provide a documented escalation plan.

**Key evidence:** [PH](https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.00879-2022) · [ASE](https://www.asecho.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/ASE-Right-Heart-Guidelines-May-2025.pdf) · [PHOP](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36924225/)

## Self-marking checklist
- Calculates PVR 5.5 WU/440 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵ correctly
- Defines precapillary PH and does not equate it automatically with group 1 PAH
- Interprets TAPSE/FAC and TR velocity with their limitations
- Explains RVSP calculation and when it approximates PASP
- Assesses cause including appropriate CTEPH screening
- Uses multiparameter clinical/RV/biomarker risk rather than mPAP bands
- Plans preop optimisation, intraop perfusion/afterload management and postoperative monitoring

items.title: 22. Group 1 PAH on epoprostenol, tadalafil and macitentan: perioperative plan
items.q: A patient with group 1 PAH receives continuous IV epoprostenol, tadalafil, macitentan and three-weekly sotatercept. She needs urgent abdominal surgery and may be unable to take oral medication afterwards. Discuss her medication management throughout the perioperative period.
items.a:
## What each treatment does

Epoprostenol augments the prostacyclin pathway; tadalafil inhibits PDE5 and macitentan blocks endothelin receptors. Sotatercept is an **activin-signalling ligand trap**, a disease-modifying add-on rather than an acute pulmonary vasodilator or replacement for the infusion. ERA/PDE5/prostacyclin combinations are selected by PAH risk and tolerance, not prescribed to every WHO PH group. [ESC/ERS](https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.00879-2022)

**Current evidence:** the ERS 2026 update recommends add-on sotatercept for already-treated PAH patients at intermediate-low, intermediate-high or high follow-up risk. It does not establish routine initial monotherapy, crisis rescue, universal use in Eisenmenger or use in pregnancy. **ZENITH** enrolled 172 high-risk patients on background treatment; the composite of death, lung transplant or PAH-worsening hospitalisation occurred in 17.4% versus 54.7% (HR 0.24, 95% CI 0.13–0.43). This is **not a 76% reduction in isolated mortality**. [ERS update](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42705705/) [ZENITH primary report](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40167274/)

## Preop

- Contact the PH service, confirm actual drugs/doses and baseline RV status; medication management must accompany haemodynamic optimisation and the surgical rescue plan.
- **Never interrupt epoprostenol**: its short action makes pump/line failure an emergency. Check dedicated labelled access, concentration, pump, drug supply, battery and a backup pump/infusion with trained staff. Do not give boluses or flush the prostacyclin line. Plan access changes with the PH team before disconnection.
- Continue the prescribed oral regimen when feasible. Define when enteral intake will cease and whether reliable enteral delivery or a specialist-directed bridge is possible. There is **no IV equivalent for every oral drug**; switching to IV sildenafil/inhaled or parenteral prostanoid is not a simple dose-equivalent substitution for tadalafil/macitentan.
- Review interactions, BP, renal function, LFTs and haemoglobin; **PDE5 inhibitors plus riociguat are contraindicated**, and nitrates are contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors/riociguat.
- For sotatercept, check timing, **Hb/haematocrit, platelets, BP and bleeding**, including interaction with antithrombotics/prostacyclin-related bleeding risk. Agree dose delay/continuation with the specialist; there is no established universal surgical washout interval. Follow product monitoring/hold criteria and fetal-harm precautions. [Prescribing information](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=21693ee2-cd23-4137-ac67-066bb3a4a9b7)

## Intraop

Maintain uninterrupted pump delivery with explicit responsibility at every transfer. Prevent systemic hypotension, hypoxaemia, hypercarbia, acidosis and RV overload. Treat suspected line/pump failure immediately with specialist support and restore reliable delivery; inhaled NO/prostacyclin may be rescue **adjuncts**, not permission to stop the baseline infusion. Prepare vasopressors/inotropy and selective pulmonary vasodilators according to risk.

## Postop

Continue infusion in an appropriately trained monitored unit. Verify delivery at handover, maintain backup supplies and monitor perfusion, oxygenation, urine/fluid balance, Hb/platelets/bleeding. Resume oral treatment when absorption is reliable using the agreed bridge/de-escalation plan. Sotatercept follow-up remains specialist-directed; it is not given as an emergency bolus for a postoperative crisis.

**Key evidence:** [PH](https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.00879-2022) · [ERS26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42705705/) · [ZENITH](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40167274/) · [SOTA](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=21693ee2-cd23-4137-ac67-066bb3a4a9b7)

## Self-marking checklist
- Explains the four pathways and current role/limits of sotatercept
- States ZENITH population and composite endpoint accurately
- Protects continuous epoprostenol delivery, dedicated line and backup arrangements
- Plans oral interruption without inventing dose-equivalent IV substitutions
- Checks PDE5/riociguat/nitrate interactions
- Reviews sotatercept Hb, platelets, BP, bleeding and pregnancy considerations
- Allocates infusion responsibility through intraop transfer and monitored postoperative care

items.title: 23. Congenital long-QT syndrome: perioperative plan and torsades rescue
items.q: A woman with congenital long-QT syndrome taking nadolol is booked for elective surgery. Outline your perioperative plan and the management of recurrent perioperative torsades de pointes.
items.a:
## Why this is high priority

Congenital LQTS is a repolarisation disorder with a risk of TdP/VF; risk depends on genotype, prior syncope/arrest, QTc, drugs and triggers. A normal QTc on one ECG does not exclude genetically proven disease. LQT1 events often follow exercise/emotion, LQT2 sudden auditory stimuli and LQT3 rest/bradycardia. [BJA Education](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7808061/)

## Preop

- Clarify phenotype, previous events, genotype, adherence, family history and cardiology advice. Record a baseline 12-lead/QTc, recognising correction limits and wide-QRS confounding.
- **Continue nadolol without missed doses**; agree an alternative if oral intake is interrupted. Review ICD/pacing history and make a procedure-specific EMI plan rather than routinely switching off every ICD for every procedure.
- Correct low K/Mg/Ca and review every new drug against a reliable QT-risk resource. Avoid dehydration, hypothermia and anxiety; provide a calm environment and suitable anxiolysis. Agree monitored postoperative care and ensure IV magnesium/defibrillation/pacing rescue are available.

## Intraop

GA or regional techniques can be used. Minimise sympathetic surges at induction, instrumentation and emergence, and avoid marked pauses/bradycardia. Propofol-based anaesthesia is commonly used; all volatiles can lengthen QT, but perioperative evidence does not establish an absolute safe/unsafe agent list. Avoid unnecessary ketamine/sympathomimetics, QT-risk antiemetics and adrenaline in local anaesthetic when suitable alternatives exist. Sugammadex may avoid anticholinesterase/anticholinergic effects. Treat hypotension promptly with a considered vasoactive plan; lifesaving drugs must not be withheld because they appear on a QT-risk list.

## TdP rescue

- **1.** Call for help, stop provoking drugs/stimulus, assess pulse/perfusion and give oxygen/ventilatory support as needed.
- **2.** **Sustained polymorphic VT: unsynchronised defibrillation even if a pulse remains**, because R-wave synchronisation is unreliable. If pulseless, immediate CPR/ALS. Do not wait for magnesium before shocking a sustained unstable rhythm.
- **3.** Give **IV magnesium** even when serum Mg is normal; ANZCOR 11.9 specifies **5 mmol over 10 min**, repeat once if necessary then an infusion. Other established TdP protocols use **MgSO4 2 g (~8 mmol)** over a rate appropriate to urgency. State the selected protocol and avoid unit confusion. Correct potassium/calcium, bradycardia and other triggers; monitor renal function and toxicity.
- **4.** Recurrent episodes need specialist review and **overdrive pacing** when indicated, with continued appropriate beta-blockade. **Isoprenaline is for selected acquired pause-dependent TdP, not routine congenital LQTS**. Avoid amiodarone for long-QT TdP. [ANZCOR](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias)

## Postop

Quiet monitored recovery, continued beta-blockade and electrolyte/drug review. The BJA Education review recommends at least 24 h monitoring in congenital LQTS; significant events require ICU/cardiology care and investigation. Restore any suspended ICD therapies before leaving monitored care and document the plan for subsequent anaesthesia.

**Key evidence:** [LQTS](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7808061/) · [ALS](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias) · [CIED](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12068544/)

## Self-marking checklist
- Assesses congenital phenotype, genotype, events, baseline ECG and device
- Continues nadolol and corrects electrolytes/drug triggers preoperatively
- Provides a stable anaesthetic with controlled induction/emergence and rescue preparation
- Shocks sustained polymorphic VT unsynchronised, with CPR if pulseless
- Gives magnesium with explicit mmol/gram distinction and a named protocol
- Avoids amiodarone and routine isoprenaline for congenital LQTS
- Uses expert pacing/beta-blocker management and postoperative monitoring/device restoration

items.title: 2026.1 Q7: Epicardial pacing in complete heart block before separation from bypass
items.q: A patient is in complete heart block prior to separation from cardiopulmonary bypass. Outline the programming considerations for epicardial pacing in this patient. (30%) Describe your approach to troubleshooting intermittent capture of the pacemaker in this patient who is pacing-dependent in the ICU. (70%)
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2026.1 Q7: choose a sensible mode and rate for a patient in complete heart block before separation from CPB, and give a structured troubleshooting approach that keeps a pacing-dependent ICU patient safe and considers alternative pacing modalities.

## Part A — programming considerations for epicardial pacing (30%)

The patient has **complete heart block** and is about to separate from bypass, so pacing must provide reliable ventricular activation and, if possible, **AV synchrony**.

- **Confirm the system:** identify atrial and ventricular wires, check polarity/connection to the pacing box, ensure a functioning generator and battery, and confirm both **electrical and mechanical capture**.
- **Choose the mode:** if sinus atrial activity and both atrial and ventricular wires are present and working, use **AV sequential pacing** (commonly **DDD** or another dual-chamber sequential mode available on the external box) to preserve AV synchrony. If atrial sensing/wires are absent or unreliable, use **ventricular pacing** (e.g. VVI; or temporarily an asynchronous ventricular mode if sensing is unreliable and there is no meaningful intrinsic ventricular rhythm).
- **Rate:** choose a rate that supports separation from CPB and cardiac output, often **about 80–100 min⁻¹**, then individualise according to perfusion, filling, ischaemia and ventricular function.
- **Output:** measure the capture threshold when practical and set an adequate safety margin, commonly **at least 2–3 × threshold** (or use a high/maximal output initially if unstable, then titrate down once capture is secure).
- **Sensitivity:** if using a sensing mode, program appropriate sensing so intrinsic atrial/ventricular activity is detected without oversensing noise.
- **AV delay:** if using AV sequential pacing, set a physiological AV delay (roughly **120–180 ms**) and optimise to arterial pressure and filling.
- **Backup planning:** before separation from bypass, have **external pacing/defibrillation pads** and vasoactive support available in case the epicardial system is unreliable.

## Part B — troubleshooting intermittent capture in the ICU (70%)

Use a **structured patient–generator–lead** approach while keeping the pacing-dependent patient safe.

### 1. Keep the patient perfused first

- Assess pulse, arterial trace, consciousness and perfusion; do **not** rely on the ECG monitor alone.
- Call for help, ensure a defibrillator is present and apply/confirm **transcutaneous pacing pads**.
- Give oxygen, treat hypotension, and provide vasopressor/chronotrope support as required.
- If unstable, increase output to **maximum immediately** and consider switching temporarily to an **asynchronous mode** if oversensing/inhibition is suspected.

### 2. Confirm the problem is truly failure to capture

- Distinguish **failure to capture** (pacing spike without a paced P wave/QRS and no corresponding pulse) from **failure to sense**, monitor artefact or complete disconnection.
- Confirm both **electrical capture** on ECG and **mechanical capture** on arterial line/plethysmography.

### 3. Check the pacing box and programming

- Ensure the box is on, battery is functioning, the correct chamber is selected, and the **rate/mode/output/sensitivity** are appropriate.
- Recheck the capture threshold and set the output above threshold.
- Review sensitivity: **oversensing** may inhibit pacing; **undersensing** may allow competition.
- If appropriate, change to **VOO/DOO** temporarily to bypass oversensing while correcting the cause.

### 4. Check the wires and connections

- Inspect all cable connections, clips and polarity.
- Look for loose terminals, fractured wires, lead/wire displacement or a faulty pacing cable/box.
- If multiple epicardial wires are present, try an **alternative ventricular wire/pair** or alternate the usable pair according to the system.

### 5. Look for causes of a rising capture threshold

- Postoperative **myocardial oedema/inflammation**.
- **Electrolyte or metabolic disturbance**, especially hyperkalaemia, acidosis and severe hypoxaemia.
- **Hypothermia**.
- **Myocardial ischaemia**, severe ventricular failure, tamponade or major haemodynamic deterioration.
- Correct reversible factors and reassess the threshold.

### 6. Escalate early if reliability is not restored

- If intermittent epicardial capture persists in a pacing-dependent patient, move to a more reliable modality such as **transvenous pacing**.
- Continue monitored ICU care; in rare cases return to theatre may be necessary if the pacing system is unusable and no alternative is satisfactory.
- Document the fault, the corrective steps taken and the definitive plan.

**Key evidence:** [TEMP](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10433321/) · [BRADY](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000628)

items.title: 2024.2 Q13: Diagnosing three ECGs (AF, LBBB, Mobitz II) and anaesthetic implications
items.q: State the diagnosis in each of the three following electrocardiograms (ECGs) and discuss their implications for anaesthesia.
items.model:
![2024.2 Q13: the three original ECGs, shown top to bottom](set12-saq-2024-2-q13.png)

> Original ECGs from the exam paper, shown top to bottom. Work out each diagnosis before revealing the model answer.

> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2024.2 report: AF/LBBB/Mobitz II; AF morbidity/stroke, Mobitz II progression and preparation for pacing. Distinguish AF from flutter, LBBB from a reflex STEMI label, and Mobitz II from complete block.

## Diagnoses (confirmed in the 2024.2 examiner report; practise the original tracings)

| ECG | Diagnosis | Key features |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Atrial fibrillation** (not flutter) | Irregularly irregular R-R intervals, no P waves, fibrillatory baseline; flutter has organised flutter waves; variable AV block can also make its ventricular rhythm irregular |
| 2 | **Left bundle branch block** | QRS 120 ms or more, broad notched R in I, aVL, V5 to V6, deep S in V1, discordant ST-T changes; do not call this a STEMI |
| 3 | **Mobitz type 2 second-degree AV block** | Constant PR interval with intermittent non-conducted P waves; the P waves still march through; often a wide QRS |

## Implications for anaesthesia

**Atrial fibrillation**
- Marker of structural heart disease; raised risk of stroke, heart failure and perioperative morbidity. Assess thromboembolic risk (CHA2DS2-VA in ESC 2024, or the locally used CHA2DS2-VASc), anticoagulation and a plan for it, rate and the cause (thyroid, electrolytes, alcohol, sepsis).
- Loss of atrial kick is poorly tolerated with stiff ventricles, mitral stenosis or aortic stenosis. Continue rate-control drugs; avoid triggers (pain, hypovolaemia, sympathetic surges). Fast AF with instability needs synchronised cardioversion.

**LBBB**
- Implies structural disease (ischaemia, cardiomyopathy, hypertension); review previous investigations; obtain an echo for new symptoms, suspected structural disease or a result that would change management. Ischaemia is hard to see on the ECG (use the clinical picture, serial ECG/troponin and modified Sgarbossa criteria for suspected occlusion; bedside echo when indicated).
- Interventricular dyssynchrony reduces output. **Right-bundle injury during pulmonary artery catheter passage can precipitate complete heart block in a patient with pre-existing LBBB**, so avoid PAC insertion or have pacing ready.

**Mobitz type 2**
- Usually infranodal disease, with a high risk of progressing to **complete heart block or asystole** and symptomatic bradycardia; this is an indication for a permanent pacemaker.
- Plan **transcutaneous pacing pads on** (for bradycardia; defibrillation remains available for a shockable arrest), pacing capability, adrenaline or isoprenaline infusion ready; atropine often fails with infranodal block. Avoid drugs that depress conduction (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, high-dose neostigmine), and correct potassium and ischaemia.
- Postpone elective surgery until a pacemaker is placed; if urgent, obtain an expert pacing plan, reliable temporary pacing when indicated, external backup and monitoring appropriate to the procedure; pads alone may be inadequate.

## General

### Preop

Define symptoms, underlying disease, rhythm and anticoagulant/device plans; seek cardiology review for high-grade block or decompensation.

### Intraop

Continuous ECG plus pulse monitoring; invasive pressure monitoring according to clinical risk. Correct reversible triggers and have the appropriate pacing/cardioversion rescue available.

### Postop

Monitor according to conduction and haemodynamic risk, investigate new changes and document anticoagulation or pacing follow-up.

**Key evidence:** [AF](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/45/36/3314/7738779) · [CIED](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12068544/) · [BRADY](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000628)

items.title: 2024.1 Q5: Preoperative assessment of an adult with a repaired congenital cardiac lesion
items.q: Discuss the preoperative assessment and risk stratification of an adult patient with a repaired congenital cardiac lesion, scheduled for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2024.1 report: stratify by lesion and functional capacity; residual pathophysiology/circulatory state; recent relevant investigations and medication. This stem is preoperative assessment, so unrelated full intra/postoperative management should not displace the requested answer.

## Approach

Adults with repaired congenital heart disease (ACHD) have a wide range of risk. The aim is to define the **lesion, the residual physiology** and the current circulatory state, then match them to the surgery and the hospital.

## Assessment

- **Lesion and repair:** the original anatomy, the type and date of each operation or intervention, operation notes and cardiology letters (simple, moderate or complex: for example, repaired tetralogy of Fallot is moderate; a Fontan or other single-ventricle circulation is complex).
- **Residual pathophysiology:** residual shunts (risk of paradoxical embolism), valve disease or conduits, outflow obstruction, pulmonary regurgitation, ventricular size and function (single, subpulmonary or systemic RV), **pulmonary hypertension**, cyanosis, polycythaemia.
- **Rhythm:** arrhythmias and conduction block, pacemaker or ICD, antiarrhythmic drugs.
- **Function and symptoms:** NYHA class, exercise tolerance, syncope, palpitations, oedema.
- **Medications and other issues:** anticoagulants, diuretics, pulmonary vasodilators, endocarditis history, renal, hepatic and neurocognitive problems, previous anaesthetics.
- **Recent investigations:** ECG, echo appropriate to the lesion and clinical course (repeat for changed symptoms or management-changing uncertainty), oxygen saturation, haemoglobin, renal function, BNP; MRI or catheter data from the ACHD service.

## Risk stratification

- **Anatomical complexity plus physiological stage** (stage A asymptomatic to D severe limitation): the same repaired lesion can be IIA or IIC, so function matters as much as anatomy.
- Adverse markers: pulmonary hypertension or Eisenmenger physiology, a failing Fontan, ventricular dysfunction, cyanosis, arrhythmia, heart failure, poor functional class.
- **Surgery:** a laparoscopic cholecystectomy is low to intermediate risk, but pneumoperitoneum reduces venous return and raises SVR and PVR, which is poorly tolerated in Fontan, pulmonary hypertension and RV failure; CO2 absorption raises PVR; air or CO2 embolism with a residual shunt is a risk.
- Urgency (elective, so time for optimisation) and anaesthetic factors.

## Plan from the assessment

Early discussion with the **ACHD cardiologist and the MDT**. Moderate or complex disease, or high-risk physiology, should be treated at a specialist centre; high-risk lesions (Eisenmenger, failing Fontan) are transferred unless surgery is immediate. Consider open surgery or low-pressure laparoscopy, and distinguish routine surgical antibiotic prophylaxis from infective-endocarditis prophylaxis. Apply local high-risk cardiac criteria; dental indications are the clearest, while selected non-dental procedures may warrant consideration under ESC 2023 guidance rather than a universal dental-only rule.

**Key evidence:** [ACHD](https://www.bjaed.org/article/S2058-5349%2825%2900066-6/pdf) · [ACHD25](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001402) · [IE](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/endocarditis/)

items.title: 2022.2 Q8: DDDR pacemaker: NBG code and perioperative assessment
items.q: A patient presenting for surgery has a DDDR pacemaker. a) Explain the NASPE/BPEG Generic (NBG) pacemaker classification system. b) Describe the assessment and preoperative management of this DDDR device.
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2022.2 report: correct DDDR interpretation; underlying rhythm, pacing burden, battery and magnet response; an organised plan based on surgery/diathermy. The report specifically states that a general cardiovascular assessment was not required.

## a) NBG code

| Position | Meaning | Letters |
|---|---|---|
| I | **Chamber paced** | O none, A atrium, V ventricle, D dual |
| II | **Chamber sensed** | O, A, V, D |
| III | **Response to sensing** | O none, I inhibited, T triggered, D dual (inhibit and trigger) |
| IV | **Rate modulation** | O none, R rate responsive |
| V | **Multisite pacing** | O, A, V, D (for example biventricular) |

**DDDR** paces and senses both atrium and ventricle, inhibits or triggers according to the intrinsic rhythm, and increases the paced rate with activity (accelerometer or minute ventilation). The ICD codes separately describe shock, antitachycardia pacing and monitoring.

## b) Assessment

- **History:** indication (AV block, sinus node disease), symptoms of malfunction (dizziness, syncope), cardiac disease and heart failure, date of insertion and the device card.
- **Last check:** review a recent interrogation and confirm current clinical/device stability. Traditional follow-up intervals (12 months for PPM; 6 months for ICD/CRT) are not universal perioperative clearance rules; AHA 2024 notes that a check within 3 months can help establish current rhythm/dependence. Obtain a report of battery life, lead thresholds and impedance, percentage pacing, and settings.
- **Underlying rhythm and dependency:** the ECG, indication, underlying escape rhythm and interrogation. A high pacing percentage does not by itself prove dependence, and anaesthesia may increase dependence. Only trained staff should test the underlying rhythm with appropriate backup.
- **Device response to a magnet:** most transvenous pacemakers go asynchronous (DOO/VOO), at a model- and battery-dependent rate; responses may be disabled or transient. Micra has no magnet response; AVEIR responses differ. Verify the actual device.
- **Chest X-ray** for lead position if in doubt; electrolytes.

## Preop management

Plan from the **site and type of surgery** and the **diathermy** used.
- Surgery below the umbilicus, or bipolar diathermy only: usually no reprogramming is required. Keep the current path away from generator/leads; the low-risk below-umbilicus rule requires the return electrode also below the umbilicus and no abdominal generator.
- Surgery above the umbilicus with monopolar diathermy: if dependent, ask for reprogramming to asynchronous (DOO) or place a magnet in a way that is practical for the field. **Consider disabling rate response when inappropriate sensor activation is likely** so that minute-ventilation sensors and diathermy do not drive tachycardia.
- Short diathermy bursts, bipolar where possible, monitor the pulse (plethysmograph or arterial line) because the ECG is distorted.
- Have external pacing and defibrillation pads available, and document postoperative restoration and the indications for interrogation (reprogramming, suspected malfunction, major EMI or external shocks); an uneventful magnet-only case does not always require full interrogation.
- If a technician is not available (emergency), manage the patient rather than the device, using a verified magnet response where appropriate, external rescue and EMI avoidance; a magnet cannot make an ICD pace asynchronously.

**Key evidence:** [CIED](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12068544/) · [NZCIED](https://nzmj.org.nz/journal/vol-137-no-1590/heart-rhythm-new-zealand-consensus-statement-on-the-practical-management-of-cardiac-implanted-electronic-devices-in-the-peri-ope)

Interprets DDDR (dual pacing, dual sensing, dual response, rate response)

Identifies underlying rhythm, pacing percentage and dependency
Describes magnet response, battery and thresholds
Plans management by site of surgery and diathermy type (bipolar, reprogramming, rate response off)
Arranges external rescue, a documented restoration plan and postoperative interrogation when indicated

items.title: 2022.1 Q6: Pulmonary hypertension on bosentan for laparoscopic bowel resection
items.q: A patient with primary pulmonary hypertension is scheduled for laparoscopic bowel resection. Their current medication is bosentan PO 125mg bd. Discuss how their condition influences your perioperative management.
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2022.1 report: laparoscopy effects on venous return/CO and CO2/PVR; current PH/RV assessment, open-versus-laparoscopic options, suitable specialist location, arterial line and the entire perioperative period.

## Why it matters

Pulmonary hypertension (PH) increases perioperative risk, but there is no universal mortality percentage: PH group, RV function, functional class, surgery and urgency determine risk. Historical cohort rates must not be applied to every patient. The RV is a low-pressure pump that fails with a sudden rise in PVR, and RV coronary flow becomes increasingly dependent on diastolic perfusion as RV pressure/wall tension rises, so **hypotension and rising PVR cause a downward spiral**.

## Preop

- **Assess severity and RV function:** functional class, syncope, signs of RV failure, 6-minute walk and BNP/NT-proBNP interpreted within a validated PAH risk assessment, BNP, echo (TAPSE ≤17 mm supports RV systolic dysfunction but is not a standalone perioperative risk grade, RV size, septal flattening, effusion, TR velocity) and recent right heart catheter data.
- **Optimise and plan:** continue **bosentan** (an endothelin receptor antagonist; check liver function, avoid interruption). Plan any enteral interruption with the PH team: there is no direct IV replacement for every oral agent, and IV sildenafil/inhaled or parenteral prostanoid is a specialist bridge rather than a bosentan-equivalent substitution. Never interrupt continuous prostacyclin: dedicated line, backup pump/drug and trained staff. Review LFTs, Hb, interactions and anticoagulation; anticoagulation is not routine for all idiopathic PAH.
- **Options:** discuss **open versus laparoscopic** surgery, or a less extensive resection, with the surgeon.
- **Location:** a centre with ICU, cardiology and PH specialist support, and planned monitored postoperative care according to severity and surgical insult, often ICU for significant PAH and major surgery.

## Intraop — laparoscopy

Raised intra-abdominal pressure **reduces venous return and cardiac output**, head-down tilt adds load, and **CO2 absorption causes hypercarbia that raises PVR**. If laparoscopy goes ahead: the lowest workable insufflation pressure (10–12 mmHg may be an agreed starting range, not a guaranteed safe limit), slow insufflation, minimal tilt, ventilation adjusted for CO2, and a low threshold to convert.

## Intraop

- **Monitoring:** arterial line before induction (essential), central line for vasopressor, TOE for RV; PAC arrhythmias are poorly tolerated.
- **Principles:** "keep them where they live", maintain SVR and RV perfusion, avoid rises in PVR (hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia, pain, N2O) and keep FRC.
- **Technique:** GA with titrated agents (a carefully titrated induction, often etomidate/opioid-based; ketamine has conflicting adult PH recommendations and is not universally preferred), vasopressor running (noradrenaline or vasopressin); positive pressure ventilation can drop venous return and cause severe hypotension. Avoid single-shot spinal; epidural only slowly titrated.
- **PH crisis:** call for help, stop the trigger/insufflation, give 100% oxygen initially, correct hypoventilation/acidaemia and optimise lung volume without injurious pressures; maintain systemic perfusion with noradrenaline or low-dose vasopressin, add inhaled nitric oxide/prostacyclin and inotropy as needed. Consider VA-ECMO as a selected rescue bridge. Do not abruptly withdraw inhaled vasodilators.

## Postop

ICU or HDU, analgesia without respiratory depression (avoid hypercarbia), oxygen, restart the drugs, VTE prophylaxis, and individualised monitoring through fluid shifts and early recovery (often 24–72 hours in higher-risk cases).

**Key evidence:** [PH](https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.00879-2022) · [PHOP](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36924225/) · [RV](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13741-024-00397-5)

items.title: 2020.1 Q9: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator for left mastectomy
items.q: A patient with an implantable cardioverter defibrillator pacemaker is scheduled for a left mastectomy. Discuss how the presence of this device affects your management of this patient.
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2020.1 report: device proximity/damage and EMI; elective technical deactivation rather than reliance on a magnet in the field; external defibrillation protection while shock therapy is disabled.

## Issues

An ICD (usually in the left pectoral region) senses ventricular activity and delivers antitachycardia pacing and shocks. **Electromagnetic interference (EMI)** from diathermy can be sensed as VF and cause an inappropriate shock, or inhibit pacing. A **left mastectomy is close to the device**, so EMI and accidental damage to the generator or leads are both real risks. This is elective surgery, so there is time to plan.

## Preop

- **History and records:** indication (primary or secondary prevention), shocks, heart failure, cardiomyopathy, and whether the patient is **pacing dependent** (ECG, underlying rhythm and interrogation; percentage pacing alone does not prove dependence).
- **Device check:** reviewed for current battery, lead data, underlying rhythm and settings; arrange recent interrogation when risk or uncertainty warrants it (a routine 6-month follow-up interval is not a guarantee of perioperative suitability). Arrange for a **cardiac technician or physiologist** to check the device before surgery.
- **Plan with the technician:** switch off the **tachyarrhythmia (shock) therapy** immediately before surgery. If pacing dependent, reprogram to asynchronous pacing for monopolar diathermy near the device. Do not rely on a magnet in the surgical field; a magnet does not alter pacing in an ICD and may be removed.
- **External pads:** apply defibrillation or pacing pads (away from the generator) **before the shock function is turned off**, with a defibrillator in the room.
- Correct electrolytes and continue antiarrhythmic drugs.

## Intraop

- ECG plus a pulse-based monitor (plethysmograph or arterial line), because EMI distorts the ECG.
- **Diathermy:** bipolar if possible; if monopolar, short bursts of 1 to 2 seconds, lowest power, return plate positioned so that the current path avoids the device (choose with the surgeon/device team for this left-sided surgical field; do not prescribe a chest/shoulder site that routes current across the generator or leads), and cables kept away. The surgeon should avoid contact with the generator and leads.
- Anaesthesia: GA or regional techniques (paravertebral or PECS block) according to cardiac function, avoiding hypoxia, acidosis and electrolyte disturbance.
- If VF/pulseless VT occurs with therapy off, defibrillate; unstable monomorphic VT with a pulse requires synchronised cardioversion, while sustained polymorphic VT requires an unsynchronised shock; if shocks are delivered, stop diathermy.

## Postop

Monitor with defibrillation available until the device is **reinterrogated and tachyarrhythmia therapy is restored**. Restore and confirm therapies **before leaving the monitored setting**, with a named person responsible for the handover.

**Key evidence:** [CIED](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12068544/) · [NZCIED](https://nzmj.org.nz/journal/vol-137-no-1590/heart-rhythm-new-zealand-consensus-statement-on-the-practical-management-of-cardiac-implanted-electronic-devices-in-the-peri-ope)

items.title: 2017.1 Q14: Anaesthesia for cardioversion in atrial fibrillation: success and safety
items.q: You are asked to provide anaesthesia for cardioversion for a 60-year-old male with atrial fibrillation. Which factors influence the success of cardioversion, and a safe outcome?
items.model:
> **Examiner alignment:** Report emphasis: both success (duration, aetiology, electrolytes, drugs) and safety (underlying disease, anticoagulation and conduct). [Official source](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106432). These checklists are not official College marking schedules.

> **Evidence:** [2024 ESC/EACTS atrial fibrillation guideline](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/45/36/3314/7738779)

## Factors affecting success

- **Duration of AF:** success falls with longer duration (below 48 hours best; more than a year poor).
- **Aetiology:** structural heart disease, larger **left atrial size/volume** (a predictor rather than a universal 5 cm threshold), valve disease, and reversible causes not corrected (thyrotoxicosis, sepsis, alcohol, hypoxia).
- **Electrolytes and drugs:** correct potassium/magnesium abnormalities; avoid arbitrary supranormal targets. Appropriate antiarrhythmic pretreatment (e.g. amiodarone in selected structural heart disease) improves conversion/maintenance. Digoxin controls rate but does not reliably restore sinus rhythm; exclude toxicity.
- **Technique:** synchronised **biphasic** shock at the device/guideline-recommended AF energy (often 200 J initially), escalating if needed. Ensure good adhesive pad contact, dry/shave excess hair, minimise impedance and use anterolateral or anteroposterior position; reposition/change vector after failure. No single pad position is universally superior. Manual pressure requires an approved electrically insulated protocol, not bare-handed pressure during shock.
- Previous failed cardioversion, obesity, COPD, and ischaemia.

## Preop: factors affecting safety

**Embolism**

- **Anticoagulation:** for elective AF cardioversion with duration **>24 hours or uncertain onset** (2024 ESC), ensure ≥3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation with verified adherence, or use TOE to exclude thrombus and establish peri-procedural anticoagulation for early cardioversion. Continue for **at least 4 weeks afterwards in most patients**, then according to long-term stroke risk (ESC uses CHA2DS2-VA; other pathways use CHA2DS2-VASc), irrespective of restored sinus rhythm. The narrow optional exception is definite <24-hour AF with no thromboembolic risk factors. If thrombus is present, defer and treat/re-image. Haemodynamic instability requires immediate synchronised cardioversion; start anticoagulation as soon as feasible without delaying rescue.

**Patient**

- Underlying disease: heart failure, ischaemia, severe valve disease, recent MI; assess LV function and thyroid.
- **Digoxin toxicity** (cardioversion can cause VF), hypokalaemia, QT-prolonging drugs.
- Pacemaker or ICD (pads away from the generator, interrogate afterwards).
- Fasting, airway risk, aspiration risk, and consent.

## Intraop: conduct of the procedure

- Suitable location with resuscitation equipment, trained assistance and a defibrillator.
- **Short anaesthetic:** monitored (ECG, SpO2, NIBP, capnography), preoxygenate, propofol or etomidate, titrated.
- Synchronised shock, clear the patient, treat **bradycardia** or asystole (atropine, pacing), VF (unsynchronised shock), hypotension, and skin burns.

## Postop

Recovery with airway/haemodynamic monitoring and a 12-lead ECG; confirm the anticoagulation and rhythm-control plan, adverse events, discharge criteria and follow-up.

items.title: 2016.2 Q2: Trifascicular block before elective hernia repair
items.q: A patient presents for an elective inguinal hernia repair and his preoperative electrocardiogram shows trifascicular block. What implications might this have for this patient in the perioperative period and how will you manage those implications?
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2016.2 Q2, p. 4: Explain the conduction abnormality and risk of complete heart block; relate urgency/complexity, causes/triggers and external/temporary pacing to this patient. Contemporary terminology distinguishes bifascicular block plus PR prolongation from proven three-fascicle disease. [Original report on Learn@ANZCA](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106431).

## What it is

The stem uses the traditional term **trifascicular block**. RBBB plus left anterior/posterior fascicular block and a prolonged PR is more accurately **bifascicular block with first-degree AV block**: PR prolongation may be AV-nodal and does not establish disease in the third fascicle. Alternating bundle-branch block is a distinct, high-risk marker of advanced His–Purkinje disease and warrants pacing assessment even without symptoms.

## Implications

- **Risk of progression to complete heart block** and asystole, which is a risk if a trigger occurs. Triggers include hypoxia, hyperkalaemia, ischaemia, drugs (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, amiodarone, digoxin), vagal stimulation, volatile and local anaesthetics in high dose, and insertion of a PAC or central line.
- The **absolute risk is low** in an asymptomatic patient, and routine prophylactic pacing is not recommended. Symptoms (syncope or presyncope) indicate a high risk of block.
- Marker of underlying disease: ischaemic, degenerative or cardiomyopathy, infiltrative, previous surgery.
- Drug and technique issues: slowed conduction, bradycardia not responding to atropine.

## Preop

- **1.** **Assess:** history (syncope, presyncope, palpitations), examination, other ECG changes, electrolytes, medications, echo if disease suspected. Compare with old ECGs.
- **2.** **Urgency and complexity:** this is elective, minor surgery, so if the patient is **symptomatic or has intermittent higher-grade block, delay and arrange cardiology review for a permanent pacemaker**. An asymptomatic patient with stable bifascicular block plus PR prolongation can usually proceed with an appropriate rescue plan; alternating BBB, Mobitz II or advanced AV block needs a different pacing pathway.
## Intraop

- **3.** **Technique:** local or regional with minimal sedation is attractive. If GA, review conduction-slowing drugs and titrate anaesthesia; do not abruptly stop indicated chronic beta-blockade without a reason, avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia and potassium or magnesium changes. Titrate neuraxial block (sympathectomy).
- **4.** **Preparation:** transcutaneous pacing and defibrillation pads on, a defibrillator and transvenous pacing available, and atropine, adrenaline and isoprenaline drawn up. Avoid a PAC.
- **5.** **Monitoring:** continuous ECG with pacing mode visible, an arterial line if there is any instability.
## Postop

- **6.** **Recovery:** continue ECG monitoring in recovery, and correct triggers.

**Key evidence:** [BRADY](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000628) · [ALS](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias)

items.q: A patient with known primary pulmonary hypertension is scheduled to undergo elective umbilical hernia repair. How will you assess the severity of this patient's pulmonary hypertension? (50%) How does this diagnosis affect your perioperative management of this patient? (50%)
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2016.1 report: severity assessment needed functional status plus another measurement; relate disease severity to facilities and anaesthetic modifications. Retain the 50:50 weighting.

## Assessing severity (50%)

PH is **mPAP >20 mmHg at rest on right-heart catheterisation**. Precapillary PH requires PAWP ≤15 mmHg and PVR >2 Wood units; PAH additionally requires a group 1 cause. Severity depends on pressure **and** RV function; a failing RV can generate lower pressures.

| Method | Findings suggesting severe disease |
|---|---|
| **Functional class and history** | WHO class III to IV, rapid progression, **syncope**, chest pain, signs of RV failure (raised JVP, V waves, hepatomegaly, oedema) |
| **Exercise tests** | WHO class, 6MWD, BNP/NT-proBNP and trends; in ESC/ERS PAH risk assessment, 6MWD <165 m and peak VO2 <11 mL/kg/min are high-risk markers, interpreted within the whole profile |
| **Echo** | TR velocity >3.4 m/s suggests high echocardiographic probability of PH; assess RV size/function (TAPSE ≤17 mm or FAC ≤35% abnormal), RV–PA coupling, septal flattening, RA size and effusion. Echo pressure alone does not grade clinical severity |
| **Right heart catheter** | RAP >14 mmHg, CI <2.0 L/min/m² and low mixed venous saturation support high-risk PAH; interpret PVR/PAWP and the clinical profile. Historical mPAP severity bands are not a modern PAH risk classification |
| **Other** | BNP, ECG (RV strain), chest X-ray, oxygen saturation, blood count, liver function |

The **cause** (WHO group) and whether the patient is on advanced therapy (bosentan, sildenafil, prostacyclin) also influence risk.

## Effect on perioperative management (50%)

PH confers increased risk, with no universal mortality/morbidity percentage. **Severity decides the facilities needed**: mild and well-controlled PH may be managed in a general hospital, while moderate to severe PH needs a centre with ICU and PH or cardiac expertise and may be better treated with local anaesthesia, or deferred.
### Preop

- **Optimisation:** continue all pulmonary vasodilators (never interrupt prostacyclin), optimise volume status and oxygen, plan HDU or ICU, anxiolysis, and VTE prophylaxis.
### Intraop

- **Technique:** local infiltration or regional block with minimal sedation is attractive for a hernia repair. Avoid single-shot spinal. If GA: avoid sympathetic surges and keep SVR (RV coronary perfusion), avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia and N2O, careful positive pressure ventilation near FRC, vasopressor ready.
- **Monitoring:** an arterial line for significant disease or haemodynamic risk (central access when vasoactive delivery or the procedure justifies it); sedation without monitoring is dangerous.
### Postop

- **Recovery:** monitored care according to severity, surgery and intraoperative course, often 24–72 hours for higher-risk patients, analgesia that avoids hypoventilation, oxygen, and a plan for a PH crisis (reduce PVR, maintain SVR, inhaled nitric oxide, milrinone, vasopressor).

**Key evidence:** [PH](https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.00879-2022) · [PHOP](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36924225/) · [ASE](https://www.asecho.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/ASE-Right-Heart-Guidelines-May-2025.pdf)

Names objective assessments (echo, exercise testing, BNP or RHC), using a multiparameter risk profile rather than pressure bands
Notes that RV function matters as well as pressure

Relates severity to the facilities and level of care needed
Describes risk-matched anaesthetic modifications, avoidance of PVR/SVR collapse and appropriate monitoring
Includes continuation of pulmonary vasodilators and postoperative care

items.title: 2014.1 Q2: Ablation of an accessory pathway in the electrophysiology laboratory
items.q: An otherwise well 35-year-old woman is scheduled for ablation of an accessory atrio-ventricular pathway in the Cardiac Electrophysiology laboratory. What are the implications for anaesthesia and how would you manage them?
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2014.1 Q2, pp. 5–6: Describe procedure duration, the isolated EP-laboratory setting, and life-threatening intra- and postprocedure complications, with prevention and management. The original answer already covered these minimum elements. [Original report on Learn@ANZCA](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106426).

## Main problems

An isolated, remote location, a long procedure (often several hours) needing a motionless patient, an arrhythmia the team wants to be **inducible**, and unique life-threatening complications.

## Preop

- **Patient:** history of the arrhythmia (AVRT, pre-excited AF, syncope), the ECG (short PR, delta wave), drugs (antiarrhythmic withdrawal is directed by the electrophysiologist to preserve inducibility; do not stop them independently), electrolytes, and a **pregnancy test** (radiation).
- **Location:** a full anaesthetic set-up as in theatre (machine, suction, airway equipment, defibrillator, pacing, emergency drugs), **radiation protection**, a clear plan for help, and good communication with the electrophysiologist through a headset or screen, because teams work in a control room.
- **Pads:** apply **external defibrillation and pacing pads** before the start, as the fluoroscopy field limits access.

## Intraop

- **GA or appropriately monitored sedation** is selected with the electrophysiologist. Immobility and airway access favour GA in some patients; simple accessory-pathway studies may suit sedation. Evidence from complex AF ablation must not be automatically extrapolated to every accessory-pathway procedure. Use agents that do not suppress the pathway (propofol, remifentanil and a low-dose volatile are acceptable); avoid unnecessary antiarrhythmic effect and **atropine or beta-agonists** unless needed.
- Monitoring: standard, with invasive pressure for long or complex cases, temperature, urinary catheter with irrigated catheters, warming (without electrical interference).
- Neuromuscular block for intubation, or remifentanil alone to maintain immobility.

## Life-threatening complications (intra- and postprocedural)

| Complication | Management |
|---|---|
| **Tamponade** (perforation; risk depends on pathway site and technique) | Echo, stop heparin and give protamine, pericardiocentesis, surgery |
| **Complete heart block** (AV node injury) | Transcutaneous or transvenous pacing, chronotropes |
| **Rapid pre-excited AF, VT or VF** | Synchronised DC cardioversion or defibrillation; **avoid all AV-nodal blockers, including IV amiodarone, adenosine, verapamil/diltiazem, beta-blockers and digoxin** in pre-excited AF |
| **Thromboembolism or stroke** | For left-heart access, use the agreed procedural heparin/ACT protocol and meticulous sheath de-airing; the requirement for postprocedure antithrombotic treatment is pathway/access-specific, not automatic aspirin or anticoagulation |
| **Vascular injury or bleeding, pneumothorax, coronary injury** | Local pressure, imaging, surgery |

## Postop

Recovery with ECG monitoring, groin and haemodynamic checks for tamponade, analgesia and antiemetics (avoiding QT prolongation), and bed rest as directed.

**Key evidence:** [ABL](https://academic.oup.com/europace/article/26/4/euae043/7639428) · [AFUS](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11104284/)

Includes postprocedure monitoring

items.title: 2011.1 Q14: Interpreting an abnormal ECG and its anaesthetic implications
items.q: (a) Describe the abnormality on this electrocardiogram. (30%) (b) What are the implications of this abnormality for anaesthesia? (70%)
items.model:
![2011.1 Q14: representative ECG for practice](set12-saq-2011-1-ecg.jpg)

> Illustrative practice ECG, not the original exam tracing (Wikimedia Commons). Describe the abnormality before revealing the model answer.

> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2011.1 Q14, p. 10: The report explicitly identifies QT prolongation not explained by QRS prolongation. Cover potentially fatal/unmasked disease, acquired peri-anaesthetic causes, existing treatment, practical monitoring/therapy, postoperative destination and rescue of life-threatening events. [Original report on Learn@ANZCA](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106420).

## a) ECG interpretation

**Diagnosis verified from the original report:** QT prolongation not accounted for by QRS widening. The archived report specifies the diagnosis but does not reproduce the ECG, so do not invent an exact QT/QTc measurement for that historical tracing.

**Prolonged QT interval** should be assessed in relation to QRS width. Measure the QT from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave, correct for rate (QTc = QT / square root of the R-R interval, Bazett), and compare: >450 ms in men and >460 ms in women is traditionally prolonged, but borderline QTc alone does not diagnose congenital LQTS; repeated QTc ≥480 ms, clinical scoring or a pathogenic variant supports diagnosis after excluding secondary causes, and above 500 ms confers a high risk of torsades de pointes. Look for notched or broad T waves, T-wave alternans, bradycardia and a normal QRS width.

## b) Implications for anaesthesia

The condition is **potentially fatal and may be unmasked by anaesthesia**: it predisposes to torsades de pointes, VF and sudden death, triggered by sympathetic surges and bradycardia or pauses.

**Causes**
- **Congenital long QT** (LQT1 to 3, ion channelopathy; symptoms of syncope, family history of sudden death).
- **Acquired:** drugs (class Ia and III antiarrhythmics, droperidol, haloperidol, ondansetron, macrolides, methadone, antipsychotics, volatile agents, suxamethonium), **hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia**, hypothermia, bradycardia, ischaemia, hypothyroidism, raised ICP.

### Preop
- Preoperative: baseline 12-lead and QTc, review drugs and electrolytes, a **cardiologist**, and the patient's treatment: **continue beta-blockers** (a single missed dose matters), check for an ICD (apply a procedure-specific EMI plan; if therapies are suspended, provide continuous monitoring and external defibrillation until reactivated), pacemaker, mexiletine, or left cardiac sympathetic denervation.
- Correct hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypocalcaemia, with renal-aware replacement; a high-normal potassium target may be chosen for TdP risk rather than imposing K >4.5 on everyone; avoid drugs that prolong the QT. Anxiolysis, good analgesia and a quiet environment to avoid sympathetic surges.
### Intraop

- **Technique:** regional is safe (no adrenaline in local anaesthetic); in GA use propofol, avoid ketamine, and recognise that all volatiles can prolong QT; isoflurane has been used successfully, but evidence does not establish one universally safest volatile; attenuate the laryngoscopy response; avoid conventional neostigmine and atropine (use sugammadex); use phenylephrine or metaraminol for hypotension rather than ephedrine or adrenaline; avoid droperidol and the antiemetics that prolong QT.
- **Monitoring:** continuous ECG with defibrillator and pads available, magnesium drawn up, arterial line if unstable.
- **Torsades:** IV magnesium (ANZCOR 11.9: 5 mmol over 10 min, repeat once if needed; other established protocols use MgSO4 2 g ≈8 mmol), correct potassium, stop the cause, overdrive pacing (or isoprenaline in acquired, bradycardia-dependent cases, not congenital LQTS), and give an **unsynchronised shock for sustained polymorphic VT even with a pulse**, or VF/pulseless VT; do not delay shock for magnesium.
### Postop

- **Recovery:** calm environment, continued beta-blockade, electrolyte and drug review, cardiology handover and monitored care matched to risk (the BJA Education review advises at least 24 hours for congenital LQTS). Restore ICD therapies before leaving the monitored setting.

**Key evidence:** [LQTS](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7808061/) · [ALS](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias)

States that it is potentially fatal (torsades, VF) and may be unmasked by anaesthesia
Recognises congenital and acquired causes (drugs, electrolytes, hypothermia)
Describes patient treatments relevant to anaesthesia (beta-blocker, ICD, pacing)
Gives practical preoperative, drug and technique choices (continue beta-blocker, correct K and Mg, avoid QT drugs)
Plans monitoring, defibrillator and treatment of torsades (magnesium, pacing, defibrillation)
Plans postoperative disposal

items.title: 2010.2 Q7: Pacemaker classification and perioperative principles
items.q: (a) Describe the common classification code for permanent pacemakers. (30%) (b) Outline the principles involved in the perioperative management of patients with a permanent pacemaker. (70%)
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2010.2 Q7, pp. 7–8: Correct code order (paced, sensed, response), positions IV/V and ICD distinctions. Assess patient and device/dependence; plan when technical staff are unavailable, explain device-specific magnet effects, display pacing spikes, use independent pulse monitoring, provide rescue and restore ICD therapies. The report states an arterial line is not mandatory for every pacemaker patient. [Original report on Learn@ANZCA](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106419).

## a) NBG code (NASPE/BPEG)

Five positions: **I chamber paced** (O, A, V, D); **II chamber sensed** (O, A, V, D); **III response to sensing** (O, I inhibited, T triggered, D dual); **IV rate modulation** (O, R); **V multisite pacing** (O, A, V, D). Examples: VVI (ventricle paced and sensed, inhibited); DDD (both chambers, dual response); AAIR; and ICDs add antitachycardia pacing and shock functions. Position IV is rate response (R).

## b) Principles (pre, intra and post)

**Manage the patient, not the pacemaker.**

### Preop
- **Patient:** indication, symptoms of malfunction, severity and stability of underlying heart disease, medications.
- **Dependency:** the ECG, indication, interrogation and adequacy of the underlying escape rhythm; spikes before every beat alone do not prove dependence; pacemaker dependence changes management.
- **Device:** review current interrogation and obtain updated specialist assessment when indicated (traditional 12-month PPM/6-month ICD follow-up intervals are not a universal perioperative clearance rule), with battery, thresholds and settings; consider reprogramming. In an emergency or after hours, proceed on clinical signs and simple investigations.
- Plan from the **type and site of surgery** and diathermy; know the **magnet response**: a magnet turns most pacemakers to asynchronous pacing (DOO or VOO), whereas a magnet over an ICD **suspends antitachycardia therapy but does not alter the pacing**.

### Intraop
- ECG plus a pulse monitor (plethysmograph or arterial line). **Select the monitor’s pacing/pacemaker-detection mode where available**, because filters may suppress pacing artefacts; confirm mechanical capture independently, and never treat a displayed spike as proof of output. This specifically addresses the examiner feedback.
- **EMI:** bipolar diathermy or short monopolar bursts, return plate positioned so that the current avoids the device, cables away from the generator; keep monopolar diathermy below the umbilicus where possible.
- Avoid myopotential inhibition (suxamethonium fasciculation) and be aware of other EMI sources (nerve stimulators, lithotripsy, ECT, MRI).
- Magnet or asynchronous mode for dependent patients with unavoidable monopolar diathermy above the umbilicus; keep rate response off if it responds to minute ventilation or vibration.
- **External pacing and defibrillation pads** and drugs (atropine, isoprenaline) on hand; correct electrolytes.

### Postop
- Continue ECG monitoring; **restore programmed settings**; reinterrogate if EMI was likely, the device was reprogrammed, or the patient had cardioversion.

**Key evidence:** [CIED](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12068544/) · [NZCIED](https://nzmj.org.nz/journal/vol-137-no-1590/heart-rhythm-new-zealand-consensus-statement-on-the-practical-management-of-cardiac-implanted-electronic-devices-in-the-peri-ope)

items.title: 2010.1 Q14: Palpitations and two ECGs in a patient for tonsillectomy
items.q: A 58 year old man presents for tonsillectomy for a tonsillar tumour. He has a 2 year history of intermittent palpitations. His electrocardiogram at diagnosis shows the following. a. What is the diagnosis? Describe the electrocardiographic changes that support your diagnosis. (30%) Following the administration of neostigmine and atropine for reversal of neuromuscular blockade, you see the following rhythm on your monitor. b. What is this rhythm? How would you manage this situation? (70%)
items.model:
![2010.1 Q14: representative ECG A](set12-saq-2010-1-ecgA.jpg)

![2010.1 Q14: representative ECG B](set12-saq-2010-1-ecgB.jpg)

> Illustrative practice ECGs A and B, not the original exam tracings (Wikimedia Commons). Name the diagnosis in each before revealing the model answer.

> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2010.1 Q14, pp. 12–13: The report explicitly identifies WPW in part A and VF in part B. Describe the ECG systematically and integrate the palpitations history; poor VF-resuscitation knowledge scored badly. The report says some candidates calling the second rhythm torsades could still pass with accurate resuscitation, but VF remains the stated diagnosis. [Original report on Learn@ANZCA](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106418).

> **Diagnoses verified from the original report:** part A **WPW syndrome**; part B **ventricular fibrillation**. The archived report names both diagnoses but does not reproduce the original ECG images. Representative educational figures appear above the model answer.

## a) Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome

With the history of **palpitations** (usually atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia), the ECG shows pre-excitation. Describe it systematically:
- Rate and rhythm (sinus), axis (may be abnormal).
- **Short PR interval** (below 120 ms).
- **Delta wave**: slurred slow upstroke of the QRS.
- **Widened QRS** (typically ≥120 ms, but may be less with minimal pre-excitation) from fusion of conduction through the accessory pathway and the AV node.
- **Secondary ST and T-wave changes** (discordant to the delta wave); pseudo-infarct patterns. Delta-wave polarity and the full 12-lead pattern suggest pathway location; V1 polarity alone does not reliably localise every pathway.

## b) The rhythm: ventricular fibrillation

Chaotic irregular activity with no QRS complexes. It can occur after **atropine** (tachycardia and rapid conduction), or when pre-excited AF is conducted rapidly over the accessory pathway and degenerates into VF. **Historical examiner feedback:** some candidates describing torsades still passed this section when resuscitation was accurate. This does not change the report’s intended diagnosis of **VF** or justify conflating its ECG appearance with TdP. Use current ALS for VF; use the separate long-QT/TdP pathway when that is the actual rhythm.

**Management (ALS algorithm)**
- **1.** **Confirm** the patient is pulseless and unresponsive; **call for help**, ask for the defibrillator and stop surgery; check the circuit and the leads.
- **2.** **Start CPR** (30:2 or continuous compressions after airway secured), 100% oxygen, secure the airway (the airway is shared with the surgeon after tonsil surgery; check for blood).
- **3.** **Defibrillate immediately** (biphasic 150 to 200 J, manufacturer's advice), resume CPR for 2 minutes, then reassess.
- **4.** **Adrenaline 1 mg** after the second shock, then every 3 to 5 minutes; **amiodarone 300 mg** after the third shock (150 mg after the fifth).
- **5.** **Reversible causes (4Hs and 4Ts):** hypoxia, hypovolaemia (bleeding), hyper- or hypokalaemia, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis.
- **6.** **After ROSC:** 12-lead ECG, oxygen and ventilation targets, haemodynamic support, temperature control, ICU, cardiology and electrophysiology review (ablation of the pathway before further surgery).
- **7.** Avoid AV node blocking drugs (including IV amiodarone, adenosine, verapamil/diltiazem, beta-blockers and digoxin) if pre-excited AF recurs; use cardioversion.

Inform the surgeon and family and document the event.

**Key evidence:** [AFUS](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11104284/) · [ALS](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias)

items.title: 2009.2 Q10: Biphasic versus monophasic defibrillators, synchronisation and hazards
items.q: 1. Describe the differences between biphasic and monophasic manual external cardiac defibrillators. (50%) 2. What is the "synchronize" button for? When would you use it? (20%) 3. List the potential hazards of defibrillation. (30%)
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2009.2 Q10, p. 8: Compare current direction, energy requirements and efficacy. Explain synchronisation to avoid repolarisation, and hazards to patient/staff. Avoid confusion between volts, amperes and joules and incorrectly labelled waveforms; preserve the 50:20:30 weighting. [Original report on Learn@ANZCA](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106417).

## 1. Biphasic versus monophasic (50%)

A defibrillator stores energy in a capacitor charged to a high voltage; energy (joules) is power over time, and it is the **current (amperes)** passing through the myocardium that depolarises it. Transthoracic impedance varies with patient, pad contact, position and waveform; a single fixed impedance is not an assumption for treatment.

| | Monophasic | Biphasic |
|---|---|---|
| **Current** | Flows **one direction** (damped sinusoid or truncated exponential) | Flows in **one direction then reverses** (truncated exponential or rectilinear) |
| **Energy** | High: 360 J | Lower: waveform/manufacturer-specific; often 150–200 J initially for adult defibrillation, escalating as indicated. Cardioversion settings are rhythm-specific |
| **Efficacy** | Lower first-shock success | **Equal or higher first-shock success** at lower energy |
| **Myocardial damage** | Higher energy requirement; injury depends on waveform, current density, contact and cumulative exposure | Lower energy requirement does not guarantee less clinical myocardial injury in every comparison |
| **Impedance** | Not compensated | Compensated: the device adjusts the waveform |
| **Status** | Largely replaced | Standard in modern devices |

Draw the waveform: monophasic is a single positive deflection decaying to zero; biphasic has a positive phase then a negative phase.

## 2. The "synchronize" button (20%)

It makes the defibrillator detect the **R wave** and deliver the shock in the QRS, avoiding the **vulnerable period** (the T wave, repolarisation) where a shock may cause VF. It is used for **elective or emergency cardioversion of a rhythm with a pulse**: AF, flutter, SVT, **monomorphic** ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. It is **not** used for VF or pulseless VT, and **sustained polymorphic VT requires an unsynchronised shock even with a pulse** because reliable R-wave synchronisation is not possible. Recheck/reselect synchronisation before every shock; device reset behaviour varies.

## 3. Hazards (30%)

- **Patient:** failure to shock, **VF or asystole** (shock on T wave, unsynchronised, or bradycardia), burns, myocardial injury, muscle and nerve damage, thromboembolism after AF cardioversion, damage to a pacemaker or ICD, aspiration or awareness with sedation.
- **Staff:** electric shock to anyone touching the patient or bed, and wet surfaces.
- **Environment and equipment:** fire in an oxygen-rich atmosphere, explosion with flammable agents, a flat battery or wrong pad placement, and delay in CPR.

**Key evidence:** [ALS](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias) · [AF](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/45/36/3314/7738779)

Explains synchronisation to the R wave to avoid the vulnerable period
