items.title: 2008.1 Q10: AICD with biventricular pacing for elective surgery
items.q: A patient with an automatic implanted cardiac defibrillator (AICD) with biventricular pacing presents for elective surgery? Describe how the presence of this device influences your perioperative management of this patient.
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2008.1 Q10, pp. 6–7: The historical marking guide allocates 3 marks to preop, 5 to intraop, 1 to postop and 1 to explaining biventricular resynchronisation in heart failure. Emphasise underlying HF/LV function, ventricular arrhythmia and dependence; preserve biventricular pacing rather than switching casually to VVIR; understand magnet effects and reactivate ICD therapy. Its near-routine arterial-line/HDU language reflects the stated HF population and is not a modern rule for every CRT recipient. [Original report on Learn@ANZCA](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106415).

**Historical marking emphasis:** device/HF understanding 1 mark, Preop 3, Intraop 5, Postop 1. Use this distribution to balance the answer; retain current, patient-specific monitoring and programming decisions.

## What the device is

A biventricular ICD (**CRT-D**) paces **both the right and left ventricle** (the left lead is usually in a coronary sinus branch) to restore ventricular synchrony in patients with **heart failure, poor LV function** (EF below 35%) and a wide QRS, and it also senses and treats VT and VF. Review the actual device configuration and current ventricular function: lead number alone neither proves severe heart failure nor establishes pacing dependence; CRT may have improved function.

## Preop

- **Assess current heart-failure and surgical risk:** and optimise heart failure (symptoms, volume, drugs, electrolytes).
- **History and examination:** heart failure and LV function (recent echo), ventricular arrhythmias and shocks, pacing dependency, and device history.
- **Device check** reviewed for current battery, lead data, underlying rhythm and settings; arrange recent interrogation when risk or uncertainty warrants it (a routine 6-month follow-up interval is not a guarantee of perioperative suitability).
- **Plan with the technician:** switch off the **antitachycardia therapy** immediately before surgery (or place a magnet over the ICD if a technician is not available). **Preserve biventricular resynchronisation**. If pacing-dependent and significant EMI is expected, programme an appropriate asynchronous mode **that retains biventricular pacing**; an ICD magnet cannot provide this. Consider rate-response deactivation according to sensor/EMI exposure. Routine disabling of tachy therapies is unnecessary for genuinely low-EMI procedures.

## Intraop

- **Invasive monitoring:** consider an arterial line according to LV function, symptoms, procedure and haemodynamic risk, rather than CRT-D alone, plus 5-lead ECG and a pulse monitor.
- **EMI precautions:** bipolar diathermy or short monopolar bursts, return plate away from the device.
- **External defibrillation and pacing pads** applied before therapy is disabled, and the defibrillator ready.
- Anaesthetic goals of heart failure: avoid hypotension, tachycardia and fluid overload, and titrate drugs.

## Postop

**Reactivate antitachycardia therapy** before the patient leaves the monitored area, with interrogation if reprogrammed or EMI was significant. Choose recovery/ward/HDU/ICU by clinical and surgical risk; CRT-D alone does not mandate HDU.

**Key evidence:** [CIED](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12068544/) · [NZCIED](https://nzmj.org.nz/journal/vol-137-no-1590/heart-rhythm-new-zealand-consensus-statement-on-the-practical-management-of-cardiac-implanted-electronic-devices-in-the-peri-ope)

![2007.1 Q10: representative ECG 2](set12-saq-2007-1-ecg2.jpg)

> Illustrative practice ECGs, not the original exam tracings (Wikimedia Commons). For ECG 1, interpret the upper tracing only; the lower panel is a separate conduction-pattern example.

> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2007.1 Q10, pp. 2, 7–8: The pass-rate table reports 53%. The guide awards credit for both ECG diagnoses and management integrating diabetes, laparoscopic/vagal and renal/bleeding causes, stopping surgery/insufflation, positional/preload measures, chronotropes/pacing, investigation and cardiology/ICU escalation. The historical question relied on two ECG figures; the available written marking commentary does not explicitly name both diagnoses. [Original report on Learn@ANZCA](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106413).

## The ECGs — interpretation of the historical question

Read each systematically: rate, rhythm, P waves, PR interval, QRS width/axis and ST–T changes.

- **ECG 1 — interpretation retained from the earlier audit:** **bifascicular conduction disease, consistent with RBBB plus left anterior fascicular block**: a predominantly positive broad right-precordial QRS/terminal rightward forces with marked left axis (positive I/aVL and predominantly negative inferior leads). The small, low-resolution atrial deflections do not permit a confident numerical PR measurement; do not add first-degree AV block or call this proven “trifascicular” disease without measuring it on an adequate original. This is the audit’s image interpretation, not a diagnosis explicitly named by the examiner’s prose.
- **ECG 2 — interpretation retained from the earlier audit:** **complete AV block with a slow broad-complex escape rhythm**. P waves march through at a faster rate independently of the QRS complexes, with no fixed PR relationship. With BP **70/30**, this is haemodynamically compromising advanced block requiring immediate support and reliable pacing preparation.

**Source distinction:** the diagnoses in this retained model answer were inferred during the earlier audit of the historical question, rather than stated in the written examiner commentary. The illustrated ECGs above are separate examples and must not be used to infer exact interval measurements or morphology from the original exam. The historical original tracing cannot be independently remeasured here.

## Context

A **diabetic** may have atherosclerosis, autonomic neuropathy and silent ischaemia; diabetes alone does not establish these diagnoses. Laparoscopy causes **vagal bradycardia** (peritoneal stretch), raised intra-abdominal pressure, head-down tilt, hypercarbia and reduced venous return; the kidney surgery adds bleeding risk.

## Management

- **1.** **Call for help**, stop the procedure and inform the surgeon; 100% oxygen, check airway, ventilation and the circuit.
- **2.** **Release the pneumoperitoneum, optimise position** and give a cautious fluid bolus only if reduced preload/bleeding is likely; do not automatically volume-load ventricular failure.
- **3.** **Drugs:** **atropine** 500–600 micrograms IV (repeat to 3 mg), **ephedrine**, then **adrenaline** boluses or an infusion, or **isoprenaline** if there is no response. Do not delay pacing for repeated atropine in advanced infranodal block. Glucagon is for suspected beta-blocker toxicity, not routine treatment simply because a beta-blocker is prescribed.
- **4.** **Pacing:** apply pads and start **transcutaneous pacing** at once if drugs fail; **transvenous pacing**, then a **permanent pacemaker** if the block persists.
- **5.** **Look for the cause:** a vagal response, hypoxia, hypercarbia, **myocardial ischaemia or infarction** (inferior MI causes AV block), pneumothorax or gas embolism, anaphylaxis, hyperkalaemia and other electrolyte disturbance, drugs (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, opioids, neostigmine, dexmedetomidine), and haemorrhage (renal bleeding).
- **6.** **Investigate:** blood gas, electrolytes, glucose, troponin, 12-lead ECG, echo.
- **7.** **Escalate:** cardiology, ICU transfer, inform relatives, and continue if CPR is needed (ALS).

If the rhythm resolves after stopping insufflation, reassess the cause and conduction risk with senior/cardiology input before deciding whether this elective major operation should continue. Do not automatically restart after complete AV block; if proceeding is justified after stabilisation, use cautious low-pressure insufflation and a reliable pacing/rescue plan.

**Key evidence:** [ALS](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias) · [BRADY](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000628)

Calls for help and includes a differential diagnosis with the effects of insufflation, vagal response and bleeding
Stops the procedure/releases pneumoperitoneum, supports perfusion and gives volume only if appropriate
Uses appropriate chronotropes and does not delay reliable pacing in advanced AV block
Gives pacing options (transcutaneous, transvenous, permanent)
Investigates the cause (ischaemia, hypoxia, hypercarbia, electrolytes, pneumothorax) and escalates

items.title: 2006.1 Q8: Permanent pacemaker for total hip replacement
items.source: Past SAQ 2006.1 Q8 · pass rate not reported
items.q: The first patient on your orthopaedic list tomorrow is scheduled for left total hip replacement. He has an implanted (permanent) cardiac pacemaker. Discuss the relevant factors in your pre-anaesthetic assessment of this patient.
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus (report directly reviewed):** 2006.1 Q8, p. 4: Obtain a cardiac history/indication, establish underlying rhythm and dependence, seek technical interrogation/programming advice and address practical surgery/diathermy issues. Avoid simply cancelling because a device was not checked within six months or asking the surgeon to avoid all diathermy. No individual Q8 pass percentage is stated in this report. [Original report on Learn@ANZCA](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106411).

## History: why does he have a pacemaker?

- **Indication:** AV block, sick sinus syndrome, bradycardia, heart failure (biventricular), or tachyarrhythmia. This tells you the **underlying rhythm** and cardiac disease.
- **Symptoms:** syncope, presyncope, dizziness, palpitations, dyspnoea, chest pain (malfunction or heart failure), and exercise tolerance for the hip replacement.
- Other cardiac disease, medications, anticoagulants, and previous anaesthetics, as well as the **date of insertion**.

## Is he pacemaker dependent?

- **Underlying rhythm:** examine the pulse and the ECG (pacing spikes before every beat suggest high pacing burden but do not prove dependence), look at the percentage paced on the last device check, and ask whether a technician can temporarily lower the rate to reveal the underlying rhythm.
- A dependent patient will be affected if **electromagnetic interference** inhibits pacing.

## Pacemaker details and technical advice

- **Device and last check:** card or record (manufacturer, model, mode such as DDD or VVI-R), review current function, with updated interrogation if uncertainty, changed symptoms or procedure risk warrants it; traditional follow-up intervals are **12 months for PPM/6 months for ICD**, not a universal clearance rule; confirm battery life, lead thresholds and impedance.
- **Magnet response:** pacemakers generally go asynchronous with a magnet; a magnet does not switch off an ICD's pacing.
- **Practical approach:** if the last check is out of date, arrange an **interrogation** or reprogramming by a pacemaker technician before surgery; do not simply cancel, and do not rely on the surgeon avoiding diathermy.

## Investigations

ECG and relevant electrolytes; CXR only if device/lead identity, position or pathology is uncertain; echo if symptoms or an unanswered question about ventricular/valve function would change management. Routine CXR/echo is not required solely for a pacemaker.

## Surgical and anaesthetic considerations

- **Site:** a hip is well **below the umbilicus**, so the risk of EMI is lower when the return path remains below the iliac crest/umbilicus and there is no abdominal generator; use bipolar diathermy or short monopolar bursts with the return plate on the thigh so that the current path avoids the chest.
- **Plan** for the technique (regional with sedation or general), pulse monitoring, **cement** hypotension and embolism, and a **peripheral nerve stimulator** (which can be sensed).
- Have a **magnet**, external pacing and defibrillator pads, and atropine and isoprenaline available, and document restoration and arrange interrogation for reprogramming, suspected malfunction, significant EMI or external shock rather than automatically after every uneventful case.

**Key evidence:** [CIED](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12068544/) · [NZCIED](https://nzmj.org.nz/journal/vol-137-no-1590/heart-rhythm-new-zealand-consensus-statement-on-the-practical-management-of-cardiac-implanted-electronic-devices-in-the-peri-ope)
rubric: Obtains the indication and cardiac history for the pacemaker
Establishes the underlying rhythm and whether the patient is pacemaker dependent
Checks the device type, last check date (12 months) and magnet response
Arranges technical advice, interrogation or reprogramming and does not simply cancel
Notes the surgical site (hip below the umbilicus), diathermy type and plate position
Plans practical precautions (pulse monitor, magnet, pads, drugs, post-op check)
Uses ECG/relevant electrolytes and CXR/echo only when clinically indicated

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
The studies below explain the evidence behind clinical decisions. They are deliberately placed after the teaching chapters: each should reinforce an already-understood concept, **not dictate the order in which the subject is taught**. Links lead to primary publications or a trustworthy trial summary when a primary free-text link is unavailable. Neutral trials are not proof of equivalence outside their population.

## A. Atrial fibrillation: rate, rhythm, ablation and anticoagulation

| Study | Result to remember | Final-exam implication |
|---|---|---|
| [AFFIRM (NEJM 2002)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa021328) | In older AF patients at stroke/death risk, five-year mortality was 23.8% with drug-led rhythm control vs 21.3% rate control (difference not statistically significant); rhythm group had more hospitalisation/adverse drug effects. | Rhythm control was not routinely superior with the older drug strategy; **continue anticoagulation based on stroke risk**, even in apparent sinus rhythm. |
| [RACE II (NEJM 2010)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1001337) | Lenient resting HR <110/min was non-inferior to strict targets in selected stable permanent AF (3-y outcome 12.9% vs 14.9%). | A heart rate of 100/min in stable chronic AF is not necessarily treatment failure; tailor for symptoms, HF, MS and ischaemia. |
| [EAST-AFNET 4 (NEJM 2020)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2019422) | Early rhythm control in 2,789 patients with recently diagnosed AF and CV conditions lowered composite CV outcomes (3.9 vs 5.0 events per 100 patient-years; HR 0.79). | Modern early rhythm control may improve prognosis in selected newly diagnosed AF; does not mean immediate drug conversion of all POAF. |
| [CASTLE-AF (NEJM 2018)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1707855) | In selected AF/HFrEF patients with an implanted defibrillator, catheter ablation reduced death or HF hospitalisation (28.5% vs 44.6%). | Arrhythmia treatment can meaningfully improve ventricular function/outcomes in carefully selected HF. |
| [CABANA (JAMA 2019)](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2019.0693) | Intention-to-treat primary composite outcome did not show a statistically significant benefit of catheter ablation over drug therapy, with substantial treatment cross-over. | Discuss symptoms, AF recurrence and the limits of ITT vs treatment-received analyses. |
| [BRIDGE (NEJM 2015)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1501035) | In warfarin-treated AF patients requiring interruption, omission of LMWH bridging was non-inferior for arterial thromboembolism and caused less major bleeding. | **Most AF does not require heparin bridging**, but recent stroke, mechanical valves and selected special populations require separate evaluation; BRIDGE excluded mechanical valves. |
| [PAUSE (JAMA Intern Med 2019)](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2019.2431) | Standardised perioperative DOAC interruption/resumption without heparin bridging produced low bleeding and arterial thromboembolism rates in AF cohorts. | Plan DOAC timing around renal function, bleeding risk and neuraxial precautions rather than routine heparin. |

## B. Pacing and device management

| Study | Result to remember | Final-exam implication |
|---|---|---|
| [MOST (NEJM 2002)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa013040) | Dual-chamber pacing did not reduce death/stroke versus ventricular pacing in sinus-node dysfunction but reduced AF and HF symptoms and improved quality of life modestly. | **Physiological AV synchrony matters**, but choice of mode does not confer a universal mortality benefit. |
| [DANPACE (Eur Heart J 2011)](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehr030) | AAIR versus DDDR in sinus-node disease: no significant difference in death; AF and need for reoperation were greater with AAIR in the study. | Atrial-only pacing needs reliably intact AV conduction; DDDR may reduce later problems for selected patients. |
| [DAVID (JAMA 2002)](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.288.24.3115) | DDDR-70 with unnecessary RV pacing in ICD patients with LV dysfunction led to more death/HF hospitalisation than backup VVI-40. | **Unnecessary RV pacing can worsen ventricular dyssynchrony and HF.** |
| [BLOCK-HF (NEJM 2013)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1210356) | In AV block with reduced/midrange LV function needing substantial pacing, biventricular pacing improved composite outcomes versus RV pacing. | CRT can prevent pacing-related deterioration in selected patients; not all pacing-dependent patients need CRT. |
| [SCD-HeFT (NEJM 2005)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa043399) | ICD reduced all-cause mortality in selected NYHA II–III HFrEF patients versus placebo; amiodarone did not improve survival. | ICD is for **sudden death prevention**, not proof that contractile function is improved. |
| [MADIT-II (NEJM 2002)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa013474) | Prophylactic ICD reduced mortality after previous MI with LVEF ≤30% in the studied population. | Primary-prevention ICD decisions require EF and eligibility/timing criteria, not an EF value alone. |
| [BRUISE CONTROL (NEJM 2013)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1302946) | Clinically significant device-pocket haematoma: **3.5% continued warfarin vs 16% heparin bridging**. | For selected device implantation patients, avoid routine heparin bridging; distinguish pocket surgery from unrelated operations. |
| [BRUISE CONTROL-2 (Eur Heart J 2018)](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy413) | Continued versus interrupted DOAC around device surgery produced similar low rates of clinically significant pocket haematoma. | Either tailored strategy may be reasonable; do not extrapolate to all surgery/neuraxial blocks. |
| [MODIFIED Valsalva / REVERT (Lancet 2015)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(15)61485-4) | Modified Valsalva improved conversion of stable SVT compared with standard technique. | Try an effective vagal manoeuvre before adenosine in suitable awake stable SVT. |

## C. Pulmonary arterial hypertension and RV disease

| Study | Result to remember | Final-exam implication |
|---|---|---|
| [AMBITION (NEJM 2015)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1413687) | Initial combination ambrisentan + tadalafil reduced clinical failure versus either monotherapy in treatment-naïve PAH. | Modern PAH often uses **combination therapy**; preserve prescribed drugs perioperatively. |
| [SERAPHIN (NEJM 2013)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1213917) | Macitentan reduced morbidity/mortality composite in PAH compared with placebo. | A patient's endothelin antagonist is disease-modifying therapy, not simply an optional vasodilator. |
| [GRIPHON (NEJM 2015)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1503184) | Selexipag reduced a composite of PAH-related complications/death in a broad treated PAH cohort. | Prostacyclin-pathway therapy has outcome evidence but requires specialist continuation planning. |
| [INCREASE (NEJM 2021)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2008470) | Inhaled treprostinil improved 6-min walk distance in PH associated with ILD. | Selected group 3 PH has disease-specific therapy; this does not justify all PAH drugs for all lung-disease PH. |
| [STELLAR (NEJM 2023)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2213558) | Add-on sotatercept improved 6-min walk distance by an estimated 40.8 m vs placebo at 24 weeks and improved secondary endpoints. | Recognise novel activin-signalling treatment and haematological/bleeding adverse effects. |
| [ZENITH (NEJM 2025)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2415160) | In high-risk PAH, add-on sotatercept reduced the trial's composite of death/transplant/worsening PAH hospitalisation; study stopped early for efficacy. | Chronic PAH management is changing; not an acute intraoperative rescue drug. |
| [HYPERION (NEJM 2025)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2508170) | Recently diagnosed PAH receiving combination treatment: clinical worsening occurred in 10.6% on sotatercept vs 36.9% placebo over median 13.2 months (early stop). | Emphasises early chronic specialist optimisation; endpoints are composites, not proof of reduced mortality alone. |
| [TRITON (JACC 2021)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.01.011) | Initial triple oral therapy in PAH did not demonstrate an advantage over dual therapy for the primary PVR endpoint in this trial. | **More medications** do not automatically mean proven benefit; phenotype and trial endpoints matter. |

## D. Resuscitation and the electrical patient

| Study | Result to remember | Final-exam implication |
|---|---|---|
| [DOSE VF (NEJM 2022)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2207304) | Cluster-randomised trial of refractory out-of-hospital VF: vector-change and double sequential defibrillation strategies improved survival to discharge compared with standard strategy, with limitations. | ANZCOR recommends considering **vector change after ≥3 shocks**; double-sequential shocks require training/equipment and are not routine first-line. |
| [PROCAMIO (Eur Heart J 2017)](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehw230) | Small RCT in tolerated wide-QRS tachycardia: procainamide caused fewer serious cardiac adverse events and more termination than amiodarone. | Procainamide is useful in expert centres but may be unavailable locally; urgent cardioversion overrides drug debates if unstable. |
| [ALPS (NEJM 2016)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1514204) | In shock-refractory out-of-hospital VF/pVT, overall discharge survival did not significantly differ with amiodarone, lignocaine or placebo; subgroup findings were exploratory. | Antiarrhythmics are adjuncts after defibrillation/CPR, not substitutes for early shocks. |

**Reading trial evidence safely:**

- Recognise whether an endpoint is mortality, a composite, surrogate haemodynamics, quality of life or rhythm recurrence.
- Do not call a nonsignificant result 'equivalent', generalise device-pocket anticoagulation trials to major surgery, or assume chronic PH therapies are emergency shock drugs.
- Apply findings alongside contemporary guidelines and patient physiology.

items.title: References by subtopic
items.body:
- The references are grouped according to their teaching value.
- **ANZCOR is the primary Australasian acute resuscitation reference** for the dosing and electrical algorithms described above; the 2025 AHA/ERC material is a useful contemporary comparator and some protocols differ.
- For drug preparation, infusion concentration and specific device programming use current local hospital guidance and the manufacturer's instructions.

## A. BJA Education — highest-yield articles for this set

- **1. Haysley J, Soliman-Aboumarie H, Huang J, Kalra DK.** [Perioperative atrial fibrillation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.10.006). BJA Education, 2025;25:99–106. **Read for:** mechanisms and perioperative triggers, risk/complications, practical prevention and postoperative management. Especially relevant to Chapters 2, 3 and 6.
- **2. Murphy E, Shelley B.** [Clinical presentation and management of right ventricular dysfunction](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2019.02.004). BJA Education, 2019;19:183–190. **Read for:** RV pressure–volume physiology, ventricular interdependence, echo clues and the rational haemodynamic treatment of RV failure (Chapters 10–12).
- **3. Bryant HC, Roberts PR, Diprose P.** [Perioperative management of patients with cardiac implantable electronic devices](https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkw020). BJA Education, 2016;16:388–396. **Read for:** fundamental pacing, sensing, generator/lead and EMI concepts. **Update** device-specific magnet actions against the 2024 AHA statement before relying on its older technical details (Chapters 7–9).
- **4. Complementary BJA article:** Price LC et al. [Perioperative management of patients with pulmonary hypertension undergoing non-cardiothoracic, non-obstetric surgery: systematic review and expert consensus](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2021.01.005). British Journal of Anaesthesia, 2021;126:774–790. **Read for:** PH perioperative mortality ranges, preoperative assessment and haemodynamic planning. This is **BJA, not BJA Education**; it is particularly valuable for Chapters 11–12.
## B. Australasian guidance, curriculum and Blue Book

- **1. ANZCOR.** [Guideline 11.9: Managing Acute Dysrhythmias](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias). **Use for:** Australasian algorithms, atropine and adrenaline infusion examples, SVT and VT management, magnesium for torsades, external pacing.
- **2. ANZCOR.** [Guideline 11.4: Electrical Therapy for Adult Advanced Life Support](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-4-electrical-therapy-for-adult-advanced-life-support). 2025 edition. **Use for:** VF/pulseless VT shocks, pad positions, **≥8 cm** from implanted generator and vector-change strategy for refractory VF.
- **3. ANZCA.** [Anaesthesia Training Program Curriculum](https://www.anzca.edu.au/resources/all-handbooks-and-curriculums/anzca-anaesthesia-training-program-curriculum.pdf), Appendix Five — Final Examination learning outcomes. **Use for:** curriculum command words and Set 12's assigned outcomes, interpreted using the master workbook.
- **4. ANZCA.** [Australasian Anaesthesia 2025 (Blue Book)](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29); **Kim JCH, Lau LSY.** [B-lines and beyond: lung ultrasound for the perioperative clinician](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1378). **Use for:** rapid lung ultrasound in the differential of acute hypoxaemia, congestion/oedema and pneumothorax during RV decompensation. This chapter supports the bedside differential, rather than replacing an echo/RHC PH guideline.
- **5. ANZCA.** [Professional documents: PG46 (perioperative echocardiography) and PG47 (perioperative diagnostic POCUS)](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents), 2025. **Use for:** scope, training and governance of perioperative echo/POCUS; not substitute numeric RV/PH cut-offs from ASE/ESC.
- **6. ANZCA Final examiner reports:** Uploaded project reports **2022.2, 2024.2, 2025.2 and 2026.1**, specifically the DDDR pacemaker SAQ, ECG identification (AF, LBBB, Mobitz II), PH in pregnancy, and epicardial pacing/troubleshooting. **Use for:** depth/structure expected and frequently missed management steps. The official reports form the exam-specific audit, not the clinical guideline authority.
## C. Major society guidelines and specialist statements

- **1. AHA.** [2025 Adult Advanced Life Support guideline](https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support). **Use for:** contemporary synchronised cardioversion decisions and energy settings, unstable AF/flutter and rescue bradycardia pacing. Some thresholds differ from ANZCOR; practise local policy.
- **2. ESC.** [2024 Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/45/36/3314/7738779). **Use for:** AF-CARE, CHA₂DS₂-VA, oral anticoagulation, cardioversion safeguards, rate/rhythm decisions and follow-up.
- **3. ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS.** [2023 Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001193). **Use for:** complementary recommendations on AF, cardioversion, thromboprophylaxis and ablation.
- **4. ACC/AHA/HRS.** [2018 Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay guideline](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000628). **Use for:** indications for permanent pacing, Mobitz II/high-grade/complete block and symptomatic sinus-node disease.
- **5. ESC.** [2021 Guideline on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronisation therapy](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/42/35/3427/6358547). **Use for:** pacing modes, permanent pacing selection and CRT indications.
- **6. AHA Scientific Statement.** [Periprocedural management and multidisciplinary pathways for CIEDs](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12068544/). Circulation, 2024. **Use for:** modern leadless/ICD/CRT systems, magnet limitations, pacing dependence, surgical EMI and post-op restoration.
- **7. ACC/AHA.** [2024 Perioperative cardiovascular management guideline](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001285). **Use for:** perioperative CIED strategy and wider cardiovascular evaluation; use current reaffirmation where relevant.
- **8. British Heart Rhythm Society.** [Guidelines for perioperative management of people with cardiac implantable devices](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.15728). Anaesthesia, 2022. **Use for:** UK practical perioperative device planning and documentation.
- **9. ESC/ERS.** [2022 Pulmonary hypertension diagnosis and treatment guidelines](https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.00879-2022). **Use for:** mPAP/PAWP/PVR definitions, five PH groups, specialist assessment and disease-specific PAH treatment.
- **10. ASE.** [2025 Right-heart and pulmonary hypertension echocardiography guideline](https://www.asecho.org/guideline/right-heart-in-adults-pulmonary-hypertension/). **Use for:** current RV systolic/diastolic assessment, pulmonary pressure estimate limitations and integration of multiple echo indices.
- **11. ESC.** [2022 Cardiovascular assessment and management for non-cardiac surgery](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/43/39/3826/6675076). **Use for:** perioperative PAH risk factors, specialist planning and avoiding treatment interruption.
## D. Textbooks and further consolidation

- **1. Miller's Anesthesia:** (latest locally available edition): cardiac electrophysiology, anaesthesia for non-cardiac surgery in patients with cardiovascular disease, pulmonary hypertension and haemodynamic management. **Recommended textbook cross-check**; edition-specific passages were not directly verified in preparing these notes.
- **2. Kaplan's Cardiac Anesthesia:** and standard perioperative echocardiography references: pacing/EP, right heart physiology, temporary epicardial pacing and TOE haemodynamic assessment. **Recommended for advanced viva extension**, particularly post-CPB pacing and RV failure; edition-specific content was not directly verified.
- **3. Yao & Artusio's Anesthesiology: Problem-Oriented Patient Management:** structured case reasoning for conduction disease, devices, congenital heart disease and PH. Useful as practice material rather than a substitute for updated device and resuscitation guidelines.
## Applying these sources to the exam

- For a **clinical-management SAQ**, begin with haemodynamic consequences and urgency before naming drugs; reference ANZCOR for acute rescue steps.
- For a **medical viva**, assess severity, stability and functional reserve before deciding on investigations and optimisation.
- For a **pacemaker question**, specify the actual device and problem (NBG code; rate, output, sensitivity; magnet/EMI; backup).
- For **PH/RV failure**, define the underlying haemodynamics and demonstrate why your choices preserve systemic perfusion, decrease PVR, avoid congestion and restore forward flow.
- This is the common reasoning thread tying the full Set 12 together.
